subtopic_detail: STEMI ECG criteria - posterior MI recognition
stem:
A 58-year-old man presents to a regional emergency department with 90 minutes of crushing central chest pain radiating to the left arm, associated with nausea and diaphoresis. He has a history of hypertension and is an ex-smoker. He took two of his wife's GTN sprays without relief.

He is in distress but mentating well. The 12-lead ECG at arrival shows 1.5 mm ST depression in V1 to V3 with prominent R waves in V2, upright T waves in V1 to V3, and 1 mm ST depression in II, III and aVF. There is no anterior ST elevation. Posterior leads recorded straight away show 1 mm ST elevation in V7, V8 and V9. The nearest primary PCI centre is 3 hours away by road, and aeromedical retrieval is unavailable for at least 2 hours because of weather. He has no contraindications to fibrinolysis.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 92/min, BP 138/86 mmHg, RR 18/min, SpO2 98% on room air, afebrile
data_table.ECG: ST depression 1.5 mm V1 to V3, dominant R in V2, upright T V1 to V3. Posterior leads V7 to V9 show 1 mm ST elevation. Inferior leads show 1 mm depression.
data_table.Investigations: hs-troponin, FBC, UEC, glucose and lipids sent, results pending

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Conservative medical management with aspirin, ticagrelor and enoxaparin only, with serial troponins
Transfer for primary PCI without giving fibrinolysis, accepting the 3 hour road transfer plus catheter-lab activation time, with full anticoagulation en route
Administer fibrinolysis with tenecteplase now, plus aspirin, clopidogrel and enoxaparin, then transfer for pharmaco-invasive PCI within 2 to 24 hours
Treat the changes as non-ST-elevation, give aspirin, ticagrelor and fondaparinux, and refer for angiography within 72 hours
Repeat ECG in 30 minutes and reassess; if persistent changes, then consider fibrinolysis

subtopic_detail: NSTE-ACS - timing of invasive strategy and GRACE risk
stem:
A 72-year-old woman presents to a tertiary metropolitan emergency department with three episodes of central chest pain over the last 12 hours, each lasting around 15 minutes, the last occurring 90 minutes ago at rest while she was reading on her couch. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 8.2%), longstanding hypertension, chronic kidney disease stage 3a (eGFR 52, baseline stable), and was admitted 18 months ago with a non-ST-elevation myocardial infarction managed conservatively at that admission.

Her current medications are aspirin 100 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg, perindopril 5 mg, metformin 1 g twice daily and gliclazide modified-release 60 mg. She is an ex-smoker (quit 8 years ago, 25 pack-years prior) and has a sister with CABG at 64. Vital signs at triage are HR 88 regular, BP 152/84, SpO2 97% on room air, RR 18, afebrile.

She is mildly distressed but well perfused with warm peripheries. Examination is unremarkable apart from a grade 2 soft systolic murmur at the apex without radiation. The 12-lead ECG shows 1 mm horizontal ST depression in V4 to V6 with biphasic T waves in V5 and V6; there is no ST elevation in any territory and no posterior or right-sided changes on additional leads.

Initial high-sensitivity troponin is 78 ng/L (reference <14) drawn at 1 hour after symptom resolution. There is no pulmonary oedema clinically or radiographically and no haemodynamic instability. The cardiology registrar has calculated a GRACE score of 158.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 152/84, SpO2 97% room air, RR 18, afebrile.
data_table.ECG: ST depression 1 mm V4 to V6, biphasic T waves V5 to V6. No ST elevation.
data_table.Investigations: hs-troponin 78 ng/L (<14) at 1 h post-symptoms. eGFR 52. HbA1c 8.2%.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate timing of coronary angiography?

options.text: Within 24 hours of presentation, as part of an early invasive strategy
Within 2 hours of presentation, as part of an immediate invasive strategy
Within 72 hours of presentation, as part of a delayed invasive strategy
Selective invasive strategy guided by non-invasive ischaemia testing after discharge
Defer angiography given CKD stage 3a; manage medically and reassess at 6 weeks

stem:
A 61-year-old man underwent successful primary PCI with a single drug-eluting stent to the proximal LAD 6 weeks ago for anterior STEMI. He has been compliant with aspirin 100 mg daily, ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily, atorvastatin 80 mg, perindopril 5 mg, and metoprolol 50 mg twice daily. He has no atrial fibrillation, no prior stroke, eGFR 78, and no prior bleeding.

He attends cardiology review and asks about antiplatelet duration. Two weeks ago he was diagnosed with a 3 cm right colonic adenocarcinoma on screening colonoscopy and is scheduled for elective laparoscopic right hemicolectomy in 4 weeks. He has had no chest pain since the procedure.

data_table.Procedure: Primary PCI LAD, 1 DES, 6 weeks ago.
data_table.Medications: Aspirin 100 mg, ticagrelor 90 mg BD, atorvastatin 80 mg, perindopril 5 mg, metoprolol 50 mg BD.
data_table.Risk factors: No AF, no prior bleed/stroke, eGFR 78, no upcoming surgery.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate antiplatelet management plan around the upcoming hemicolectomy?

options.text: Continue aspirin perioperatively, stop ticagrelor 5 days before surgery, and restart ticagrelor as soon as surgical haemostasis allows (typically 24 to 72 hours postoperatively)
Stop both aspirin and ticagrelor 5 days before surgery and resume both after discharge
Continue both aspirin and ticagrelor throughout the perioperative period without interruption
Bridge ticagrelor with prophylactic low molecular weight heparin from 5 days pre-op until restart of ticagrelor
Proceed with surgery now without changing antiplatelet therapy because the stent was placed more than a month ago

stem:
An 82-year-old woman attends her general practice for review of newly diagnosed non-valvular atrial fibrillation found on a 24 hour Holter for palpitations. Her history includes essential hypertension on perindopril-indapamide, ischaemic stroke 3 years ago with full recovery, and no diabetes or heart failure. She weighs 56 kg. Current medications: perindopril-indapamide 5/1.25 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg, paracetamol as required.

BP 132/80, HR 78 irregularly irregular. Bloods today: creatinine 138 micromol/L, eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m^2, HCO3 24. She has no prior bleeding and her HAS-BLED score is 2. She prefers an oral medication strategy without routine INR monitoring.

data_table.Risk factors: Age 67, female, HTN treated, prior TIA, no DM, no HF, no vascular disease.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril/indapamide 5/1.25 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, paracetamol PRN.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate stroke-prevention prescription?

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily as standard non-valvular AF dose
Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily based on age, weight, and creatinine criteria
Warfarin titrated to INR 2.0 to 3.0 with point-of-care monitoring
Rivaroxaban 20 mg once daily with the main meal of the day
Aspirin 100 mg daily as sole long-term antithrombotic therapy

subtopic_detail: Rate vs rhythm control in AF with heart failure
stem:
A 58-year-old man with HFrEF (LVEF 32% on TTE 4 weeks ago) and persistent atrial fibrillation diagnosed 7 months ago is reviewed in the dedicated heart failure clinic of a metropolitan tertiary hospital. He is on sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily, bisoprolol 7.5 mg daily, spironolactone 25 mg daily, dapagliflozin 10 mg daily and apixaban 5 mg twice daily, all at maximum tolerated doses with documented adherence on pharmacy refill records.

Despite these guideline-directed therapies, he reports NYHA class III symptoms with breathlessness when flat-walking 50 metres on level ground and orthopnoea requiring two pillows at night, with one episode of paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnoea in the past week. Resting heart rate is 78 in AF on the clinic ECG; 6 minute walk test today is 280 metres (down from 360 m at his last review 3 months ago).

He had one direct current cardioversion 4 months ago, which restored sinus rhythm initially with relapse to AF within 6 weeks despite continuation of beta-blocker therapy. He has no significant comorbidities (no diabetes, no CKD, no prior stroke) and lives 30 minutes from a metropolitan electrophysiology centre with established AF ablation program. Symptoms have not improved despite optimal heart failure medical therapy for 3 months and adequate rate control.

data_table.Echo: LVEF 32%, mild LA dilatation, no significant valve disease.
data_table.Medications: Sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 BD, bisoprolol 7.5 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, dapagliflozin 10 mg, apixaban 5 mg BD.
data_table.Functional: NYHA III, 6MWT 280 m, resting HR 78 in AF, BP 118/72.
data_table.Procedural history: DCCV 4 months ago, AF relapse at 6 weeks.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step to improve symptoms and outcomes?

options.text: Increase bisoprolol to 10 mg daily for tighter rate control and continue current management
Add amiodarone 200 mg daily after loading, for pharmacological rhythm control
Repeat DCCV and load amiodarone for maintenance
AV node ablation with biventricular pacing
Refer for catheter ablation of atrial fibrillation as the rhythm-control strategy of choice in his HFrEF

stem:
A 79-year-old man with persistent non-valvular atrial fibrillation diagnosed 4 years ago has worsening chronic kidney disease with a current eGFR of 22 mL/min/1.73m2 (CKD-EPI), serum creatinine 218 micromol/L, and stable weight of 64 kg (BMI 22.4). His comorbidities include hypertension on perindopril, type 2 diabetes mellitus on basal insulin (HbA1c 7.1%), and a prior ischaemic stroke 2 years ago with mild residual right hemiparesis but functional independence.

His calculated CHA2DS2-VASc score is 6 (age >=75 = 2, HTN = 1, DM = 1, prior CVA = 2) and HAS-BLED score is 3 (age >65, HTN, abnormal renal function). He has been on rivaroxaban 20 mg daily for 3 years, but his renal function has progressively declined over the past 6 months from an eGFR of 38 to the current 22.

He is not yet on dialysis and his treating nephrologist estimates he is 12 to 18 months from requiring renal replacement therapy. He has no mechanical heart valve and no moderate-to-severe mitral stenosis on his last echocardiogram. He has had one prior epistaxis requiring nasal packing 18 months ago but no other bleeding.

data_table.Other: No mechanical valve, no significant MS, no active malignancy.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate anticoagulation strategy?

options.text: Continue rivaroxaban 20 mg daily
Switch to apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily with periodic renal function monitoring
Switch to dabigatran 110 mg twice daily
Switch to warfarin with INR target 2.0 to 3.0
Stop all anticoagulation and refer for left atrial appendage occlusion

subtopic_detail: HFrEF - four pillars guideline-directed medical therapy
stem:
A 62-year-old man with newly diagnosed HFrEF (LVEF 28% on transthoracic echocardiogram performed during admission) presents to the heart failure clinic at a metropolitan tertiary centre 2 weeks after discharge from his index admission with acute pulmonary oedema. The admission echocardiogram showed global hypokinesis without focal wall motion abnormality, mild left atrial dilatation and no significant valvular disease. Cardiac MRI during admission excluded an infiltrative cardiomyopathy and showed no late gadolinium enhancement suggestive of myocarditis.

Coronary angiography demonstrated non-obstructive coronary artery disease. He is in sinus rhythm. Current medications post-discharge are ramipril 5 mg daily, bisoprolol 5 mg daily, and furosemide 40 mg daily. He has type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 7.4%, on metformin 1 g twice daily), no atrial fibrillation, no significant valve disease, eGFR 64, potassium 4.2 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, BP 122/76 supine and 118/74 standing, HR 64 sinus rhythm, and NYHA class II symptoms when walking up two flights of stairs.

He has no history of angio-oedema, no symptomatic hypotension or dizziness, and no recent gout flare. His weight is 88 kg (down 4 kg since admission with diuresis) and he is keen to optimise medical therapy following written education from the heart failure nurse practitioner.

data_table.Echo: LVEF 28%, no significant valve disease, mild LA dilatation.
data_table.Bloods: eGFR 64, K 4.2 mmol/L, HbA1c 7.4%, Hb 138.
data_table.Vitals: BP 122/76, HR 64 sinus rhythm, NYHA II.
data_table.Current Rx: Ramipril 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, furosemide 40 mg, metformin.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next addition or modification to his heart failure regimen?

options.text: Switch ramipril to sacubitril/valsartan and add spironolactone 12.5-25 mg daily and dapagliflozin 10 mg daily over subsequent visits
Add digoxin 125 micrograms daily for symptom relief without optimising disease-modifying therapy with ARNI, MRA and SGLT2i first
Add ivabradine 5 mg twice daily as a heart-rate-lowering addition to current beta-blocker therapy, with electrocardiogram review at four weeks
Increase furosemide to 80 mg daily and add metolazone 2.5 mg as required for fluid control rather than disease modification today
Refer for cardiac resynchronisation therapy with defibrillator (CRT-D) without further uptitration of guideline-directed medical therapy

subtopic_detail: HFpEF - SGLT2 inhibitor as first-line disease-modifying therapy
stem:
A 73-year-old woman presents to a community cardiology clinic with progressive exertional dyspnoea over 6 months, now limiting her ability to walk to her letterbox without stopping. She has longstanding essential hypertension, type 2 diabetes mellitus (HbA1c 7.6%, on metformin 1 g twice daily and gliclazide modified-release 60 mg daily), obesity (BMI 34, weight 92 kg), and moderate obstructive sleep apnoea well-controlled on nightly CPAP at 9 cmH2O with good compliance documented.

She had a hospital admission 3 months ago for fluid overload requiring intravenous diuresis and was discharged on oral furosemide as needed. Her examination today shows BP 138/82, HR 76 sinus, JVP not elevated, mild bibasal end-inspiratory crackles, and no peripheral oedema. Transthoracic echocardiogram performed last week shows preserved LVEF 58%, grade II diastolic dysfunction, left atrial volume index 38 mL/m2 (dilated), septal e' velocity 6 cm/s, E/e' ratio of 14, and no significant valvular disease.

NT-proBNP is 612 pg/mL (elevated for her age and BMI, after BMI correction). Her current medications are perindopril 10 mg daily, indapamide 2.5 mg, metformin 1 g BD, gliclazide MR 60 mg, and atorvastatin 40 mg. Renal function: eGFR 58, K 4.3 mmol/L, creatinine 92 micromol/L. There is no history of gout, recurrent urinary infection, or genital fungal infection. She is keen on therapies that will reduce hospitalisation and would prefer to avoid additional injectable medications.

data_table.Echo: LVEF 58%, grade II diastolic dysfunction, LAVI 38, E/e' 14.
data_table.Bloods: NT-proBNP 612 pg/mL, eGFR 58, K 4.3, HbA1c 7.6%.
data_table.Current Rx: Perindopril 10, indapamide 2.5, metformin, gliclazide MR, atorvastatin.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate addition to her management for heart failure outcomes?

options.text: Add sacubitril/valsartan 49/51 mg twice daily
Add spironolactone 25 mg daily
Add bisoprolol 2.5 mg daily
Add empagliflozin 10 mg daily as first-line disease-modifying therapy for HFpEF
Increase furosemide as required and emphasise weight loss and CPAP adherence only

subtopic_detail: Acute pulmonary oedema - early NIV and IV nitrate
stem:
A 78-year-old woman with known HFrEF (LVEF 30% on her most recent echocardiogram 4 months ago) and a background of long-standing hypertension, permanent atrial fibrillation rate-controlled on bisoprolol and apixaban, and chronic kidney disease stage 3a (baseline eGFR 48) is brought to a busy metropolitan emergency department by paramedic ambulance with severe dyspnoea. She has been progressively breathless over the previous 24 hours after dietary indiscretion at a family birthday and woke with acute orthopnoea 2 hours ago.

On arrival to the resuscitation bay she is sitting upright bolt-upright, gasping, with marked accessory muscle use, tracheal tug, and visible pink frothy sputum at the lips. Vital signs at triage: HR 132 in atrial fibrillation, BP 192/108, RR 36, SpO2 86% on 15 L non-rebreather mask, afebrile at 36.6 degrees Celsius. Examination shows JVP elevated to the angle of the jaw, widespread bilateral fine inspiratory crackles to the mid-zones, gallop rhythm with audible S3, and cool peripheries with capillary refill of 3 seconds.

ECG shows atrial fibrillation with ventricular rate 130 to 140 and no acute ischaemic changes. Chest x-ray shows bilateral alveolar infiltrates with Kerley B lines and bilateral pleural effusions. Initial high-sensitivity troponin is 38 ng/L (<14), creatinine 142 micromol/L (up from baseline 110), potassium 4.6, lactate 2.4 mmol/L. She has a current Resuscitation Plan documenting a wish for full active treatment short of invasive intubation if it can be avoided.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132 AF, BP 192/108, RR 36, SpO2 86% on NRB 15 L, afebrile.
data_table.Examination: Sitting upright, pink frothy sputum, JVP to jaw, widespread crackles, gallop, cool peripheries CRT 3 s.
data_table.ECG: AF rate 130 to 140, no ST changes.
data_table.Investigations: hs-troponin 38 ng/L, Cr 142, K 4.6, lactate 2.4. CXR: bilateral alveolar oedema, Kerley B.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management combination?

options.text: IV furosemide 80 mg bolus, IV morphine 5 mg for anxiolysis and venodilation, with low-flow oxygen at 4 L via nasal prongs
Intubate immediately for invasive mechanical ventilation
IV digoxin 500 micrograms loading and IV metoprolol 5 mg for rate control
Commence IV nesiritide and IV dobutamine infusion
Commence BiPAP (e.g., IPAP 12 to 14, EPAP 6 to 8 cmH2O), IV GTN infusion titrated to BP, and IV furosemide 40 mg bolus

subtopic_detail: Cardiac vs vasovagal syncope - high-risk features
stem:
A 72-year-old man with hypertension and a 30 pack-year smoking history presents to ED after collapsing without warning while shopping. Bystanders report he became briefly stiff with a few arm jerks; he was unresponsive for around 30 seconds and recovered immediately on the floor with no confusion. He had two similar episodes in the past 2 months, one while sitting watching television.

Examination: BP 142/82 lying, 140/82 standing, HR 60 sinus, no postural drop, normal cardiovascular and neurological exam. ECG: sinus rhythm 58, PR 220 ms, QRS 110 ms, RBBB plus left anterior fascicular block. Bloods within reference. He drives a private car daily for his work as a courier.

data_table.ECG: Sinus 58, PR 220 ms, QRS 110 ms, RBBB + LAFB (bifascicular block).
data_table.Investigations: FBC, UEC, glucose, hs-troponin, TSH all within reference.

lead_in: Which combination is most appropriate as his next steps?

options.text: Admit for telemetry and TTE, advise him not to drive a private vehicle until cause is identified and treated, and notify him of his obligation to inform the licensing authority
Admit for telemetry and TTE but allow private driving once telemetry is normal for 48 hours
Discharge with reassurance, advise hydration and counterpressure manoeuvres for vasovagal syncope, and continue driving
Arrange outpatient CT brain and EEG for suspected new-onset seizure disorder and advise no driving for 6 months under epilepsy rules
Discharge home for outpatient 24-hour Holter and tilt-table testing within 4 weeks; continue driving in the interim

subtopic_detail: Brugada syndrome - type 1 ECG with syncope
stem:
A 34-year-old male software engineer of South-East Asian background is brought to a tertiary hospital emergency department after a single witnessed episode of syncope at 0300 hours while sleeping next to his wife. His wife reports that he became briefly stiff for around 10 seconds with gasping agonal-type respirations and then recovered spontaneously over 1 minute with no confusion or post-event lethargy.

He drinks approximately 4 standard drinks twice weekly, takes no regular medications, and has had a non-specific febrile illness over the previous 48 hours with paracetamol use for symptomatic relief of myalgia. He has had no previous episodes of syncope, pre-syncope, or palpitations. Family history is notable: a paternal first cousin died suddenly at age 28 during sleep with no clear cause identified at coronial autopsy; his father is well at age 62 with no cardiac history.

Examination today is unremarkable; he is fully oriented with no neurological deficit. BP 124/72, HR 64 sinus, RR 14, T 37.8 degrees Celsius (febrile), SpO2 99% room air. The 12-lead ECG demonstrates a coved-type ST elevation of 2.5 mm in V1 and V2 with negative T waves and a J point >=2 mm, type 1 pattern present in two right precordial leads, persisting on repeat ECG with leads in standard and high (second intercostal space) positions.

The QTc interval is 410 ms (normal). Cardiac troponin, electrolytes, magnesium and TSH are all within reference range. Echocardiogram is structurally normal with no regional wall motion abnormality. Urine toxicology screen is negative. There is no history of cocaine, tricyclic antidepressant, or sodium channel blocker exposure.

data_table.ECG: Type 1 Brugada pattern: coved ST elevation >=2 mm with negative T in V1 and V2. QTc 410 ms.
data_table.Family Hx: Paternal cousin sudden death age 28 during sleep.
data_table.Investigations: Troponin, electrolytes, Mg, TSH normal. Echo structurally normal. Tox screen negative.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate definitive management?

options.text: Reassure, advise paracetamol for fever, and arrange outpatient cardiology review in 6 weeks
Refer for implantable cardioverter-defibrillator (ICD) implantation under the symptomatic Brugada syndrome Class I indication
Commence flecainide 100 mg twice daily for arrhythmia suppression
Commence amiodarone 200 mg daily for arrhythmia suppression
Arrange genetic testing for SCN5A and other Brugada-associated variants, and await the result before deciding on further definitive management

stem:
A 46-year-old woman is referred to a metropolitan hypertension clinic with progressively worsening hypertension that has resisted intensification over 18 months. Her home blood pressure log, taken with a validated upper-arm device twice daily, averages 162/96 mmHg despite perindopril 10 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, and indapamide 2.5 mg taken daily with documented adherence on pharmacy refill records over the past 12 months.

She has no obstructive sleep apnoea symptoms (no snoring, no witnessed apnoeas, Epworth 4), no flushing or palpitations, no abdominal bruit on examination, and no family history of phaeochromocytoma, paraganglioma or thyroid medullary carcinoma. She has had intermittent hypokalaemia (lowest documented potassium 3.1 mmol/L) attributed by her referring GP to indapamide. Her most recent UEC shows: Na 142, K 3.4, Cl 102, HCO3 28 mmol/L, urea 5.6, creatinine 72 micromol/L, eGFR 89.

Fasting glucose 5.4 mmol/L, HbA1c 5.7%. TSH and free T4 within reference range. Urinary catecholamine and metanephrine screen normal on two separate 24-hour collections. Renal artery Doppler ultrasonography shows no evidence of renal artery stenosis bilaterally. ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy by voltage criteria (Sokolow-Lyon positive). She is keen to investigate a potentially reversible secondary cause given her young age and target-organ damage on ECG.

data_table.BP: Home average 162/96 on perindopril 10, amlodipine 10, indapamide 2.5.
data_table.Bloods: Na 142, K 3.4 (low end), HCO3 28, Cr 72, eGFR 89, HbA1c 5.7%, TSH normal.
data_table.Other workup: Urinary catecholamines normal, renal Doppler no RAS, ECG LVH.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: 24-hour urinary metanephrines (repeat)
MR angiography of renal arteries
Overnight 1 mg dexamethasone suppression test
Plasma aldosterone-to-renin ratio after appropriate medication adjustment
Add spironolactone 25 mg empirically and reassess BP at 12 weeks

subtopic_detail: NHFA hypertension - lifestyle as first-line for grade 1 low-risk
stem:
A 38-year-old man presents to his GP for a workplace medical. He is asymptomatic, exercises twice a week, drinks 8 standard drinks weekly, has BMI 28, does not smoke, has no diabetes, and no family history of premature CVD. Three separate clinic BP readings over 6 weeks average 156/96, and home BP averaged over 7 days is 152/94. Bloods: total cholesterol 4.6, LDL 2.8, HDL 1.4, triglycerides 1.2, fasting glucose 5.1, eGFR over 90, normal urea/electrolytes and urine ACR.

ECG normal. His Australian absolute 5-year CV risk (NVDPA calculator) is 4 percent. He has tried 12 weeks of structured lifestyle change with his GP including reduced salt, DASH-style diet, alcohol reduction to 8 standard drinks per week, and increased exercise; BP today remains 154/94.

data_table.Bloods: Chol 4.6, LDL 2.8, HDL 1.4, TG 1.2, FBG 5.1, eGFR >90, ACR normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence perindopril 5 mg daily and continue ongoing lifestyle measures, with home BP review at 6 weeks
Continue lifestyle modification for another 6 months before considering pharmacotherapy
Refer for 24-hour ambulatory BP monitoring to exclude white-coat hypertension before any pharmacotherapy
Commence atorvastatin 20 mg daily for global CV risk reduction in addition to lifestyle
Investigate for secondary hypertension with plasma aldosterone-renin ratio, renal artery imaging and 24-hour urinary metanephrines today

subtopic_detail: Complete heart block with haemodynamic compromise - immediate management
stem:
A 74-year-old man is brought to a metropolitan emergency department by paramedic ambulance after a witnessed syncopal episode at home. His wife reports that he stood from his armchair, became pale, and collapsed without warning, hitting his head lightly on the carpeted floor; he was unresponsive for approximately 90 seconds before recovering some awareness. On arrival to the resuscitation bay he is confused (GCS 13: E4 V3 M6), cool peripherally, pale and diaphoretic.

Vital signs at triage: HR 28, BP 76/40, RR 22, SpO2 95% on room air, temperature 36.8 degrees Celsius, blood glucose 7.8 mmol/L on point-of-care testing. Capillary refill is prolonged at 4 seconds. The 12-lead ECG demonstrates complete atrioventricular dissociation with an atrial rate of 84 and a ventricular escape rhythm of 28 with broad QRS complexes (160 ms) and a left bundle branch block morphology consistent with an infra-nodal escape.

There are no acute ischaemic ST changes and no Q waves. He has no known cardiac history. His regular medications are amlodipine 10 mg daily and metformin 1 g twice daily. He has had no recent illness, no diarrhoea(no recent prescription changes, no access to other medications), and no environmental exposures. Initial bloods drawn at arrival: troponin pending, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, glucose 7.8, urea and creatinine within normal limits, calcium and magnesium normal.

data_table.Vitals: HR 28, BP 76/40, RR 22, SpO2 95% room air, GCS 13.
data_table.Examination: Cool peripherally, CRT 4 s, pale, diaphoretic, confused.
data_table.ECG: Complete AV dissociation. Atrial rate 84, ventricular escape rate 28, broad QRS 160 ms (LBBB morphology). No acute ischaemic changes.
data_table.Bloods: K 4.4, glucose 7.8, troponin pending.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate intervention while awaiting cardiology?

options.text: IV adrenaline 1 mg bolus stat and prepare for immediate rapid sequence intubation as the airway intervention takes priority over rate restoration
Atropine 600 micrograms IV, repeated every 3 to 5 minutes to a maximum cumulative dose of 3 mg, as the sole pharmacological strategy while awaiting cardiology review
Commence transcutaneous pacing with analgesia/sedation, set rate 70 to 80, increase output until electrical and mechanical capture confirmed, while arranging emergent transvenous pacing
1 L 0.9% saline bolus over 15 minutes to optimise preload and reassess perfusion and conscious state before considering rate-restoring measures
IV calcium gluconate 10 mL of 10% solution given over 10 minutes empirically while awaiting biochemistry, with repeat ECG at 5 minutes

stem:
A 58-year-old man presents to a rural hospital ED with 90 minutes of crushing central chest pain radiating to the left jaw, associated with diaphoresis and nausea. He has a 30 pack-year smoking history, dyslipidaemia on atorvastatin 40 mg, and untreated hypertension. He took two GTN sprays at home with minimal relief. He has no prior bleeding history, no recent surgery, and is not on anticoagulation.

Initial ECG shows 3 mm ST elevation in V1 to V4 with reciprocal inferior ST depression. The nearest PCI-capable centre is 180 minutes away by road, and the local rural transfer team estimates first-medical-contact-to-balloon time of 200 minutes if transferred immediately. The local ED can administer fibrinolysis within 20 minutes. Troponin I has been sent; bedside echocardiogram shows anteroseptal hypokinesis.

The team specifically asks whether transfer for primary PCI is still preferred even with predicted door-to-balloon exceeding 120 minutes, whether to delay reperfusion pending troponin confirmation, whether IV unfractionated heparin alone with next-day angiography would be safe, and whether conservative anti-ischaemic therapy with high-dose nitrates and beta-blockade is acceptable given only minor reciprocal changes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 148/92 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, RR 20, SpO2 95% RA, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Diaphoretic, GCS 15, chest clear, S4 gallop, no murmur, calves soft.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: 3 mm ST elevation V1 to V4 with reciprocal inferior ST depression. CXR clear.
data_table.Medications: Atorvastatin 40 mg nocte. GTN spray PRN.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Transfer immediately for primary PCI even though first-medical-contact-to-balloon time will exceed 120 minutes
Administer fibrinolysis with tenecteplase now and arrange transfer for angiography within 3 to 24 hours
Withhold reperfusion and load with ticagrelor and aspirin while awaiting troponin result
Give intravenous unfractionated heparin alone and transfer for elective angiography next day
Treat conservatively with high-dose nitrates and beta-blockade given the small reciprocal change

subtopic_detail: Acute coronary syndrome - reperfusion choice and timing in STEMI

stem:
A 64-year-old woman presents with 4 hours of intermittent retrosternal chest tightness, worse on exertion, partially relieved by rest. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin, hypertension on perindopril, and is a current smoker. She has had two similar episodes in the past week. On arrival she is pain-free. Her ECG is in sinus rhythm with non-specific T-wave flattening in the lateral leads, no ST elevation or depression, no Q-waves, and is unchanged from a tracing 6 months ago.

Initial high-sensitivity cardiac troponin I (hs-cTnI) drawn 4 hours after pain onset is 14 ng/L (99th percentile cut-off 16 ng/L; algorithm low-rule-out less than 5, rule-in greater than 52). A 1-hour repeat is 18 ng/L (absolute change 4 ng/L; algorithm rule-in delta greater than 6). Her renal function is normal, and she has no prior cardiac history or stress test.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA, T 36.5 degC.
data_table.Examination: Pain-free, chest clear, heart sounds dual no murmur, calves soft.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: SR, non-specific lateral T-wave flattening, unchanged from 6 months ago. hs-cTnI 0h 14 ng/L, 1h 18 ng/L (delta 4). Creatinine 72 micromol/L, Hb 132 g/L, eGFR greater than 90.
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD, perindopril 5 mg daily.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with GP follow-up within 48 hours because the 0/1 hour algorithm rules her out given the trivial 1-hour delta
Admit and proceed to inpatient invasive coronary angiography within 24 hours with adjunctive dual antiplatelet loading and fondaparinux
Repeat troponin at 3 hours from presentation and admit to a cardiac observation unit pending the result and further risk stratification
Commence fibrinolysis with weight-adjusted tenecteplase given high cardiovascular risk profile and the early presentation to a non-PCI capable facility today
Refer for outpatient exercise stress echocardiogram in 2 weeks and discharge home tonight with safety-netting and short-term GTN spray as required

stem:
A 67-year-old man presents with 2 hours of severe central chest pain radiating to the back, associated with diaphoresis and nausea. He has a history of hypertension on amlodipine and a 40 pack-year smoking history. He has no prior cardiac history. On arrival he is in pain, clammy and pale. The 12-lead ECG shows horizontal ST depression of 2 mm in V1, V2 and V3 with prominent upright R-waves in V1 and V2 (R/S greater than 1), tall upright T waves in V1 to V3, and no ST elevation or depression in any other lead.

There is no Q-wave. A posterior 15-lead ECG with leads V7, V8 and V9 placed below the left scapula shows 1 mm ST elevation in V8 and V9. Troponin I is pending. Bedside echocardiogram shows inferolateral wall hypokinesis. The ED registrar asks whether to manage as NSTEMI with conservative pathway and 24-hour angiography, whether the ECG could represent Wellens syndrome, right bundle branch block, or digoxin effect, and whether emergency cath lab activation is justified for a STEMI equivalent in the absence of overt ST elevation on the standard 12-lead.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/64 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 96% RA, T 36.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: Pale, diaphoretic, JVP not elevated, chest clear, dual heart sounds no murmur.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: 2 mm horizontal ST depression V1 to V3, dominant R in V1/V2, upright T waves. Posterior leads V8, V9: 1 mm ST elevation.
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine 10 mg daily.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Manage as NSTEMI with conservative pathway and angiography within 24 hours
Activate the cath lab for emergency primary PCI as a STEMI equivalent
Treat as Wellens syndrome with urgent outpatient cardiology referral
Diagnose right bundle branch block and arrange echocardiogram in the morning
Diagnose digoxin effect and check digoxin level urgently

subtopic_detail: Posterior STEMI - ECG recognition with isolated ST depression in V1 to V3

stem:
A 62-year-old woman undergoes successful primary PCI with a single drug-eluting stent to the proximal LAD for an anterior STEMI. She has hypertension on perindopril, dyslipidaemia, no diabetes, and no prior bleeding. Pre-procedure haemoglobin was 138 g/L and platelets 240 x 10^9/L. She was loaded with aspirin 300 mg and ticagrelor 180 mg in the ED. Post-procedurally she is haemodynamically stable, has no ongoing chest pain, and an echocardiogram shows an LVEF of 42 percent with anteroseptal hypokinesis.

She has no history of stroke, intracranial haemorrhage, peptic ulcer disease, or anticoagulant use. The cardiology team plans discharge on day 3. She has private cover and no PBS concerns about device or drug choice.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/76 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, RR 14, SpO2 98% RA.
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, dual heart sounds, no signs of heart failure.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 132 g/L, platelets 232 x 10^9/L, creatinine 76 micromol/L, LVEF 42 percent.
data_table.Medications: Loaded with aspirin 300 mg and ticagrelor 180 mg; ramipril 5 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg, bisoprolol 2.5 mg started inpatient.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate ongoing antiplatelet regimen?

options.text: Aspirin 100 mg daily plus ticagrelor 90 mg twice daily for 12 months, then aspirin alone indefinitely
Aspirin 100 mg daily plus clopidogrel 75 mg daily for 12 months, then aspirin alone
Aspirin 100 mg daily alone, with clopidogrel added only if recurrent ischaemia occurs
Aspirin 100 mg daily plus prasugrel 10 mg daily for 6 months, then aspirin alone
Aspirin 100 mg daily plus apixaban 5 mg twice daily for 12 months

subtopic_detail: ACS - DAPT choice and duration post-PCI

stem:
A 74-year-old man with known HFrEF (LVEF 32 percent) presents to the ED with 2 days of progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and 3 kg weight gain. He admits to non-adherence with his furosemide for 1 week. He has a background of ischaemic cardiomyopathy, hypertension, and CKD stage 3 (baseline creatinine 140 micromol/L). On arrival he is sitting upright, working hard to breathe, and unable to complete sentences.

He has bibasal crackles to the mid-zones and elevated JVP. He has no chest pain and his ECG shows old anterior Q-waves without acute ischaemic changes. His usual medications are furosemide 40 mg BD, perindopril 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, and dapagliflozin 10 mg. The team specifically asks whether IV fluid bolus and IV metoprolol for the tachycardia would help, whether IV morphine with high-flow nasal cannula at 60 L/min is appropriate, whether to withhold his ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker indefinitely while starting dobutamine, and whether oral diuretics would suffice.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 162/94 mmHg, HR 108 bpm, RR 32, SpO2 88% RA improving to 94% on 6 L Hudson, T 36.5 degC.
data_table.Examination: Sitting upright, accessory muscle use, bibasal crackles to mid-zones, JVP 8 cm, peripheral oedema to mid-shins.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: SR with old anterior Q-waves. Troponin I 28 ng/L (cut-off less than 16). NT-proBNP 4200 ng/L. Creatinine 175 micromol/L, potassium 4.2 mmol/L.
data_table.Medications: Furosemide 40 mg BD, perindopril 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, dapagliflozin 10 mg.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: IV furosemide 80 mg bolus, GTN infusion, and non-invasive ventilation with CPAP
IV fluid bolus 500 mL Hartmann's and IV metoprolol 5 mg for the tachycardia
IV morphine 5 mg with high-flow nasal cannula oxygen at 60 L/min and observation
Withhold his ACE inhibitor and beta-blocker indefinitely and start a dobutamine infusion
Oral furosemide 80 mg, oral metolazone 5 mg, and admit to a monitored bed

subtopic_detail: Acute decompensated heart failure - initial management priorities

stem:
A 66-year-old woman with HFrEF (LVEF 28 percent, ischaemic aetiology) attends the heart failure clinic. She is NYHA class II to III with mild exertional dyspnoea climbing one flight. She has type 2 diabetes (HbA1c 7.2 percent), hypertension, and CKD stage 3a (eGFR 52, baseline). She has been on stable doses for 3 months of perindopril 8 mg daily, bisoprolol 7.5 mg daily, furosemide 40 mg daily, and atorvastatin 80 mg.

Her BP is 118/72 mmHg, HR 64 bpm, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, creatinine 118 micromol/L. She has no symptomatic hypotension. She is keen to optimise prognosis-modifying therapy and has private cover for medication cost. She specifically asks whether to add digoxin for prognosis, whether to increase her furosemide and add amlodipine for blood pressure, whether to refer for cardiac resynchronisation now, or whether to switch to candesartan with ivabradine instead of the ARNI and MRA approach. She has private cover and PBS access to all four pillars.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 64 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA.
data_table.Examination: JVP not elevated, chest clear, dual heart sounds with soft S3, trace ankle oedema.
data_table.Investigations: LVEF 28 percent. eGFR 52, potassium 4.4 mmol/L, sodium 138 mmol/L, HbA1c 7.2 percent, NT-proBNP 980 ng/L.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 8 mg, bisoprolol 7.5 mg, furosemide 40 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step to optimise prognosis?

options.text: Add spironolactone 25 mg daily and dapagliflozin 10 mg daily, and plan switch of perindopril to sacubitril/valsartan after a 36-hour washout
Add digoxin 125 micrograms daily as the next prognostic agent, continuing perindopril and bisoprolol at their current doses
Increase furosemide to 80 mg daily and add amlodipine 5 mg daily for tighter blood pressure control without adding any additional prognosis-modifying agent
Refer for cardiac resynchronisation therapy now, given the persistent NYHA class II to III symptoms on her current triple-therapy regimen
Switch perindopril to candesartan 8 mg daily and add ivabradine 5 mg twice daily for additional symptomatic and prognostic benefit in HFrEF management

subtopic_detail: Chronic HFrEF - guideline-directed medical therapy escalation

stem:
A 68-year-old woman is referred for symptomatic palpitations and exertional dyspnoea over the past 3 weeks. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of 118 bpm at rest. She has hypertension on perindopril, no diabetes, no prior stroke, and no heart failure. Her LVEF on echo done last week is 58 percent with a mildly dilated left atrium (44 mm) and no significant valvular disease.

She is otherwise active and reports the palpitations are interfering with her hiking. Her current symptom burden is EHRA class IIb. Her TSH and electrolytes are normal. She specifically asks whether rate control alone is acceptable, whether early electrical cardioversion is preferred, whether anticoagulation alone is sufficient pending spontaneous reversion, whether digoxin monotherapy without anticoagulation would be appropriate given her age, or whether amiodarone loading without anticoagulation is reasonable in someone with such low overall stroke risk.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 118 bpm irregular, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, dual heart sounds no murmur, chest clear, no peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: AF with rate 118. Echo: LVEF 58 percent, LA 44 mm. TSH 2.1 mIU/L, K 4.0 mmol/L.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management strategy for her atrial fibrillation?

options.text: Rate control only with bisoprolol, with rhythm control reserved for two or more recurrences after rate-control optimisation
Commence apixaban and a rate-controlling beta-blocker, then refer for early electrical cardioversion with consideration of catheter ablation
Anticoagulation alone with apixaban; AF often spontaneously reverts without further intervention
Digoxin monotherapy for rate control without anticoagulation as her CHA2DS2-VA score is 1
Amiodarone loading orally for 4 weeks followed by maintenance, with no anticoagulation given low stroke risk

subtopic_detail: Atrial fibrillation - rate vs rhythm control strategy

stem: A 76-year-old woman with newly diagnosed persistent non-valvular atrial fibrillation attends a cardiology clinic. She has type 2 diabetes on metformin, hypertension on amlodipine, and a transient ischaemic attack 3 years ago with full recovery. She has CKD stage 3b with creatinine 138 micromol/L, eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73 m2, and weighs 58 kg. Her haemoglobin is 122 g/L, platelets 230 x 10^9/L, and she has no history of GI bleeding or peptic ulcer.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 82 bpm irregular, RR 14.
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, chest clear, no neurological deficit, no peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 138 micromol/L, eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73 m2, weight 58 kg, Hb 122 g/L, platelets 230 x 10^9/L, ALT/AST normal.
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD, amlodipine 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate anticoagulation?

options.text: Apixaban 2.5 mg twice daily indefinitely
Apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely
Dabigatran 150 mg twice daily indefinitely
Warfarin titrated to INR 2.0 to 3.0 indefinitely
Aspirin 100 mg daily plus clopidogrel 75 mg daily

subtopic_detail: Atrial fibrillation - CHA2DS2-VA scoring and DOAC selection

stem:
A 28-year-old woman presents with sudden palpitations for 50 minutes. She has had similar self-terminating episodes since her teens. She is haemodynamically stable. Her past history includes moderate persistent asthma managed with budesonide-formoterol; she had a hospital admission with status asthmaticus 3 years ago and reports wheeze with viral illnesses. She takes the combined oral contraceptive pill and drinks 2 to 3 coffees daily.

On arrival she is anxious but well perfused. ECG shows a regular narrow-complex tachycardia at 184 bpm with no clearly visible P waves and a normal QRS axis. A modified Valsalva manoeuvre with leg elevation has been attempted twice without success.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 184 bpm regular, RR 18, SpO2 99% RA.
data_table.Examination: Warm well-perfused peripheries, GCS 15, chest clear, no signs of heart failure.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: narrow-complex regular tachycardia 184 bpm, no clear P waves, normal axis. K 4.2 mmol/L, TSH normal.
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: IV adenosine 6 mg rapid push followed by 20 mL saline flush with continuous ECG recording
IV verapamil 5 mg slowly over 2 minutes with continuous ECG and blood pressure monitoring
Synchronised DC cardioversion at 50 joules under procedural sedation with continuous monitoring
Oral metoprolol 25 mg with discharge home and cardiology outpatient follow-up if symptoms persist
IV amiodarone 300 mg loading dose over 60 minutes via a peripheral large-bore cannula

stem:
A 72-year-old man presents with exertional dyspnoea, one episode of syncope while climbing stairs last week, and a 2-month history of chest tightness on hills. He has hypertension on amlodipine, hyperlipidaemia on atorvastatin, and is otherwise well. On auscultation there is an ejection systolic murmur best heard at the right second intercostal space, radiating to both carotids, with a soft S2 and a slow-rising carotid pulse.

The murmur is intensity grade 3/6, peaks late in systole, and is louder on squatting. There is no S3, no opening snap, no MR jet, and no pulmonary congestion clinically. His ECG shows left ventricular hypertrophy with strain pattern. CXR shows a borderline-enlarged cardiac silhouette without pulmonary oedema. He has never had an echocardiogram.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/72 mmHg (narrow pulse pressure), HR 76 bpm regular, RR 16, SpO2 97% RA.
data_table.Examination: Slow-rising carotid pulse, soft S2, late-peaking ejection systolic murmur 3/6 RUSB radiating to carotids, louder on squatting. No S3. No mid-systolic click. JVP not elevated. No peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: LVH with strain. CXR: borderline cardiomegaly, clear lungs. Normal troponin and TSH.

lead_in: Which finding most strongly distinguishes severe aortic stenosis from hypertrophic obstructive cardiomyopathy in this patient?

options.text: Murmur intensity increases on squatting and falls with Valsalva strain
Presence of an ejection systolic murmur at the right upper sternal edge today
ECG showing left ventricular hypertrophy with associated strain pattern in lateral leads
Exertional syncope as a presenting symptom in this elderly patient with murmur
Presence of a slow-rising carotid pulse and a narrow pulse pressure today

subtopic_detail: Valvular DDx - aortic stenosis vs HCM vs mitral regurgitation

stem:
A 68-year-old man with a 50 pack-year smoking history attends his GP for review. Spirometry 4 weeks ago confirmed COPD with post-bronchodilator FEV1/FVC 0.58 and FEV1 62 percent predicted (GOLD 2). Over the past year he has had 2 exacerbations managed in the community with prednisolone and amoxicillin, and no hospital admissions. His mMRC dyspnoea score is 2 (stops for breath after about 100 m on the flat) and CAT score is 18.

He is currently on as-needed salbutamol inhaler only. He stopped smoking 6 months ago, is up to date with influenza and pneumococcal vaccines, and is enrolled in a pulmonary rehabilitation program. He has no diagnosis of asthma, no significant atopy, and a blood eosinophil count of 120 cells/microL. His GP specifically asks whether to add a LAMA alone, to add a fixed-dose LAMA/LABA combination, to add a LABA/ICS combination, to commence triple therapy with LAMA/LABA/ICS, or to add oral theophylline.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 95% RA.
data_table.Examination: Mild barrel chest, reduced air entry bilaterally, prolonged expiration, no peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: Post-bronchodilator FEV1 62 percent predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.58. Eosinophils 120 cells/microL. CXR hyperinflation without infiltrate.
data_table.Medications: Salbutamol 100 microg pMDI PRN.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next inhaled therapy?

options.text: Add tiotropium 18 microg daily (LAMA)
Add a LAMA/LABA combination inhaler
Add a fixed-dose LABA/ICS combination
Triple therapy with LAMA/LABA/ICS in a single inhaler
Add oral theophylline 200 mg twice daily

subtopic_detail: COPD - GOLD group classification and inhaler escalation

stem:
A 71-year-old woman with severe COPD (FEV1 38 percent predicted) is brought to ED by ambulance with worsening dyspnoea, productive cough with greenish sputum, and confusion over the past 24 hours. She is a current smoker. On arrival she was placed on 8 L/min Hudson mask oxygen by paramedics; SpO2 is now 98 percent. She is drowsy with bounding peripheral pulses, flapping tremor, and warm sweaty palms.

She is using salbutamol/ipratropium nebulisers continuously since arrival. An arterial blood gas is taken on the current oxygen flow rate. Her usual inhalers are tiotropium and salmeterol/fluticasone, and she has had 3 prior admissions for COPD exacerbations in the past year, two requiring non-invasive ventilation. The ED registrar specifically asks whether to maintain current oxygen and proceed straight to intubation, to reduce oxygen to nasal prongs 2 L/min without ventilatory support, to administer IV doxapram to stimulate respiration, or to switch to nasal high-flow oxygen at 60 L/min and continue nebulisers as definitive management before any non-invasive ventilation trial is attempted. A BiPAP machine is available now in resus. ICU has been notified of likely admission.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 148/86 mmHg, HR 108 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 98% on 8 L Hudson mask, T 37.4 degC, GCS 13.
data_table.Examination: Drowsy, flapping tremor, warm peripheries, accessory muscle use, widespread polyphonic wheeze, prolonged expiration.
data_table.Investigations: ABG (on 8 L Hudson): pH 7.21, pCO2 88 mmHg, pO2 110 mmHg, HCO3 32 mmol/L, BE +3. CXR: hyperinflation, no consolidation or pneumothorax.
data_table.Medications: Tiotropium 18 microg daily, salmeterol/fluticasone 50/500 BD.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Titrate oxygen down to a target SpO2 of 88 to 92 percent and initiate non-invasive ventilation with BiPAP
Maintain the current 8 L/min Hudson mask oxygen flow rate and proceed straight to endotracheal intubation and invasive mechanical ventilation
Reduce oxygen to nasal prongs at 2 L/min and observe in resus without ventilatory support pending repeat arterial blood gas in 1 hour
Administer intravenous doxapram infusion to stimulate respiratory drive and continue current Hudson mask oxygen flow rate while awaiting ICU review
Switch to nasal high-flow oxygen at 60 L/min, FiO2 0.6, and continue back-to-back salbutamol/ipratropium nebulisers without BiPAP

subtopic_detail: COPD exacerbation - acute management and ABG interpretation

stem:
A 24-year-old woman with known moderate persistent asthma presents to ED with 6 hours of progressively worsening dyspnoea, wheeze, and dry cough. She had a viral URTI 3 days ago. She has been using her salbutamol inhaler every 30 minutes for the last 2 hours with minimal relief. She has a background of eczema and rhinitis, no other medical history, and her usual inhaler is budesonide/formoterol 200/6 maintenance and reliever.

Her best-ever PEF is 460 L/min. On arrival she can only speak in short phrases, is sitting upright, and is using accessory muscles. There is widespread polyphonic expiratory wheeze without focal crackles. There is no chest pain, no haemoptysis, and no calf swelling. The ED registrar asks specifically whether the exacerbation is mild-moderate, severe, or life-threatening, and which initial treatment bundle applies under the Australian Asthma Handbook for this patient today.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/78 mmHg, HR 124 bpm, RR 30, SpO2 91% RA, T 37.0 degC.
data_table.Examination: Sitting upright, accessory muscle use, short-phrase speech, widespread polyphonic wheeze, prolonged expiration.
data_table.Investigations: PEF 180 L/min (39 percent of personal best). CXR: hyperinflation, no consolidation/pneumothorax. K 3.6 mmol/L.
data_table.Medications: Budesonide/formoterol 200/6 BD maintenance and reliever.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate classification of severity and corresponding initial treatment?

options.text: Mild to moderate exacerbation - salbutamol pMDI 4 to 12 puffs via spacer and reassess in 20 minutes for ongoing wheeze
Severe exacerbation - continuous salbutamol nebulisers with ipratropium, IV hydrocortisone, and oxygen titrated to SpO2 93 to 95 percent
Life-threatening exacerbation - immediate intubation and mechanical ventilation in the resus bay regardless of clinical response to bronchodilator therapy
Moderate exacerbation - oral prednisolone 50 mg and discharge home with safety-net advice and GP review in 24 hours for reassessment
Severe exacerbation - IV magnesium sulfate 2 g as first-line and observe response before commencing salbutamol nebulisers or systemic corticosteroid

stem:
A 31-year-old woman is reviewed by her GP for asthma. Over the past 3 months she has had daytime symptoms 3 to 4 times per week, nocturnal waking once weekly, and uses her salbutamol inhaler roughly 4 times per week. She has had no exacerbations requiring oral steroids in the past year. Her inhaler technique is excellent on observation. She is currently on salbutamol 100 microgram pMDI as needed only.

She is planning pregnancy in the next 6 months and asks specifically about whether she can keep using her reliever as her only inhaler in pregnancy. FEV1 is 88 percent predicted with bronchodilator reversibility of 14 percent. She has no rhinitis, reflux, or known occupational trigger.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, RR 14, SpO2 99% RA.
data_table.Examination: Chest clear, no wheeze, no signs of allergic rhinitis.
data_table.Investigations: FEV1 88 percent predicted, BDR 14 percent, normal CXR.
data_table.Medications: Salbutamol 100 microg pMDI PRN only.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Continue salbutamol PRN alone with a written asthma action plan and review after conception
Commence low-dose budesonide-formoterol 200/6 used as anti-inflammatory reliever only with written action plan
Commence daily montelukast 10 mg nocte with continued salbutamol PRN as reliever
Commence high-dose fluticasone-salmeterol 500/50 twice daily with salbutamol PRN
Commence oral prednisolone 25 mg daily for 2 weeks then taper with continued salbutamol PRN

stem:
A 78-year-old woman presents with 2 days of progressively worsening dyspnoea and pleuritic right-sided chest pain. She had a right total knee replacement 4 weeks ago with delayed mobilisation. She has hypertension on amlodipine, osteoarthritis, and no prior VTE. She is on no anticoagulation since stopping enoxaparin 1 week post-op. She has had no haemoptysis but her right calf is mildly swollen with 2 cm difference compared with the left.

On arrival she is haemodynamically stable, SpO2 92 percent RA improving to 96 percent on 2 L. ECG shows sinus tachycardia at 102 bpm with no S1Q3T3 and no right heart strain pattern. CXR is unremarkable. D-dimer is 720 microg/L (laboratory standard cut-off 500 microg/L; age-adjusted cut-off age x 10 microg/L for age greater than 50).

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 102 bpm, RR 22, SpO2 92% RA improving to 96% on 2 L NP, T 36.8 degC.
data_table.Examination: Right calf swollen with 2 cm circumference difference, chest clear, no JVP elevation, S1 S2 no S3.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: sinus tachycardia 102 bpm, no S1Q3T3. CXR: unremarkable. D-dimer 720 microg/L. Troponin pending. Creatinine 84 micromol/L.
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Based on Wells score and D-dimer interpretation, which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home because the D-dimer sits below the age-adjusted threshold of 780 microg/L and therefore excludes the diagnosis
Order CT pulmonary angiogram and commence empirical therapeutic anticoagulation while awaiting imaging
Order V/Q scan as first-line imaging given the normal CXR
Repeat D-dimer in 24 hours and arrange outpatient CTPA if it rises
Arrange bilateral lower-limb compression ultrasound first and only proceed to CTPA if positive

subtopic_detail: Pulmonary embolism - Wells score and age-adjusted D-dimer

stem:
A 52-year-old man is diagnosed with acute segmental pulmonary embolism on CTPA, performed for pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea after a long-haul flight from London 5 days ago. He has no prior VTE, no malignancy, and no recent surgery. On arrival he is haemodynamically stable, ambulating, eating, and drinking. His vital signs are stable as below. His troponin I and NT-proBNP are normal, and the CTPA reports no right heart strain.

He has stable home circumstances, lives 10 minutes from the hospital, and has a partner at home. He is not pregnant. He has no significant bleeding history and is not on antiplatelets or NSAIDs. His haemoglobin is 142 g/L, platelets 230 x 10^9/L, and creatinine 78 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 86 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 96% RA, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Comfortable at rest, chest clear, calves soft, no peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: CTPA: right segmental PE, no right heart strain. Troponin I normal. NT-proBNP normal. Hb 142 g/L, platelets 230, creatinine 78.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management strategy?

options.text: Outpatient management with apixaban 10 mg twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily for 3 months
Inpatient management on a therapeutic enoxaparin bridge to warfarin titrated to INR 2.0 to 3.0 for at least 3 months of continued anticoagulation
Systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours followed by therapeutic heparin infusion and admission to a coronary care monitored bed
Inferior vena cava filter insertion without therapeutic anticoagulation given the recent long-haul flight as a transient provoking factor
Aspirin 100 mg daily indefinitely without therapeutic anticoagulation given the segmental clot burden and absence of right heart strain

subtopic_detail: Pulmonary embolism - risk stratification and outpatient management

stem: A 64-year-old man presents to ED with 3 days of fever, productive cough with rusty sputum, right-sided pleuritic chest pain, and progressive dyspnoea. He has a 25 pack-year smoking history, hypertension on perindopril, and no known drug allergies. On arrival he is alert but unwell-looking. His CXR shows dense right middle lobe consolidation with a small parapneumonic effusion. Bloods show WCC 18.4 x 10^9/L with neutrophilia, CRP 280 mg/L, albumin 28 g/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L, urea 9.2 mmol/L, glucose 7.8 mmol/L. ABG on room air shows pH 7.42, pO2 58 mmHg, pCO2 36 mmHg, HCO3 24 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/64 mmHg, HR 116 bpm, RR 28, SpO2 90% RA, T 38.6 degC.
data_table.Examination: Alert, dehydrated, dullness and bronchial breathing right lower zone, no neck stiffness, no focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: CXR: dense right middle lobe consolidation with small effusion. WCC 18.4, CRP 280, albumin 28 g/L, creatinine 96, urea 9.2, glucose 7.8. ABG: pH 7.42, pO2 58, pCO2 36, HCO3 24.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate disposition and initial empirical antibiotic therapy?

options.text: Admit to general ward today with oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily plus doxycycline 100 mg twice daily for atypical cover
Admit to high-dependency or ICU; IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus IV azithromycin 500 mg daily, with empirical cover for atypicals
Discharge home with a 7-day course of oral moxifloxacin 400 mg once daily based on a CURB-65 of only 1 today
Admit to general ward today with intravenous benzylpenicillin 1.2 g six-hourly monotherapy and review at 48 hours for response to therapy
Admit to ICU today with intravenous vancomycin 1.5 g twelve-hourly plus intravenous meropenem 1 g eight-hourly for empirical broad-spectrum coverage

subtopic_detail: Community-acquired pneumonia - SMART-COP severity and antibiotic choice

stem:
An 82-year-old nursing home resident with advanced Parkinson disease and known dysphagia is brought to ED with 24 hours of fever, productive cough, and confusion. The nursing home reports she was found coughing during dinner the previous evening. She was hospitalised 3 weeks ago for a urinary tract infection and received IV ceftriaxone and oral ciprofloxacin during that admission. She has no documented multi-drug-resistant organism.

On examination she is febrile and tachypnoeic with right lower zone crackles. CXR shows right lower lobe consolidation. Bloods show neutrophilic leukocytosis and creatinine 96 micromol/L. She has no penicillin allergy.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/72 mmHg, HR 102 bpm, RR 24, SpO2 92% on 2 L NP, T 38.4 degC, GCS 14.
data_table.Examination: Right lower zone crackles and dullness, no neck stiffness, mild dehydration.
data_table.Investigations: CXR: right lower lobe consolidation. WCC 14.6 x 10^9/L. CRP 180 mg/L. Creatinine 96 micromol/L.
data_table.Medications: Levodopa/carbidopa 100/25 mg QID, no antibiotics in past 6 months.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic therapy?

options.text: IV amoxicillin-clavulanate 1.2 g eight-hourly empirically without antipseudomonal cover
IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g six-hourly empirically with daily microbiology review
Oral amoxicillin 1 g three times daily as monotherapy without anaerobic cover
IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus IV metronidazole 500 mg twelve-hourly empirically
IV vancomycin 1.5 g twelve-hourly plus IV ciprofloxacin 400 mg twelve-hourly empirically

subtopic_detail: Aspiration pneumonia - antibiotic choice and risk factors

stem:
A 58-year-old man presents to ED with palpitations and mild dyspnoea that began approximately 32 hours ago, but he reports a similar but milder episode 4 days ago that he ignored. He has hypertension on perindopril and no other medical history. He is haemodynamically stable. ECG confirms atrial fibrillation at 102 bpm. Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram shows preserved LV function (LVEF 60 percent), mild left atrial dilatation (LA 42 mm), and no significant valvular disease.

He has no prior stroke, peripheral vascular disease, diabetes, or heart failure, and has never been anticoagulated. CHA2DS2-VA score is 1 (hypertension). The team would like to attempt rhythm control on this presentation.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 102 bpm irregular, RR 16, SpO2 98% RA.
data_table.Examination: Irregularly irregular pulse, chest clear, no neurological deficit, no peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: AF rate 102. Echo: LVEF 60 percent, LA 42 mm, no valve disease. TSH normal, K 4.2 mmol/L.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg daily.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate approach to cardioversion?

options.text: Proceed to electrical cardioversion now without anticoagulation since current episode is under 48 hours
Commence therapeutic anticoagulation and perform TOE-guided cardioversion, then continue anticoagulation for at least 4 weeks regardless of CHA2DS2-VA
Commence aspirin 100 mg daily and proceed to elective electrical cardioversion in 24 hours
Defer cardioversion indefinitely and use rate control with metoprolol without anticoagulation
Discharge home, commence flecainide pill-in-pocket strategy and review in clinic next week

subtopic_detail: Atrial fibrillation - cardioversion timing and anticoagulation

stem:
A 76-year-old woman presents at 3 am with 8 hours of progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea, and a dry cough. She has HFrEF (LVEF 35 percent) on perindopril, bisoprolol, furosemide, and dapagliflozin; type 2 diabetes on metformin; and known paroxysmal AF on apixaban 5 mg twice daily. She was discharged 10 days ago after a 5-day admission for cellulitis. Since then she has been less mobile, sitting in her chair most of the day.

She denies fever, chest pain, or haemoptysis. On arrival she is afebrile but distressed. JVP is elevated to the angle of the jaw at 60 degrees. There are fine bibasal crackles to the mid-zones and trace ankle oedema bilaterally. Her ECG shows AF at 118 bpm without acute ischaemic changes. CXR shows bilateral interstitial opacities with upper lobe blood diversion.

Troponin I is 22 ng/L (cut-off less than 16, stable on repeat). NT-proBNP is 6800 ng/L. D-dimer is 1800 microg/L. Bedside lung ultrasound shows bilateral B-lines and small bilateral pleural effusions. Creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 110).

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/92 mmHg, HR 118 bpm AF, RR 28, SpO2 89% RA improving to 94% on 6 L Hudson, T 36.7 degC.
data_table.Examination: Sitting upright, JVP elevated, bibasal crackles to mid-zones, trace ankle oedema bilaterally, right calf 1 cm greater than left.
data_table.Investigations: ECG: AF rate 118, no acute ischaemia. CXR: bilateral interstitial opacities with upper lobe diversion. Troponin I 22 ng/L (stable). NT-proBNP 6800 ng/L. D-dimer 1800 microg/L. POCUS: bilateral B-lines and small pleural effusions. Creatinine 142 (baseline 110).
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, furosemide 40 mg, dapagliflozin 10 mg, apixaban 5 mg BD, metformin 1 g BD.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial diagnostic and management step?

options.text: Treat as acute decompensated heart failure with IV furosemide and GTN, and arrange CT pulmonary angiogram only if response is inadequate within 6 hours
Treat as suspected pulmonary embolism with immediate CT pulmonary angiogram and empirical therapeutic-dose enoxaparin, withholding all diuretics until the imaging result is available for review
Treat as severe community-acquired pneumonia with intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus intravenous azithromycin 500 mg daily and admit to a high-dependency monitored bed for observation

Activate the cardiac catheter lab for emergency primary percutaneous coronary intervention given the troponin elevation, AF with rapid ventricular response and bibasal pulmonary congestion on examination

Defer all imaging and start broad empirical combination therapy targeting pulmonary embolism, community-acquired pneumonia and acute decompensated heart failure simultaneously without further bedside diagnostic disambiguation today

subtopic_detail: Acute breathlessness - integrative diagnosis between PE, ADHF, and CAP
STEMI - reperfusion choice with rural transfer window
stem:
A 64-year-old man presents to a small rural emergency department in regional NSW with 70 minutes of central crushing chest pain radiating to the jaw. He has hypertension and is a current smoker. He is in pain but well perfused. The 12-lead electrocardiogram (ECG) shows 3 mm ST elevation in II, III and aVF with reciprocal depression in I and aVL.

Right-sided leads show 1 mm ST elevation in V4R. A high-sensitivity troponin is pending. There are no fibrinolysis contraindications. The closest primary percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) centre is a 90-minute road transfer; the local helicopter retrieval team estimates first medical contact to balloon at 150 minutes. The nurse asks how to proceed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 58, BP 96/62, SpO2 96% room air, RR 18, afebrile.
data_table.ECG: ST elevation 3 mm II/III/aVF, reciprocal depression I/aVL, V4R ST elevation 1 mm.
data_table.Investigations: hs-troponin pending. FBC, UEC unremarkable.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Aspirin, clopidogrel, enoxaparin, tenecteplase now, then transfer for angiography within 3 to 24 hours
Transfer directly for primary PCI without fibrinolysis
Aspirin, ticagrelor, enoxaparin, tenecteplase now, then transfer for angiography
Aspirin and intravenous glyceryl trinitrate, defer reperfusion until troponin returns
Aspirin, ticagrelor and unfractionated heparin infusion, observe for spontaneous reperfusion

stem: A 68-year-old woman presents with two episodes of central chest pain over 6 hours, the last 90 minutes ago at rest. She has type 2 diabetes, hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3a. The 12-lead ECG shows 1.5 mm horizontal ST depression in V4 to V6 with dynamic T-wave inversion. High-sensitivity troponin rises from 62 to 180 ng/L over 3 hours (reference <14). She is comfortable, normotensive and well perfused. The Global Registry of Acute Coronary Events (GRACE) score is 162.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 148/82, SpO2 97% room air, RR 18, afebrile.
data_table.ECG: ST depression 1.5 mm V4-V6, dynamic T-wave inversion.
data_table.Investigations: hs-troponin 62 then 180 ng/L (<14). eGFR 48.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate timing of coronary angiography?

options.text: Within 2 hours
Within 24 hours
Within 72 hours
Selective invasive strategy after stress imaging
Defer angiography because of CKD stage 3a

subtopic_detail: Narrow complex tachycardia - stable SVT management
stem: A 28-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 45 minutes of palpitations and mild light-headedness that began abruptly while sitting at work. She has no past cardiac history. The 12-lead ECG shows a regular narrow complex tachycardia at 188 bpm without visible P waves. She is alert and well perfused with cool peripheries; BP 112/74. Continuous monitoring is in place and intravenous access has been obtained.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 188 regular, BP 112/74, SpO2 99% room air, RR 18.
data_table.ECG: Regular narrow complex tachycardia, no visible P waves, QRS 92 ms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Synchronised direct current cardioversion at 100 J
Modified Valsalva manoeuvre
Intravenous adenosine 6 mg rapid push
Intravenous metoprolol 5 mg
Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg loading

subtopic_detail: Broad complex tachycardia - stable VT management
stem: A 67-year-old man with prior anterior myocardial infarction and an ejection fraction of 32% presents with 20 minutes of palpitations and chest tightness. The 12-lead ECG shows a regular broad complex tachycardia at 168 bpm with QRS duration 168 ms, northwest axis, concordance across the precordial leads, and capture beats visible in lead II. He is alert, BP 108/68, SpO2 97% room air, no pulmonary oedema. He has tolerated symptoms without syncope or chest pain at rest.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 168 regular, BP 108/68, SpO2 97% room air, RR 20.
data_table.ECG: Broad complex regular tachycardia QRS 168 ms, northwest axis, precordial concordance, capture beats.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate pharmacological agent?

options.text: Intravenous adenosine 6 mg
Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg over 20 to 60 minutes
Intravenous verapamil 5 mg
Intravenous metoprolol 5 mg
Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g

stem: A 74-year-old woman presents with 30 minutes of palpitations and chest pain. The monitor shows a regular broad complex tachycardia at 200 bpm. She becomes increasingly unwell: BP 78/42, cool peripheries, drowsy, with crackles to the mid-zones. Pads are placed and the defibrillator is set to synchronised mode.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 200, BP 78/42, SpO2 92% on 6 L oxygen, RR 28, GCS 14.
data_table.ECG: Regular broad complex tachycardia QRS 160 ms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial cardioversion energy?

options.text: 50 J biphasic synchronised
100 J biphasic synchronised
200 J biphasic unsynchronised
360 J monophasic synchronised
Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg before cardioversion

subtopic_detail: Polymorphic VT and torsades de pointes
stem: A 56-year-old woman with depression admitted overnight on citalopram and quetiapine develops recurrent self-terminating runs of polymorphic ventricular tachycardia with a twisting QRS axis. Between runs the ECG shows sinus rhythm at 52 bpm with corrected QT interval (QTc) 612 ms. Potassium is 3.1 mmol/L and magnesium 0.62 mmol/L. She is conscious between episodes.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 52 sinus between runs, BP 102/64, SpO2 98%, RR 18.
data_table.ECG: Polymorphic VT runs; sinus QTc 612 ms.
data_table.Investigations: K 3.1 mmol/L, Mg 0.62 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 10 minutes
Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg loading
Intravenous sotalol 80 mg
Intravenous adenosine 6 mg
Synchronised DC cardioversion 100 J

stem: A 78-year-old man with chronic heart failure and reduced ejection fraction presents with two hours of progressive dyspnoea, orthopnoea and pink frothy sputum after running out of his furosemide a week earlier. He is sitting upright, distressed and unable to speak in full sentences. Crackles extend to the mid-zones bilaterally. BP 168/96, HR 118 sinus, SpO2 86% on room air, RR 32. He is alert.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 168/96, SpO2 86% room air, RR 32, afebrile.
data_table.Examination: Upright, accessory muscle use, bibasal to mid-zone crackles, raised JVP, peripheral oedema.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial combination?

options.text: Intravenous furosemide 40 mg, sublingual glyceryl trinitrate, non-invasive ventilation
Intravenous morphine 5 mg, intravenous furosemide 40 mg, intubation
Intravenous noradrenaline infusion and intravenous furosemide 40 mg
Intravenous fluid bolus 500 mL and intravenous furosemide 40 mg
Oral metoprolol 25 mg and intravenous furosemide 40 mg

stem:
A 66-year-old man presents 6 hours after onset of anterior STEMI to a tertiary centre. Primary percutaneous coronary intervention to the proximal left anterior descending artery has restored flow. After return to coronary care he becomes hypotensive with cool, mottled peripheries and oliguria. BP 78/54 despite a 500 mL crystalloid bolus, HR 112 sinus, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, urine output 8 mL/h.

Bedside echocardiography shows a severely impaired left ventricle (ejection fraction 20%), no tamponade, no acute mitral regurgitation, no ventricular septal defect. Pulmonary artery catheter shows cardiac index 1.6 L/min/m2, pulmonary capillary wedge 24 mmHg, systemic vascular resistance 1800 dyn s cm-5.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 112, BP 78/54, SpO2 94% on 6 L oxygen, RR 26, urine 8 mL/h.
data_table.Investigations: Lactate 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 142 µmol/L.
data_table.Haemodynamics: CI 1.6 L/min/m2, PCWP 24 mmHg, SVR 1800 dyn s cm-5.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate first-line vasoactive agent?

options.text: Noradrenaline infusion titrated to MAP 65 mmHg
Dopamine infusion at 10 mcg/kg/min
Adrenaline infusion at 0.1 mcg/kg/min
Dobutamine infusion as monotherapy
Vasopressin infusion at 0.04 units/min

stem: A 62-year-old man with ischaemic cardiomyopathy (ejection fraction 28%) presents with decompensated heart failure and is admitted to the Hunter New England LHD coronary care unit. After 48 hours of intravenous furosemide his weight has fallen 4 kg, BP 118/72, HR 76 sinus, creatinine has improved from 142 to 108 µmol/L, potassium 4.4 mmol/L. He has been euvolaemic for 24 hours. His current medications are perindopril 5 mg and furosemide intravenously. He is asymptomatic at rest.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76, BP 118/72, SpO2 97% room air, afebrile.
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 108 µmol/L, K 4.4 mmol/L, Hb 132 g/L.

lead_in: Which additional therapy is most appropriate to commence before discharge?

options.text: Bisoprolol, spironolactone and dapagliflozin
Digoxin and ivabradine
Amlodipine and isosorbide mononitrate
Bisoprolol alone, defer other agents to outpatient
Switch perindopril to candesartan

stem: A 60-year-old man with inferior ST-elevation myocardial infarction has 2 mm ST elevation in V4R confirming right ventricular involvement. He is bradycardic at HR 48 and hypotensive at BP 84/52 with clear lungs. The cardiology registrar has given 250 mcg of atropine without effect. There is no pulmonary oedema. Primary PCI has been activated.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 48 sinus brady, BP 84/52, SpO2 97% room air, RR 20.
data_table.ECG: II/III/aVF ST elevation 3 mm, V4R ST elevation 2 mm.
data_table.Examination: Clear lungs, raised JVP, no peripheral oedema.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before cardiac catheterisation transfer?

options.text: Intravenous normal saline 250 to 500 mL bolus
Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion
Intravenous furosemide 40 mg
Intravenous noradrenaline infusion
Transcutaneous pacing

stem: A 71-year-old woman with chronic heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (EF 30%) on oral furosemide 80 mg twice daily at home presents with worsening dyspnoea and 5 kg weight gain over 10 days. She is admitted to a general medical ward, comfortable on 2 L oxygen, BP 124/76, HR 88, with crackles to the mid-zones. Renal function is at her baseline (creatinine 116 µmol/L).

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 124/76, SpO2 95% on 2 L oxygen, RR 22.
data_table.Home meds: Furosemide 80 mg PO BD, bisoprolol, perindopril, spironolactone.
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 116 µmol/L (baseline), K 4.2 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial diuretic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous furosemide 40 mg twice daily
Intravenous furosemide 80 mg twice daily
Continue oral furosemide 80 mg twice daily
Intravenous hydrochlorothiazide 50 mg daily
Hold spironolactone and start oral metolazone 5 mg daily

subtopic_detail: Post-MI mechanical complication - acute mitral regurgitation
stem: A 70-year-old woman is on day 4 of admission for inferior STEMI managed with thrombolysis and uncomplicated angiography (single-vessel right coronary artery disease, no intervention required). She suddenly develops severe dyspnoea and pink frothy sputum. BP 92/60, HR 124, SpO2 84% on 8 L oxygen, RR 32. Auscultation reveals widespread crackles and a new soft apical systolic murmur. Bedside echocardiography shows flail posteromedial papillary muscle leaflet with severe mitral regurgitation; left ventricular ejection fraction is preserved at 55%.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 124, BP 92/60, SpO2 84% on 8 L oxygen, RR 32.
data_table.Echo: Flail posteromedial papillary muscle, severe MR, LVEF 55%.
data_table.Examination: Widespread crackles, soft apical systolic murmur.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent cardiothoracic referral for mitral valve surgery
Repeat coronary angiography and percutaneous intervention
Intravenous furosemide and observation
Intravenous metoprolol and intravenous furosemide
Intra-aortic balloon pump as definitive treatment

subtopic_detail: Atrial fibrillation with rapid ventricular response - rate vs rhythm
stem: A 64-year-old man with hypertension presents with palpitations of 6 hours duration. He has had a similar episode 12 months ago that self-terminated.
