ECG shows atrial fibrillation at ventricular rate 142. He is comfortable, BP 142/86, no chest pain, no heart failure features. He has had no oral anticoagulation. CHA2DS2-VASc is 1.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 142 irregular, BP 142/86, SpO2 98% room air, RR 18.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral metoprolol 25 mg as initial rate control
Electrical cardioversion at 150 J biphasic
Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg
Intravenous digoxin 500 mcg loading
Aspirin 100 mg daily for stroke prevention

subtopic_detail: ACS antiplatelet selection with high bleeding risk
stem: A 79-year-old woman has been diagnosed with NSTEMI and proceeds to invasive angiography with drug-eluting stent insertion to the right coronary artery. Her past history includes prior gastrointestinal bleed on dual antiplatelet therapy 3 years ago, current oral anticoagulation with apixaban 5 mg twice daily for atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VASc 5), eGFR 48, and weight 58 kg. She has no mechanical valve.

data_table.History: Prior GIB on DAPT, AF on apixaban, CHA2DS2-VASc 5, eGFR 48, weight 58 kg.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate antithrombotic regimen at discharge?

options.text: Aspirin, clopidogrel and apixaban for 12 months, then aspirin plus apixaban
Clopidogrel plus apixaban 5 mg twice daily for 12 months, then apixaban alone
Aspirin, ticagrelor and warfarin for 12 months
Apixaban alone, no antiplatelet
Aspirin and apixaban for 1 month, then apixaban alone

stem: A 54-year-old man with extensive anterior STEMI 8 hours after primary PCI remains in cardiogenic shock despite noradrenaline 0.5 mcg/kg/min and dobutamine 10 mcg/kg/min. BP 84/52, lactate 6.2 mmol/L (rising from 4.8 mmol/L), urine output 5 mL/h, peripheries cool and mottled to mid-thigh. He is intubated and ventilated. Echocardiography shows severely impaired left ventricular function (ejection fraction 15%), no mechanical complication, no tamponade. He is 54 years old with no significant comorbidity.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 84/52, SpO2 92% ventilated, lactate 6.2 mmol/L, urine 5 mL/h.
data_table.Echo: LVEF 15%, no MR, no VSD, no tamponade.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Increase noradrenaline and add adrenaline infusion
Veno-arterial extracorporeal membrane oxygenation (VA-ECMO) referral
Intra-aortic balloon pump insertion
Intravenous milrinone bolus and infusion
Repeat coronary angiography

stem: A 73-year-old man with known severe aortic stenosis presents to a Central Coast LHD emergency department with acute dyspnoea. He has crackles to the apices bilaterally and is using accessory muscles. BP 86/58, HR 104 sinus, SpO2 88% on 10 L oxygen, RR 30. He is alert. Bedside echocardiography confirms severe aortic stenosis with peak velocity 4.6 m/s and moderately impaired left ventricular function.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 104, BP 86/58, SpO2 88% on 10 L oxygen, RR 30.
data_table.Echo: Severe AS (peak V 4.6 m/s), moderately impaired LV.
data_table.Examination: Crackles to apices, accessory muscle use, ejection systolic murmur.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial intervention?

options.text: Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion
Intravenous furosemide 40 mg and non-invasive ventilation
Intravenous morphine 5 mg and fluid bolus 500 mL
Intravenous metoprolol 5 mg for tachycardia
Intravenous noradrenaline infusion

stem: An 82-year-old woman is admitted with community-acquired pneumonia. She has had no chest pain. Heart rate has been 118 sinus for 24 hours and oxygen saturation has dipped to 89% on room air. Routine high-sensitivity troponin returns at 145 ng/L, rising to 210 ng/L on a 3-hour repeat (reference <14). ECG shows sinus tachycardia, no ST changes. She remains afebrile after 24 hours of antibiotics, but is dyspnoeic. Echocardiography shows a structurally normal left ventricle.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118 sinus, BP 124/76, SpO2 89% room air, RR 24.
data_table.Investigations: hs-troponin 145 then 210 ng/L (<14).

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Treat the underlying pneumonia and hypoxia; do not commence dual antiplatelet therapy
Commence dual antiplatelet therapy and refer for angiography within 24 hours
Commence aspirin alone and observe
Thrombolysis with tenecteplase
Coronary angiography after pneumonia resolves

subtopic_detail: Post-discharge bridge therapy and clinic follow-up
stem: A 70-year-old woman is discharged after a 5-day admission with decompensated heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (ejection fraction 32%). She has been initiated on bisoprolol, perindopril, spironolactone, dapagliflozin and furosemide. She lives alone in a Hunter New England LHD rural town 90 minutes from the cardiology clinic.

data_table.Context: Lives alone, rural, 90 min from cardiology clinic.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate follow-up plan?

options.text: Heart failure nurse review within 7 to 14 days and cardiology clinic within 6 weeks
Cardiology clinic review at 3 months
General practitioner review when symptoms recur
Discharge with no scheduled follow-up
Inpatient referral for cardiac transplantation assessment

stem: A 68-year-old man with no prior cardiac history presents with light-headedness and one syncopal episode. ECG shows complete heart block with broad QRS escape at 32 bpm. BP 78/48, HR 32, SpO2 96% room air. He is alert but pale and clammy. Intravenous atropine 600 mcg has been given with no response.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 32, BP 78/48, SpO2 96% room air, RR 18.
data_table.ECG: Complete heart block, broad QRS escape 32 bpm.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat atropine 1 mg and observe
Transcutaneous pacing with sedation
Permanent pacemaker insertion in the next routine catheter laboratory list
Intravenous amiodarone 300 mg
Intravenous fluid bolus 1 L crystalloid

subtopic_detail: Spontaneous coronary artery dissection - young female presentation
stem: A 42-year-old woman 3 weeks post-partum presents with 2 hours of chest pain. She has no cardiovascular risk factors. ECG shows 2 mm ST elevation in V3 to V5. She is haemodynamically stable. Urgent coronary angiography reveals a long smooth tapering stenosis in the mid left anterior descending artery without atherosclerotic plaque; intracoronary imaging confirms a Type 2 spontaneous coronary artery dissection. Flow is preserved (TIMI 3). She has no ongoing ischaemia.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 122/74, SpO2 98% room air.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Conservative management with aspirin and beta-blocker; admit for observation
Emergency percutaneous coronary intervention with stent placement
Emergency coronary artery bypass surgery
Thrombolysis with tenecteplase
Dual antiplatelet therapy for 12 months and high-intensity statin

subtopic_detail: DKA - initial fluid and insulin protocol
stem:
A 19-year-old man with type 1 diabetes mellitus presents to a HNE LHD emergency department with 24 hours of polyuria, abdominal pain and vomiting after a viral gastroenteritis. He is drowsy but rousable. Examination: dry mucous membranes, deep sighing respirations, capillary refill 4 seconds. Heart rate 122, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, SpO2 99% room air, respiratory rate 28. Capillary blood glucose 28.4 mmol/L, capillary ketones 5.6 mmol/L.

Venous blood gas: pH 7.08, HCO3 7 mmol/L, base excess -22. Sodium 132, potassium 5.2, chloride 98, urea 9.2, creatinine 118 micromol/L. He weighs 70 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122, BP 96/58, RR 28, SpO2 99% RA, GCS 14, weight 70 kg.
data_table.Electrolytes: Na 132, K 5.2, Cl 98, urea 9.2, creatinine 118 mcmol/L.
data_table.Hydration: Dry mucosae, CRT 4 s, BP 96/58, HR 122.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial fluid and insulin order?

options.text: Sodium chloride 0.9% 1000 mL over 60 minutes, then start insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/h
Sodium chloride 0.9% 1000 mL over 60 minutes plus bolus insulin 10 units intravenously
Insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/h before commencing intravenous fluids
Compound sodium lactate 1000 mL over 60 minutes plus insulin infusion
Sodium bicarbonate 8.4% 100 mL over 30 minutes, then insulin and fluid

stem: A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes mellitus is being managed for diabetic ketoacidosis. She has received 1 L of 0.9% saline over the first hour and insulin infusion at 7 units/h has been running for 60 minutes. Her second bag of 0.9% saline is being set up. Current results: pH 7.14, HCO3 9, BGL 22 mmol/L, sodium 138, potassium 4.6, urea 8.0, creatinine 92 micromol/L. Urine output 60 mL in the past hour.

data_table.Status: 1 h into DKA treatment, hour 2 fluid being set up.
data_table.Bloods now: pH 7.14, HCO3 9, BGL 22, Na 138, K 4.6, urea 8.0, creatinine 92.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate potassium addition to the next litre of saline?

options.text: No potassium added; recheck after this bag
Add 40 mmol potassium chloride to the second-hour fluid
Add 20 mmol potassium chloride to the second-hour fluid
Stop insulin infusion until potassium rises to 5.0
Give oral potassium 40 mmol slow-release tablet

stem: An 82-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin and gliclazide is brought by family who report 5 days of progressive lethargy, polyuria and reduced oral intake during a urinary tract infection. She is drowsy and dry. Heart rate 108, blood pressure 102/64, capillary refill 4 seconds. Investigations: capillary glucose 42.6 mmol/L, capillary ketones 0.8 mmol/L. Venous blood gas: pH 7.34, HCO3 22, base excess -2, lactate 2.4. Sodium 158, potassium 4.0, urea 22, creatinine 198 micromol/L. Calculated serum osmolality 348 mOsm/kg. No focal neurology.

data_table.Background: T2DM, metformin + gliclazide, intercurrent UTI.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate distinction and management priority?

options.text: Hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state; slow fluid replacement with sodium chloride 0.9% titrated to gradual osmolality reduction
Diabetic ketoacidosis; start insulin infusion 0.1 unit/kg/h and rapid fluid
Euglycaemic ketoacidosis from SGLT2 inhibitor; investigate medication history
Acute kidney injury from osmotic diuresis; haemodialysis to lower glucose and osmolality
Sepsis-driven hyperglycaemia; broad-spectrum antibiotics and source control take priority over glucose

stem: A 46-year-old woman with known Addison disease on hydrocortisone 20 mg morning and 10 mg afternoon plus fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily presents to the emergency department with 36 hours of vomiting from gastroenteritis. She is drowsy, hypotensive and hyperpigmented. Heart rate 128, blood pressure 78/42 mmHg unresponsive to 500 mL of compound sodium lactate. Capillary blood glucose 2.8 mmol/L. Sodium 128, potassium 5.8, urea 14, creatinine 142 micromol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 128, BP 78/42 after 500 mL CSL, GCS 13.
data_table.Background: Addison disease, on hydrocortisone 20/10 mg + fludrocortisone 100 mcg, vomiting 36 h.
data_table.Examination: Hyperpigmented, dry, peripherally shut down.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenously plus 1 L 0.9% saline with 5% glucose
Dexamethasone 4 mg intravenously and await random cortisol result
Noradrenaline infusion via central line for refractory hypotension
Double the patient's usual oral hydrocortisone and continue oral fludrocortisone
Insulin and glucose bolus to manage hyperkalaemia urgently

stem: A 38-year-old man with secondary adrenal insufficiency following pituitary adenoma resection 2 years ago is on hydrocortisone 15 mg morning and 5 mg afternoon. He calls the endocrine clinic at the start of an influenza-like illness with fever 38.7 degrees Celsius and myalgia but is tolerating oral fluids and small meals.

data_table.Background: Secondary adrenal insufficiency post pituitary surgery, on hydrocortisone 15/5 mg.
data_table.Current illness: Influenza-like illness, fever 38.7, myalgia, tolerating oral intake.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate sick day advice?

options.text: Double oral hydrocortisone (30 mg morning, 10 mg afternoon) for the duration of fever
Continue usual dose and only escalate if symptoms worsen significantly
Inject intramuscular hydrocortisone 100 mg immediately and present to emergency
Switch to prednisone 10 mg daily for simpler dosing during illness
Add fludrocortisone 100 mcg daily during illness

subtopic_detail: Thyroid storm - recognition and pharmacology sequence
stem: A 32-year-old woman with poorly controlled Graves disease presents to emergency 4 days after stopping carbimazole because of a presumed allergy. She is agitated, confused, tremulous and diaphoretic. Temperature 39.8 degrees Celsius, heart rate 168 atrial fibrillation, blood pressure 162/88, respiratory rate 28. Free thyroxine (T4) 64 pmol/L, free triiodothyronine (T3) 24 pmol/L, thyroid stimulating hormone (TSH) <0.01 mU/L. Burch-Wartofsky Point Scale (BWPS) is 65, consistent with thyroid storm.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.8, HR 168 AF, BP 162/88, RR 28, agitated/confused.
data_table.Thyroid: fT4 64 pmol/L, fT3 24 pmol/L, TSH <0.01 mU/L.
data_table.Background: Graves disease, stopped carbimazole 4 days ago (presumed allergy).

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate sequence of pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Propylthiouracil 200 mg orally, then 1 hour later potassium iodide oral solution, plus propranolol and hydrocortisone
Potassium iodide oral solution immediately, then thionamide 1 hour later
Total thyroidectomy after rapid optimisation with beta-blockade
Radioactive iodine ablation as immediate definitive therapy
Carbimazole 60 mg orally with concurrent ibuprofen for pyrexia

stem: An 80-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department in winter after being found unresponsive at home. She has known hypothyroidism but is reported to have stopped levothyroxine some months ago because she 'felt fine'. She is hypothermic and obtunded. Temperature 31.4 degrees Celsius (rectal), heart rate 42, blood pressure 86/52, respiratory rate 8 and shallow. Sodium 122, potassium 4.4, glucose 3.1, cortisol 198 nmol/L (random). TSH 102 mU/L, free T4 3 pmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: T 31.4 (rectal), HR 42, BP 86/52, RR 8 shallow, GCS 6.
data_table.Bloods: Na 122, K 4.4, glucose 3.1, random cortisol 198 nmol/L.
data_table.Background: Known hypothyroidism, stopped levothyroxine months ago, winter.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Intravenous hydrocortisone 100 mg, then intravenous levothyroxine 200-400 mcg loading
Intravenous levothyroxine 500 mcg loading, then hydrocortisone if cortisol low
Active external rewarming with forced-air blanket and observation
Oral levothyroxine 200 mcg via nasogastric tube and supportive care
Hypertonic 3% saline correction for severe hyponatraemia

stem: A 72-year-old woman is brought to the emergency department after a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure at home. She has had progressive lethargy and confusion over 5 days. She is on hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension and was started on a thiazide-sparing antidepressant (escitalopram) 2 weeks ago. Heart rate 88, blood pressure 138/84, post-ictal Glasgow Coma Score 12. Sodium 108 mmol/L, potassium 3.6, urea 4.2, creatinine 64 micromol/L. Serum osmolality 232 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 480 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 58 mmol/L. Euvolaemic on examination.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 138/84, post-ictal GCS 12, euvolaemic.
data_table.Medications: HCTZ, escitalopram started 2 weeks ago.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Hypertonic 3% saline 150 mL bolus over 20 minutes, repeat up to twice if symptoms persist, aiming sodium rise of 4-6 mmol/L in first hour
0.9% sodium chloride 1 L over 4 hours and fluid restriction to 1 L/24 h
Fluid restriction to 800 mL/day plus oral salt tablets
Tolvaptan 15 mg orally daily and monitor sodium 6-hourly
Demeclocycline 600 mg orally daily for chronic SIADH management

stem: A 64-year-old man is reviewed in the outpatient clinic for incidentally noted sodium of 124 mmol/L on routine bloods. He has small cell lung carcinoma diagnosed 3 weeks ago, recently commenced platinum-based chemotherapy. He is asymptomatic. He is clinically euvolaemic. Serum osmolality 258 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 520 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 62 mmol/L. Thyroid stimulating hormone 1.8 mU/L, morning cortisol 380 nmol/L.

data_table.Background: Small cell lung carcinoma, on chemotherapy.

lead_in: What is the most likely cause of his hyponatraemia?

options.text: Syndrome of inappropriate antidiuretic hormone secretion from small cell lung carcinoma
Pseudohyponatraemia from hyperlipidaemia
Hypovolaemic hyponatraemia from chemotherapy-induced vomiting
Hypothyroidism-related impaired free water clearance
Adrenal insufficiency with cortisol deficiency

subtopic_detail: Haemolysed specimen as a cause of a spuriously raised potassium
stem: A 58-year-old woman attends for routine review of stage 3 chronic kidney disease. She feels well and takes perindopril. The laboratory has flagged this morning's specimen and telephoned the result.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 74 /min, blood pressure 128/76 mmHg, SpO2 98% room air
data_table.Investigations: Potassium 6.6 mmol/L, haemolysis index high; creatinine 132 micromol/L; ECG normal

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Repeat the potassium on a fresh free flowing sample
Give intravenous calcium gluconate and attach cardiac monitoring
Start insulin with dextrose and recheck in one hour
Prescribe oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate and review tomorrow
Cease perindopril today and arrange review in one week

stem: A 74-year-old woman with hypertension and chronic kidney disease stage 3b (estimated glomerular filtration rate 38) presents with serum potassium 6.4 mmol/L. She takes the following: perindopril 4 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, paracetamol 1 g 6-hourly, ibuprofen 400 mg 8-hourly (started last week for knee pain), trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole (commenced 4 days ago for a urinary tract infection).

data_table.Recent additions: Ibuprofen 1 week ago; trimethoprim/sulfamethoxazole 4 days ago for UTI.

lead_in: Which combination of medications has most likely contributed to the hyperkalaemia?

options.text: Perindopril, spironolactone, ibuprofen, trimethoprim
Atorvastatin and paracetamol
Amlodipine and atorvastatin
Perindopril and atorvastatin
Spironolactone and amlodipine

stem: A 54-year-old man with type 2 diabetes mellitus on metformin, empagliflozin and sitagliptin presents the day after laparoscopic cholecystectomy with 12 hours of progressive nausea, abdominal pain and dyspnoea. He fasted for 18 hours before surgery and has eaten little since. Capillary blood glucose 8.4 mmol/L, capillary ketones 4.8 mmol/L. Venous blood gas: pH 7.16, HCO3 10, base excess -16, lactate 2.1. Sodium 137, potassium 4.2, chloride 102, anion gap 25.

data_table.Background: T2DM on metformin + empagliflozin + sitagliptin, post-op day 1 cholecystectomy, 18 h fast.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Treat as DKA with insulin-dextrose infusion plus saline, withhold empagliflozin
Treat as starvation ketosis with intravenous glucose alone
Investigate as post-operative sepsis and start broad-spectrum antibiotics
Continue empagliflozin and add NPH insulin twice daily
Resume oral metformin and observe for symptom improvement

stem: A 15-year-old girl is being managed for severe DKA in a HNE LHD emergency department. After 4 hours of treatment (3 L 0.9% saline at 1 L/h then 500 mL/h, insulin infusion 5 units/h, potassium replacement, BGL down from 35 to 14 mmol/L), she develops a headache, then becomes drowsy and irritable. Her glasgow coma score has dropped from 15 to 11 in 30 minutes. Heart rate 62 (was 110), blood pressure 152/92 (was 96/56). Pupils equal, briskly reactive.

data_table.Trajectory: Hour 4 of DKA Rx: GCS dropped 15 to 11 over 30 min, headache then drowsiness.
data_table.Fluids: 3 L 0.9% saline (1 L/h x 1 then 500 mL/h x 4), insulin 5 units/h.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Hypertonic 3% saline 5 mL/kg bolus, reduce fluid rate, urgent CT head and paediatric ICU referral
Increase fluid rate to treat presumed dehydration and worsening shock
Increase insulin infusion to 0.15 unit/kg/h to drive glucose down further
Administer sodium bicarbonate 1 mmol/kg to reverse acidosis faster
Give intramuscular promethazine for nausea and reassess in 30 minutes

stem: A 70-year-old man on amiodarone 200 mg daily for 4 years for atrial fibrillation presents with thyrotoxicosis. TSH <0.01 mU/L, free T4 48 pmol/L, free T3 12 pmol/L. Thyroid antibody panel negative. Colour Doppler thyroid ultrasound shows reduced vascularity with patchy parenchymal changes. Iodine-123 uptake scan shows very low uptake. Interleukin-6 elevated.

data_table.Thyroid: TSH <0.01 mU/L, fT4 48 pmol/L, fT3 12 pmol/L.
data_table.Imaging: Colour Doppler US: reduced vascularity, patchy parenchymal change; I-123 uptake very low.
data_table.Background: 4 years on amiodarone 200 mg/day for AF.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: High-dose oral prednisolone 40-60 mg daily
Carbimazole 40 mg orally daily as first-line
Total thyroidectomy as immediate definitive therapy
Radioactive iodine ablation
Discontinue amiodarone and observe for spontaneous resolution

subtopic_detail: Interfering medicine behind a modestly raised plasma metanephrine result
stem: A 48-year-old woman with hypertension has plasma metanephrines measured after several months of episodic headache and sweating. She takes amitriptyline at night for neuropathic pain. No adrenal imaging has been arranged.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 84 /min, blood pressure 148/92 mmHg seated
data_table.Investigations: Plasma normetanephrine 1.7 times the upper reference limit; metanephrine within range

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Withhold amitriptyline and repeat the plasma metanephrines
Arrange adrenal computed tomography before any repeat testing
Start phenoxybenzamine while further investigation proceeds
Accept the result as normal and stop further investigation
Arrange a meta-iodobenzylguanidine scan of the adrenal glands

stem: A 67-year-old woman with metastatic breast cancer presents to a Central Coast LHD emergency department with confusion, polyuria, polydipsia and constipation. Heart rate 112, blood pressure 102/64. Corrected calcium 3.84 mmol/L (reference 2.10-2.60), phosphate 0.78, parathyroid hormone (PTH) 0.6 pmol/L (reference 1.6-6.9), parathyroid hormone-related peptide (PTHrP) elevated, 25-hydroxyvitamin D 62 nmol/L. Creatinine 142 micromol/L (baseline 78).

data_table.Background: Metastatic breast cancer.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment sequence?

options.text: Aggressive intravenous 0.9% saline rehydration, then intravenous zoledronic acid 4 mg
Furosemide 40 mg intravenously to promote calcium excretion
Oral cinacalcet 30 mg twice daily for symptomatic control
Prednisolone 60 mg daily for first-line management
Phosphate replacement orally to chelate serum calcium

stem: A 38-year-old man with severe alcohol use disorder is admitted after 3 weeks of negligible oral intake. Body mass index 15.8 kg/m2. He has lost 9 kg over the past 2 months. Initial bloods: phosphate 0.62 mmol/L (reference 0.75-1.50), magnesium 0.58 mmol/L (0.70-1.10), potassium 3.4, sodium 138, glucose 4.2, albumin 28. The dietitian recommends commencing enteral nutrition.

data_table.Nutrition risk: BMI 15.8, 9 kg loss in 2 months, negligible oral intake 3 weeks.
data_table.Background: Severe alcohol use disorder.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step before initiating feeds?

options.text: Replace phosphate, magnesium and potassium plus give intravenous thiamine 200 mg 8-hourly, then start feeds at 5-10 kcal/kg/day
Start full enteral feeds at 25 kcal/kg/day with daily electrolyte monitoring
Start oral feeds with high-protein supplements and oral thiamine 100 mg daily
Start total parenteral nutrition at standard rates and monitor electrolytes daily
Defer feeding for 48 hours and replace electrolytes alone

stem: Five hospitalised patients are noted to have hypoglycaemia. The endocrinology registrar is asked to identify which patient most likely has a sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycaemia requiring prolonged observation and octreotide rather than the standard short observation after glucose correction.

data_table.Patient 1: Type 1 diabetic on insulin pump, BGL 2.4 at 6am after exercise yesterday evening.
data_table.Patient 2: Type 2 diabetic on metformin and gliclazide, BGL 2.1 at 4pm, recurrent episodes overnight despite glucose.
data_table.Patient 3: Post-bariatric surgery patient, BGL 2.6 90 minutes after a high-carbohydrate meal.
data_table.Patient 4: Adrenal insufficient patient who missed hydrocortisone dose, BGL 2.8.
data_table.Patient 5: End-stage liver disease patient with BGL 2.5 fasting.

lead_in: Which patient requires prolonged observation and octreotide?

options.text: Patient 1 - exercise-related insulin pump hypoglycaemia
Patient 2 - gliclazide-associated recurrent hypoglycaemia
Patient 3 - post-bariatric reactive hypoglycaemia
Patient 4 - adrenal insufficiency-related hypoglycaemia
Patient 5 - hepatic failure hypoglycaemia

stem: A 31-year-old woman presents 4 months postpartum with palpitations, anxiety, heat intolerance and weight loss of 3 kg over 6 weeks. She is breastfeeding. Examination: small diffuse goitre without bruit, no eye signs, no pretibial myxoedema, fine tremor. Heart rate 102, blood pressure 122/72. TSH <0.01 mU/L, free T4 32 pmol/L, free T3 9 pmol/L. TSH receptor antibodies negative, anti-thyroid peroxidase (anti-TPO) antibodies 480 IU/mL (raised). Iodine-123 uptake very low at 1.2% (reference 5-25%).

data_table.Symptoms: Palpitations, anxiety, heat intolerance, 3 kg weight loss in 6 weeks.
data_table.Examination: Small diffuse goitre (no bruit), no eye signs, fine tremor.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Propranolol 20-40 mg orally 8-hourly for symptom control without thionamide
Carbimazole 10 mg orally 8-hourly with regular thyroid function monitoring
Radioactive iodine ablation as definitive therapy
Total thyroidectomy because of suspected Graves disease
Levothyroxine 50 mcg daily for the hyperthyroid phase

stem: A 42-year-old man 5 days after pituitary macroadenoma resection develops polyuria (8 L in 24 hours) and increasing thirst. Urine output is consistent over time. Plasma sodium has risen from 138 to 152 mmol/L over the same 24 hours. Plasma osmolality 312 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 122 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 28 mmol/L. He is conscious, drinking water voluntarily, but is unable to keep up with urine losses.

data_table.Osmolality: Plasma 312 mOsm/kg, urine 122 mOsm/kg, urine Na 28.
data_table.Hydration: Conscious, drinking, but losing more than able to replace.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate diagnosis and immediate management?

options.text: Central diabetes insipidus; commence desmopressin 1-2 mcg subcutaneously and free water replacement
SIADH; fluid restrict to 800 mL/day and consider tolvaptan
Cerebral salt wasting; replace volume with 0.9% saline at 200 mL/h
Osmotic diuresis from hyperglycaemia; check BGL and start insulin
Primary polydipsia; restrict free water to 1.5 L per day

stem: A 56-year-old man attends his GP for review of fatigue and nocturia over the last three months. He has hypertension on perindopril 5 mg, BMI 31, and his father has T2DM. He has had two haemoglobinopathy screens incidentally documented in the past (beta thalassaemia minor). He is not on glucocorticoids and has had no transfusions or recent illness. A fasting venous plasma glucose taken in a NATA-accredited laboratory two weeks ago was 7.3 mmol/L; today's laboratory HbA1c is 50 mmol/mol (6.7 percent); a random venous glucose today is 9.4 mmol/L. He has acanthosis nigricans and is otherwise well, with no polyuria, weight loss, or vomiting.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/84 mmHg, HR 78 bpm, BMI 31 kg/m^2.
data_table.Examination: Acanthosis nigricans over the posterior neck. No ketotic breath. Hydrated.
data_table.Investigations: Fasting venous glucose 7.3 mmol/L (two weeks ago, NATA lab); HbA1c 50 mmol/mol (6.7 percent) today, standardised assay; random glucose 9.4 mmol/L today; eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73m^2; ACR 1.2 mg/mmol.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step to establish or refute the diagnosis of type 2 diabetes?

options.text: Diagnose type 2 diabetes now on the basis of HbA1c 50 mmol/mol plus fasting glucose 7.3 mmol/L and commence metformin
Repeat the fasting venous plasma glucose in a NATA-accredited laboratory on a separate day to confirm fasting glucose at least 7.0 mmol/L
Discharge without diagnosis because the random glucose of 9.4 mmol/L is below 11.1 mmol/L
Order fructosamine as the primary diagnostic test since HbA1c is unreliable in haemoglobinopathy
Order an oral glucose tolerance test with 2-hour glucose at 75 g load, but commence metformin today regardless of result

stem:
A 64-year-old man with type 2 diabetes for 9 years attends his GP for diabetes review. He is on metformin XR 2 g daily and has been adherent for 18 months. He has heart failure with reduced ejection fraction (LVEF 35 percent) on echocardiography after an anterior STEMI two years ago, treated with stented LAD, and is on perindopril 8 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg and aspirin 100 mg.

He has chronic kidney disease with eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m^2 and ACR 6.4 mg/mmol on two occasions. He has no symptoms of urinary tract infection, no recurrent thrush and no history of diabetic foot ulceration. BMI is 29 kg/m^2 and he is normotensive. His most recent HbA1c is 62 mmol/mol (7.8 percent), up from 56 mmol/mol six months ago. He denies hypoglycaemic episodes and is keen to optimise his cardiovascular and renal protection in addition to glycaemic control.

He has no history of pancreatitis and no personal or family history of medullary thyroid carcinoma or MEN2. He has never had a diabetic foot ulcer, retinal laser or amputation. He is on no NSAID, no potassium-sparing diuretic and has no documented contrast allergy. He fully understands sick-day rules and is independently mobile, performs his own injections if needed and has reliable transport for monitoring bloods.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/72 mmHg, HR 64 bpm.
data_table.Examination: JVP not elevated. Chest clear. No peripheral oedema. Feet warm, pulses present, monofilament intact.
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 62 mmol/mol (7.8 percent); eGFR 48 mL/min/1.73m^2; ACR 6.4 mg/mmol; potassium 4.2 mmol/L; LFTs normal; LVEF 35 percent.
data_table.Medications: Metformin XR 2 g, perindopril 8 mg, bisoprolol 5 mg, atorvastatin 80 mg, aspirin 100 mg.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in pharmacological management?

options.text: Add a sulfonylurea such as gliclazide MR 30 mg daily
Add an SGLT2 inhibitor such as empagliflozin 10 mg daily
Add basal insulin glargine starting 10 units nocte
Add a DPP4 inhibitor such as sitagliptin 100 mg daily
Add pioglitazone 15 mg daily for insulin sensitisation

stem:
A 71-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes for 14 years attends her GP. She is on metformin XR 2 g, empagliflozin 25 mg and dulaglutide 1.5 mg weekly. She has tolerated triple therapy for 18 months without hypoglycaemia, weight loss has plateaued and her HbA1c has risen from 58 to 76 mmol/mol (9.1 percent) over the last six months. She has no acute illness, drinks no alcohol and lives independently with her husband who can assist with injections.

She is willing to start insulin but anxious about night-time hypoglycaemia. Her eGFR is 62 mL/min/1.73m^2, weight 78 kg, and she has retinopathy on annual review. Fasting capillary glucose self-monitoring shows readings of 11 to 14 mmol/L; pre-dinner readings are 8 to 10 mmol/L. There is no significant post-prandial glucose excursion documented. She drives a private car only and her vision is corrected to 6/9. She is up to date with her sick-day plan for the SGLT2 inhibitor.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 134/78 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, weight 78 kg.
data_table.Examination: Unremarkable. No injection sites yet.
data_table.Investigations: HbA1c 76 mmol/mol (9.1 percent); eGFR 62; fasting capillary glucose 11 to 14 mmol/L; pre-dinner 8 to 10 mmol/L.
data_table.Medications: Metformin XR 2 g, empagliflozin 25 mg, dulaglutide 1.5 mg weekly.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate insulin regimen to commence?

options.text: Premixed biphasic insulin (e.g. NovoMix 30) twice daily before breakfast and dinner
Basal-bolus regimen with insulin glargine nocte and rapid-acting insulin with each meal
Long-acting basal insulin glargine 10 units nocte titrated by 2 units every 3 days
Twice-daily NPH insulin in equal split doses administered each morning and again each night
Prandial-only rapid-acting insulin aspart given with only the largest carbohydrate meal of the day

stem:
An 18-year-old woman with newly diagnosed type 1 diabetes is admitted to a regional ED with severe DKA. Capillary glucose is 38 mmol/L, ketones 6.4 mmol/L, venous pH 6.98, HCO3 5 mmol/L, sodium 128 mmol/L, potassium 3.6 mmol/L, urea 11 mmol/L, creatinine 132 micromol/L. She received 2 L of 0.9 percent saline over the first hour for shock, followed by 0.9 percent saline at 500 mL/hour and a fixed-rate insulin infusion at 0.1 units/kg/hour.

Five hours into treatment, blood glucose has fallen to 12 mmol/L and bicarbonate has risen to 11 mmol/L, but she develops a worsening frontal headache, increasing drowsiness with a GCS drop from 15 to 11, a single episode of vomiting and a slowing heart rate. Her blood pressure has risen from 102/64 to 142/86 mmHg. Capillary glucose is now 11 mmol/L and ketones 2.4 mmol/L. The receiving consultant is concerned about a deteriorating neurological picture. A bedside neurological exam reveals sluggish pupils and brisk lower limb reflexes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/86 mmHg (up from 102/64), HR 58 bpm (down from 118), RR 18, SpO2 99 percent, T 36.6, GCS 11 (E3 V3 M5).
data_table.Examination: Drowsy. Sluggish pupillary response, no focal weakness. Brisk LL reflexes.
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 11 mmol/L (was 38); ketones 2.4; pH 7.18, HCO3 11; Na 130, K 3.8.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step?

options.text: Increase the IV fluid infusion rate to correct the remaining estimated deficit much faster
IV mannitol over 20 minutes, reduce fluids, nurse head up, then CT and ICU review
Stop the IV insulin infusion entirely and simply observe her for any spontaneous improvement
Give IV 50 percent dextrose 50 mL because the cause of drowsiness is hypoglycaemia
Administer IV ceftriaxone 2 g and dexamethasone 10 mg for presumed bacterial meningitis

stem:
A 78-year-old man with type 2 diabetes is brought from his nursing home with one week of progressive confusion and reduced oral intake. He has hypertension, chronic kidney disease and a recent UTI treated with trimethoprim. His regular medications include metformin 500 mg BD, gliclazide MR 60 mg and lisinopril 10 mg. Staff report he has been refusing to drink for the last two days.

On arrival he is drowsy, severely dehydrated and has a temperature of 38.4 degrees. Capillary glucose is 48 mmol/L. Venous gas shows pH 7.34, bicarbonate 20 mmol/L, anion gap 14, lactate 1.8. Capillary ketones are 0.6 mmol/L. Sodium 152 mmol/L, potassium 4.1, urea 24, creatinine 198 micromol/L (baseline 110), corrected sodium for glucose 158 mmol/L. Calculated effective serum osmolality is 348 mosm/kg. Urinalysis confirms leucocytes and nitrites; he is on no SGLT2 inhibitor. There are no Kussmaul respirations and no ketotic breath.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/56 mmHg, HR 112, RR 18, T 38.4, SpO2 96 percent on RA, GCS 13.
data_table.Examination: Severely dehydrated, dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 4 seconds. No Kussmaul breathing.
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 48 mmol/L; ketones 0.6 mmol/L; pH 7.34, HCO3 20, AG 14; Na 152, K 4.1, Cr 198 (baseline 110); effective osmolality 348 mosm/kg.

lead_in: Which feature best distinguishes this presentation as hyperosmolar hyperglycaemic state (HHS) rather than DKA?

options.text: The blood glucose level of 48 mmol/L on bedside capillary testing today
Effective osmolality above 320, capillary ketones under 3 and pH above 7.30 without acidosis
The acute kidney injury with creatinine rising from baseline 110 to 198 micromol/L
The presence of a urinary tract infection acting as the precipitating event here
The reduced Glasgow Coma Scale score on arrival to the emergency department

stem:
A 74-year-old woman with T2DM on metformin 1 g BD, gliclazide MR 120 mg daily and insulin glargine 22 units nocte is brought to ED by paramedics after her daughter found her diaphoretic and confused. Capillary glucose was 1.8 mmol/L pre-hospital. She received IM glucagon 1 mg followed by oral juice with rapid clinical improvement; her glucose now is 6.4 mmol/L and she is fully oriented.

Over the last week she has reported anorexia, fatigue and unintentional weight loss of 2 kg. She started cefalexin five days ago for a urinary tract infection and the same day her GP added trimethoprim 300 mg daily after sensitivities returned. She has CKD stage 3b (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m^2 baseline). She lives alone and reports occasional missed meals. Her last HbA1c three months ago was 49 mmol/mol (6.6 percent). She has no chest pain. ECG shows sinus rhythm rate 78 with no acute ischaemic changes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/72 mmHg, HR 78, T 36.6, SpO2 98 percent, GCS 15.
data_table.Examination: Now alert and oriented. No focal neurology. Mild dry mucous membranes.
data_table.Investigations: Glucose now 6.4 mmol/L; eGFR 38; HbA1c 49 mmol/mol; UEC otherwise normal.

lead_in: Which factor is most likely to have precipitated this hypoglycaemic episode?

options.text: The basal insulin glargine dose, which should be reduced as the default first action
Trimethoprim potentiating gliclazide via reduced clearance in CKD plus the reduced oral intake
Direct metformin-induced hypoglycaemia from her usual twice-daily 1 g metformin dose
Cefalexin-induced hypoglycaemia from the recently started urinary tract infection antibiotic
Inadequate paramedic glucagon dose given prior to her arrival in the emergency department

stem:
A 38-year-old woman is brought to ED with two days of worsening agitation, vomiting and fever after stopping carbimazole 10 days ago because she ran out of her script. She was diagnosed with Graves disease six months ago. On arrival she is agitated, sweaty and tremulous. She is in atrial fibrillation at 152 bpm with a blood pressure of 96/52 mmHg.

Temperature is 39.6 degrees and she has had one episode of vomiting in ED. She has bilateral exophthalmos and a smooth diffuse goitre. Her last TSH four weeks ago was <0.01 mIU/L with free T4 48 pmol/L. She is alert but confused (GCS 14) and not following commands consistently. There is no chest pain. Bedside echo at the bedside shows preserved LV function.

Capillary glucose is 7.2 mmol/L. She has no recent travel, no respiratory symptoms and clear chest on auscultation. Beta-hCG is negative. CRP is 18 mg/L and white cell count is 11.2 x10^9/L without left shift. There is no rash and no neck stiffness. The endocrinology registrar has been called. She has no documented allergy to iodine, propranolol, propylthiouracil, carbimazole or hydrocortisone.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/52 mmHg, HR 152 (AF), RR 28, T 39.6 degC, SpO2 97 percent, GCS 14.
data_table.Examination: Agitated, tremulous, diaphoretic. Lid lag, exophthalmos, smooth goitre with bruit. Warm peripheries.
data_table.Investigations: TSH <0.01, fT4 48 (4 weeks ago); ECG AF rate 152; CXR clear; CRP 18; WCC 11.2; LFTs mildly deranged ALT 78.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate initial medical management?

options.text: IV propranolol, oral propylthiouracil, Lugol's iodine after PTU, hydrocortisone, paracetamol and active cooling
IV amiodarone 300 mg for prompt rate control of her new atrial fibrillation
Empirical IV ceftriaxone 2 g and aciclovir for presumed sepsis or encephalitis
IV levothyroxine 200 microgram and IV hydrocortisone 100 mg for presumed myxoedema coma
Oral carbimazole 60 mg single dose only and immediate discharge home with outpatient endocrinology follow-up

stem:
A 34-year-old woman is referred by her GP for definitive management of Graves disease diagnosed 14 months ago. She was treated with carbimazole 20 mg daily for 12 months, achieving biochemical euthyroidism, but TSH-receptor antibody titres remain markedly elevated (TRAb 8 IU/L) and she relapsed within six weeks of stopping carbimazole. She has moderate active Graves orbitopathy with proptosis, mild diplopia on upgaze and intermittent retro-orbital pain; CAS (Clinical Activity Score) is 4/7.

She has not yet completed her family and would like to conceive within the next 12 months. She is a non-smoker now (ex-smoker, ceased six months ago). Her thyroid is moderately enlarged without nodularity, and ultrasound shows no discrete nodules. She has no compressive symptoms.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 88, weight 62 kg.
data_table.Examination: Diffuse smooth goitre, no nodules, no compressive symptoms. Proptosis with diplopia on upgaze, CAS 4/7.
data_table.Investigations: TSH 1.2 mIU/L, fT4 14 pmol/L on carbimazole 20 mg; TRAb 8 IU/L (relapsed off treatment); thyroid US no nodules.
data_table.Medications: Carbimazole 20 mg daily.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate definitive treatment option?

options.text: Radioactive iodine 131I ablation arranged within the next month as definitive therapy
Total thyroidectomy after pre-operative carbimazole and Lugol's iodine plus calcium and vitamin D loading
Indefinite low-dose carbimazole 5 mg once daily as long-term outpatient monotherapy
Switch to propylthiouracil 100 mg three times daily continued indefinitely for ongoing control
High-dose IV methylprednisolone 500 mg weekly for 6 weeks given alone as definitive treatment

stem: A 32-year-old woman attends her GP for preconception counselling. She is planning pregnancy in the next 3 months. Blood tests ordered 8 weeks ago showed TSH 5.6 mIU/L with normal free T4. A repeat panel today shows TSH 5.4 mIU/L, free T4 13 pmol/L (normal), and TPO antibodies markedly elevated at 540 IU/mL. She has no goitre, no compressive symptoms, and no other thyroid history. She has hypercholesterolaemia on atorvastatin and is otherwise well. She has no constipation or weight change.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/76, HR 68, weight 72 kg.
data_table.Examination: No goitre. No dry skin. Reflexes normal.
data_table.Investigations: TSH 6.8 mIU/L (was 7.2); fT4 14 pmol/L; TPO Ab 540 IU/mL (positive); lipids stable.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence levothyroxine to target a pre-conception TSH below 2.5 mIU/L and review TFTs in 6 to 8 weeks
Repeat TFTs and TPO antibodies in 6 to 12 months with no treatment now and advise contraception until reassessed
Stop atorvastatin and recheck thyroid function in 6 weeks since statin may interfere with the TSH assay
Refer for ultrasound-guided fine needle aspiration of the thyroid for cytology
Commence T3 (liothyronine) 20 microgram daily as primary thyroid replacement

stem:
A 52-year-old woman is reviewed on the surgical ward 14 hours after total thyroidectomy for a multinodular goitre with compressive symptoms. She reports peri-oral and finger tingling for the last hour and one episode of carpal spasm when the cuff was inflated. She is otherwise well, with no airway compromise and no haematoma at the wound. She is on regular paracetamol and prophylactic enoxaparin.

Bloods drawn at the onset of symptoms show: corrected calcium 1.78 mmol/L (corrected for albumin 38 g/L), ionised calcium 0.92 mmol/L, magnesium 0.74 mmol/L, phosphate 1.6 mmol/L, parathyroid hormone 0.4 pmol/L (low), 25-OH vitamin D 64 nmol/L, potassium 4.1, creatinine 76. Her ECG shows a prolonged QTc of 510 ms. She has no history of renal stones, no malignancy and her pre-operative calcium was 2.34 mmol/L. She is alert with GCS 15. There is no respiratory distress.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 128/78 mmHg, HR 84, RR 16, SpO2 98 percent on RA, T 36.7.
data_table.Examination: Peri-oral and finger paraesthesiae. Positive Chvostek and Trousseau signs. No stridor. Wound dry.
data_table.Investigations: Corrected Ca 1.78 mmol/L, ionised Ca 0.92; Mg 0.74; PTH 0.4 pmol/L; ECG QTc 510 ms.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Oral calcium carbonate 1.5 g elemental calcium with calcitriol 0.5 microgram and clinical review in 4 hours
IV 10 percent calcium gluconate 10 mL bolus followed by infusion, replace magnesium, then oral calcium plus calcitriol
IV 10 percent calcium chloride 10 mL given via a peripheral cannula stat dose
IV magnesium sulfate 10 mmol over 20 minutes given as the only acute therapy
IV cinacalcet 30 mg given as a single calcimimetic dose for acute symptom control

stem:
A 52-year-old man is on day 7 of his admission to neurosurgery after a Hunt-Hess 3 aneurysmal subarachnoid haemorrhage clipped on day 1. On the morning ward round his nurse reports increased confusion and lethargy. His urine output over the last 24 hours has been 4.2 L. He has been on free water orally without IV fluids since day 4.

Bloods today: sodium 122 mmol/L (was 134 on day 4), potassium 3.6, urea 9.4 mmol/L, creatinine 96 micromol/L, serum osmolality 258 mosm/kg, glucose 5.4 mmol/L. Urine: sodium 95 mmol/L, osmolality 540 mosm/kg, specific gravity 1.022. Clinically he has dry mucous membranes, BP 102/64 mmHg (was 128/74 yesterday) lying with a 14 mmHg systolic drop on standing, HR 96, normal JVP and no oedema. Bedside lung ultrasound shows A-lines bilaterally. Weight is down 2 kg from admission.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 102/64 lying with 14 mmHg systolic postural drop, HR 96, T 36.7, SpO2 98 percent.
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, JVP not visible, no oedema, weight down 2 kg.
data_table.Investigations: Na 122 mmol/L (was 134), K 3.6, urea 9.4, Cr 96, serum osm 258; urine Na 95, urine osm 540; UO 4.2 L/24h.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial fluid management?

options.text: Fluid restriction to 800 mL per day with daily sodium monitoring on the ward
IV 0.9% sodium chloride 125 mL/hour with oral salt, escalating to 3% saline if sodium fails to rise
Oral tolvaptan 15 mg given today with hourly sodium monitoring on the ward
IV 3 percent hypertonic saline 150 mL bolus over 10 minutes only, with no further fluid
IV 5 percent dextrose at 100 mL/hour to reduce osmotic stress on the brain

subtopic_detail: SIADH vs cerebral salt wasting after SAH

stem:
A 68-year-old right-handed man is brought to a metropolitan ED by ambulance. He was last seen well at 0815 by his wife; she returned at 1005 to find him slumped on the kitchen floor with right-sided weakness and aphasia. Time of arrival is 1110 (2 hours 55 minutes after last seen well). He has hypertension, ischaemic heart disease, atrial fibrillation (CHA2DS2-VA 4) on apixaban 5 mg BD with his last dose at 0700.

He has no history of recent surgery, head injury, bleeding or stroke. On arrival his blood pressure is 198/112 mmHg, glucose 6.8 mmol/L, GCS 12 (E3 V3 M6) and NIHSS is 18 (gaze preference, right hemiplegia, global aphasia, left neglect). Non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage and an ASPECTS of 8 in the left MCA territory. CT angiography demonstrates a proximal left M1 occlusion with reasonable collaterals. There is a comprehensive stroke centre with thrombectomy capability 15 minutes away by road.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 198/112, HR 92 (AF), T 36.8, SpO2 97 percent on RA, GCS 12.
data_table.Examination: Right hemiplegia, global aphasia, left gaze preference. NIHSS 18.
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 6.8 mmol/L; INR not on warfarin; apixaban 5 mg BD with last dose 0700; CT brain no haemorrhage, ASPECTS 8; CTA proximal M1 occlusion.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate next step in acute reperfusion management?

options.text: Administer IV alteplase immediately and then transfer for mechanical thrombectomy at the comprehensive stroke centre
Lower BP to under 140/90 mmHg with IV labetalol before making any reperfusion decision
Activate stroke team and arrange urgent transfer for thrombectomy without thrombolysis, BP <185/110
Administer aspirin 300 mg orally and admit to the stroke unit for conservative management
Administer IV idarucizumab to reverse apixaban first, then proceed to IV thrombolysis with alteplase

stem: A 72-year-old woman attends her GP three hours after an episode of left arm and face weakness lasting 35 minutes, now completely resolved. She has hypertension on amlodipine, T2DM on metformin, current smoker (20 pack-years), and no prior atrial fibrillation. Examination is now normal. BP today 168/96, blood glucose 9.2, ECG sinus rhythm, no carotid bruit. She has no anticoagulation, no bleeding tendency, and no recent head injury.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 168/96, HR 78, weight 76 kg.
data_table.Examination: Normal neurological examination now. No carotid bruit. ECG sinus rhythm.
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 9.2 mmol/L.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate combination of management steps?

options.text: Same-day ED transfer for non-contrast CT brain and CT angiography of head and neck, load with aspirin 300 mg now, and arrange admission to a stroke unit with cardiac monitoring
Calculate ABCD2 and refer urgently only if 4 or more; otherwise manage in primary care with aspirin and review in 1 week
Reassure and arrange outpatient specialist clinic review in 2 weeks with aspirin 100 mg daily today
Commence rivaroxaban 20 mg daily empirically for presumed paroxysmal AF and arrange outpatient Holter monitor
Arrange a carotid Doppler within the next 4 weeks and review her again after the result is back

stem:
A 34-year-old man is brought to ED by his partner after a witnessed generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds while watching television. He has no prior seizures, no head injuryo medications. He was confused for about 20 minutes after the event and bit the side of his tongue. On arrival he is back to his baseline. Capillary glucose, electrolytes, calcium, magnesium and a urine drug screen are normal.

ECG is normal sinus rhythm. He works as a self-employed delivery driver using a standard private licence (no commercial endorsement). His non-contrast CT brain is normal. He wants to know when he can drive and what investigations are needed. He has no fever, no headacherology. He has no family history of epilepsy and no recent travel. He is otherwise well and has not started any new medications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78, HR 76, T 36.8, SpO2 99 percent, GCS 15.
data_table.Examination: Normal neurology. Lateral tongue bite. No focal weakness.
data_table.Investigations: Glucose normal; electrolytes, Ca, Mg, drug screen all normal; CT brain normal; ECG normal.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate combination of next investigation and driving advice?

options.text: MRI brain and EEG as outpatient; no driving for at least 6 months (Austroads private standard)
Commence sodium valproate immediately and clear him to return to driving in 1 month
Lumbar puncture today and start IV ceftriaxone for presumed bacterial meningitis empirically
Continuous video-EEG admission for 72 hours starting today as the immediate next investigation
Cleared to return to commercial driving as soon as he feels well, neurology in 6 weeks

stem:
A 56-year-old man with known epilepsy on sodium valproate is brought to ED in convulsive status epilepticus. The seizure started 25 minutes ago in the ambulance. Paramedics gave 10 mg IM midazolam at 12 minutes and another 10 mg IV at 20 minutes without resolution; he continues to have generalised tonic-clonic activity. On arrival his airway is maintained with nasopharyngeal airway and SpO2 96 percent on 15 L non-rebreather.

BP is 156/92, HR 124, temperature 37.1. Capillary glucose is 7.4 mmol/L. He has IV access and is now 27 minutes into the seizure. He has no recent head injury and his valproate level is pending. There is no fever, no rash, and no obvious focal sepsis. His airway position is maintained and there is no audible stridor. His pupils are equal and reactive. Bedside ECG shows sinus tachycardia without ischaemic changes.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 156/92, HR 124, RR 18 (assisted), T 37.1, SpO2 96 percent on 15 L NRB, GCS 3 during seizure.
data_table.Examination: Generalised tonic-clonic seizure continuing. Airway maintained with NPA.
data_table.Investigations: Glucose 7.4 mmol/L; valproate level pending; ECG sinus tachycardia.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Repeat a further IV midazolam 10 mg bolus dose as third benzodiazepine attempt
IV levetiracetam 60 mg/kg (maximum 4.5 g) given over 10 minutes as second-line agent
IV propofol 2 mg/kg induction and intubate without any further antiepileptic drug given
Oral phenytoin 300 mg administered via nasogastric tube as the next antiepileptic agent
IV thiamine 200 mg and 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose given as the next intervention

stem:
A 74-year-old woman presents to her GP with a three-week history of new bilateral temporal headache progressively worsening, with scalp tenderness on hair brushing and jaw pain with chewing tough food. Yesterday she had a 10-minute episode of curtain-like vision loss in her right eye that has now resolved. Today on examination her right eye visual acuity is 6/9 (was 6/6 four months ago at optometry) with a relative afferent pupillary defect; left eye 6/6.

Temporal arteries tender and pulsatile bilaterally. Bloods: ESR 92 mm/hr, CRP 84 mg/L, Hb 108 g/L, platelets 484. She has hypertension on perindopril and T2DM on metformin (HbA1c 58 mmol/mol). Bone mineral density was T-score -1.4 at the lumbar spine 6 months ago.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/82, HR 72, T 36.9, SpO2 98 percent.
data_table.Examination: Tender pulsatile bilateral temporal arteries. Normal fundoscopy. VA 6/9 R, 6/6 L.
data_table.Investigations: ESR 92, CRP 84, Hb 108 (NCNC), platelets 484.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Admit for IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days followed by oral prednisolone 60 mg daily, with same-day ophthalmology and rheumatology review and arrangement of temporal artery biopsy within 1 to 2 weeks

Commence oral prednisolone 60 mg daily today, arrange same-day ophthalmology and rheumatology review, and book temporal artery biopsy within 1 to 2 weeks, with bone-protection planning at the next GP visit
Order urgent CT brain today, defer prednisolone until temporal artery biopsy returns positive within 2 weeks, and arrange same-day ophthalmology and rheumatology review for further workup
Commence tocilizumab 162 mg subcutaneously weekly as first-line steroid-sparing monotherapy, with same-day ophthalmology and rheumatology review and temporal artery biopsy within 1 to 2 weeks
Treat empirically as migraine with sumatriptan 50 mg orally, prescribe regular simple analgesia, and arrange outpatient neurology follow-up within 2 weeks for further headache workup

stem:
A 28-year-old woman is brought to ED 25 minutes after eating a peanut-containing dessert. She has a known peanut allergy. On arrival: stridor and dyspnoea, widespread urticaria and lip swelling, BP 78/42, HR 132, SpO2 91 percent on 15 L non-rebreather, RR 28, alert but distressed. You give IM adrenaline 0.5 mg into the anterolateral mid-thigh and lie her supine with legs elevated.

Five minutes later, BP is 82/46, HR 130, RR 28, SpO2 92 percent, with persistent stridor. A second IM adrenaline 0.5 mg is given. Five minutes after that, BP is 84/48, HR 128, SpO2 92 percent, stridor persists. Two large-bore IVs are in. She has no past cardiac history and takes no regular medications.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 78/42, HR 132, RR 28, SpO2 91 percent on 15 L NRB, T 36.6, GCS 15.
data_table.Examination: Stridor, widespread urticaria, lip swelling, accessory muscle use.
data_table.Investigations: Bedside investigations pending.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence IV adrenaline infusion at 5 microgram per minute titrated to clinical response, give 20 mL/kg IV crystalloid bolus, and prepare for advanced airway management
Continue IM adrenaline 0.5 mg every 5 minutes indefinitely as the sole vasoactive agent, avoid IV adrenaline regardless of response, and continue resuscitation with crystalloid as tolerated
Give IV hydrocortisone 200 mg and IV promethazine 25 mg as the next escalation, continue IM adrenaline at current frequency, and observe for further response over 15 minutes
Give IV glucagon 1 to 5 mg bolus as the next escalation step, continue IM adrenaline at current frequency, and prepare for advanced airway management if no response
Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg and nebulised adrenaline 5 mg via oxygen-driven nebuliser as the next escalation, give 20 mL/kg IV crystalloid bolus, and reassess in 5 minutes

stem: An 82-year-old woman with osteoporosis (previous Colles fracture and L1 vertebral compression fracture) and mild cognitive impairment is reviewed at her general practice for medication review. She has been taking temazepam 20 mg nightly for 9 years for insomnia. She lives alone. Her gait is steady but she has fallen twice in the past 6 months getting up to the toilet at night. Her other medications are perindopril 5 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, denosumab 6-monthly, calcium 600 mg with colecalciferol 1000 IU daily.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, BP 132/78 lying, 118/72 standing (no symptoms).
data_table.Falls: Two falls in 6 months, both nocturnal.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next prescribing action?

options.text: Continue temazepam 20 mg nightly unchanged; prescribe hip protectors, arrange occupational therapy home falls assessment, and recommend a night-light to address fall risk
Switch to zopiclone 7.5 mg nightly as a safer Z-drug alternative, with sleep diary review and ongoing falls precautions at 6 weeks
Taper temazepam over 8 to 12 weeks (10 to 25% dose reduction every 1 to 2 weeks) and provide cognitive behavioural therapy for insomnia
Stop temazepam abruptly tonight with no taper and arrange weekly GP review for rebound insomnia, withdrawal anxiety and seizure risk over 4 weeks
Add melatonin prolonged-release 2 mg nightly and continue temazepam 20 mg nightly, with review of insomnia response at 4 weeks

stem: A 78-year-old woman is reviewed for ankle oedema. Her medications are amlodipine 10 mg daily (started 4 weeks ago for hypertension), perindopril 5 mg daily, atorvastatin 40 mg, metformin 1 g BD, and pantoprazole 40 mg daily. Her general practitioner is considering adding furosemide 20 mg for the oedema. Lower-limb examination shows symmetrical pitting oedema to mid-shin. JVP is not elevated. Heart sounds dual. Chest is clear. Renal function and serum albumin are normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 70, BP 124/78, SpO2 98% room air.
data_table.Examination: Symmetric pitting oedema to mid-shin. JVP normal. No crackles, no S3.
data_table.Investigations: eGFR 64, albumin 38 g/L, BNP 42 pg/mL.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next action?

options.text: Reduce or stop amlodipine and substitute another antihypertensive (e.g. up-titrate perindopril)
Add furosemide 20 mg daily as planned
Add compression stockings and continue all current medications
Investigate for cardiac failure with echocardiogram
Increase amlodipine to control BP further

stem: An 81-year-old man with Parkinson disease and benign prostatic hyperplasia presents with new urinary retention, confusion (Mini-Mental State Examination dropped from 26 to 19), constipation, and dry mouth over 2 weeks. Medications introduced in the last month include oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily for urge incontinence, amitriptyline 25 mg nocte for neuropathic pain, and promethazine 25 mg nocte for sleep, added by different prescribers. He continues levodopa-carbidopa and tamsulosin.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 96, BP 128/72 lying, 96/64 standing (symptomatic).
data_table.Examination: Confused, dry mucous membranes, palpable bladder, reduced bowel sounds.
data_table.New medications: Oxybutynin, amitriptyline, promethazine - all started in last month.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate intervention?

options.text: Stop all three new anticholinergic agents; review with substitutes that lack anticholinergic burden (e.g. mirabegron, gabapentin, melatonin)
Continue all medications and add donepezil to counter the cognitive decline
Catheterise for retention and continue all medications
Stop tamsulosin to address orthostasis only
Halve all three new doses without stopping any

stem: A 79-year-old woman presents to her general practitioner after three falls in 6 months. She has osteoarthritis of both knees, type 2 diabetes mellitus, and bilateral cataracts. Medications include metformin, gliclazide modified-release, perindopril, simvastatin and paracetamol. Visual acuity is 6/24 in both eyes. Timed up-and-go is 18 seconds. Lying blood pressure 138/78, standing 112/70 with mild dizziness. Vitamin D is 38 nmol/L (deficient). She is socially isolated and walks unaided indoors.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 70, lying BP 138/78, standing BP 112/70 with dizziness.
data_table.Examination: Visual acuity 6/24 bilateral, TUG 18 s, no neurological deficit.
data_table.Investigations: Vitamin D 38 nmol/L (deficient), HbA1c 7.2%, eGFR 58.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-priority intervention?

options.text: Comprehensive multifactorial falls intervention including medication review with deprescribing of gliclazide if hypoglycaemia documented, vitamin D supplementation, vision optimisation referral, strength and balance exercise program, and home hazard assessment
Refer for hip protectors only as the sole intervention for falls prevention, without medication review, vitamin D replacement, vision optimisation, exercise prescription or home hazard assessment
Prescribe alendronate 70 mg orally weekly for fracture prevention without measuring bone mineral density, vitamin D status or addressing the immediate falls risk factors driving the recurrent falls

Start fludrocortisone 0.1 mg orally daily for orthostatic hypotension without first reviewing perindopril dose, hydration status, exercise tolerance, footwear, vision, or other reversible orthostatic contributors driving recurrent falls

Provide a four-wheeled walker in isolation without strength-and-balance exercise prescription, vision review, vitamin D replacement or medication review, on the basis that mobility support alone will prevent further falls indoors

stem: An 84-year-old man with Alzheimer disease (baseline MMSE 22, lives at home with wife) is brought to a metropolitan emergency department because of acute behavioural change over the last 24 hours. He is alternately drowsy and agitated, sees insects on the wall, does not recognise his wife who is usually familiar, and is incontinent of urine for the first time. Examination reveals warm flushed skin, suprapubic tenderness, and crackles at the right base. Urinalysis shows leucocytes ++, nitrites positive.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 108, BP 132/76, SpO2 92% room air, T 38.4 C, RR 22.
data_table.Examination: Fluctuating arousal, visual hallucinations, suprapubic tenderness, right basal crackles.

lead_in: Which feature best discriminates delirium from a stepwise dementia decline in this patient?

options.text: Acute onset over 24 hours with fluctuating attention and altered arousal
Visual hallucinations
Urinary incontinence
Reduced visuospatial function
Forgetting his wife's name

stem: A 78-year-old woman with post-operative hyperactive delirium on day 2 after right total hip replacement is shouting, attempting to pull out her IV, and trying to climb out of bed despite reorientation, presence of family, ambient lighting, and management of pain, constipation and retention. She has not slept overnight. She has no Parkinson disease. ECG QTc is 440 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 138/82, SpO2 96% room air, afebrile.
data_table.Background: Day 2 post right THR. Pain controlled (paracetamol + oxycodone PRN). No retention, normal bowels.
data_table.Non-pharm: Reorientation, family present, lighting, hearing aids - tried.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate pharmacological intervention?

options.text: Haloperidol 0.5 mg orally or intramuscular, repeated 2-hourly as needed to a maximum of 2 mg in 24 hours
Diazepam 5 mg orally with hourly nursing observation and a maximum of 10 mg in 24 hours
Olanzapine 10 mg intramuscular as a single stat dose with cardiac and respiratory observations
Quetiapine 100 mg orally nocte with continuation as a regular sedative for the duration of admission
Physical restraint with bedrails and limb restraints, without any sedating medication

subtopic_detail: Opioid conversion - morphine PO to subcutaneous
stem: A 72-year-old man with metastatic pancreatic cancer is taking oral sustained-release morphine 60 mg twice daily plus oral immediate-release morphine 10 mg for breakthrough (using 4 doses in 24 hours). He is now unable to swallow due to oral mucositis and needs conversion to a continuous subcutaneous infusion (CSCI) via syringe driver. He has stable pain on the current regimen.

data_table.Current regimen: MS Contin 60 mg PO BD + morphine IR 10 mg PRN x4 doses in 24 h.
data_table.Total 24 h oral morphine: 120 mg sustained + 40 mg breakthrough = 160 mg PO.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate 24-hour dose of subcutaneous morphine for the syringe driver, with breakthrough plan?

options.text: Morphine 80 mg subcutaneous over 24 hours via syringe driver; breakthrough morphine 10 to 15 mg subcutaneous 1-hourly as needed
Morphine 160 mg subcutaneous over 24 hours; breakthrough morphine 20 mg subcutaneous 4-hourly
Morphine 40 mg subcutaneous over 24 hours; breakthrough morphine 5 mg subcutaneous 4-hourly
Hydromorphone 4 mg subcutaneous over 24 hours; no breakthrough
Fentanyl patch 100 mcg/h with no breakthrough plan

subtopic_detail: Opioid rotation - morphine to hydromorphone in renal impairment
stem: A 68-year-old woman with metastatic ovarian cancer and chronic kidney disease stage 4 (eGFR 22) is on continuous subcutaneous morphine 40 mg over 24 hours. She has developed myoclonic jerks, generalised allodynia, and worsening confusion over 3 days. The palliative care team plans opioid rotation. Pain control was adequate prior to neurotoxicity.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 86, BP 124/74, SpO2 95% room air.
data_table.Examination: Myoclonic jerks at rest, allodynia (lightest touch painful), confused.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate opioid rotation choice and starting dose?

options.text: Hydromorphone subcutaneous, starting at 4 mg over 24 hours via syringe driver (with dose reduction for incomplete cross-tolerance), with appropriate breakthrough dosing
Increase the morphine continuous subcutaneous infusion to 60 mg over 24 hours to control the agitation and myoclonus in this opioid-naive scenario
Apply a fentanyl 25 microgram/h transdermal patch with no syringe driver, on the basis that fentanyl is renally safe and the patch provides analgesia within hours
Pethidine 25 mg subcutaneously every 4 hours as the new opioid for the rotation in this patient with CKD stage 4 and ongoing pain control needs
Codeine 60 mg orally four-hourly as the rotation choice, with paracetamol cover and reassessment at 24 hours for analgesic adequacy

stem: An 82-year-old man with end-stage chronic obstructive pulmonary disease is unconscious and recognised to be in the last 48 hours of life. He has audible upper-airway bubbling secretions causing his family distress. He is not in respiratory distress himself and is comfortable. He has a continuous subcutaneous infusion of morphine and midazolam running.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 92, BP 96/58, SpO2 88% room air, RR 14 unlaboured.
data_table.Examination: Unconscious, audible airway rattle, comfortable expression.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management?

options.text: Reposition (lateral or semi-prone), gentle oral suction if needed, explain to family that rattle does not distress the patient, and consider hyoscine butylbromide 20 mg subcutaneous if rattle persists and family find it distressing

Perform deep oropharyngeal and tracheal suctioning with a Yankauer catheter to clear the airway, every 1 to 2 hours regardless of distress to the patient or family, continuing throughout the dying phase as the primary intervention for the rattle

Arrange endotracheal intubation and transfer to the intensive care unit for mechanical ventilation to control the upper airway secretions and protect the airway in this dying patient, despite the previously documented goals of comfort care

Cease all parenteral fluids immediately, restrict any oral intake, and withhold subcutaneous medication infusions to dry up airway secretions and reduce the audible rattle at the bedside over the next few hours
Administer intravenous furosemide 40 mg as a stat dose to reduce upper airway secretions through diuresis and decongestion of the airway mucosa, with consideration of a follow-up dose 6 hours later

stem: A 75-year-old woman with end-stage metastatic colorectal cancer is in the last 48 hours of life on the palliative care ward. She develops restless picking at the bedclothes, calling out, and brief periods of agitation despite reorientation by her daughter. She has a continuous subcutaneous infusion of morphine 60 mg/24 h. There is no urinary retention, no constipation, no obvious pain trigger, and no signs of opioid neurotoxicity.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, BP 102/64, SpO2 92% room air, T 37.4 C, RR 18.
data_table.Reversibles checked: Bladder empty, bowel opened yesterday, opioid-rotation considered (no neurotoxic signs), no clear pain spike.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate pharmacological management?

options.text: Add midazolam 2.5 to 5 mg subcutaneous as needed, with consideration of continuous infusion 10 to 30 mg over 24 hours if recurrent
Increase the morphine continuous subcutaneous infusion from 60 mg to 120 mg over 24 hours and add a PRN breakthrough dose every hour
Administer haloperidol 10 mg subcutaneously as a stat dose, then repeat 2-hourly as needed for ongoing terminal agitation overnight
Apply soft wrist physical restraint to prevent self-harm from bedclothes-picking and to keep the subcutaneous line in place overnight
Provide verbal reassurance only with no pharmacological intervention, despite ongoing distress, and re-review on the daytime ward round

stem: A 70-year-old woman with end-stage idiopathic pulmonary fibrosis is at home with a community palliative care team. She is opioid-naive. She describes constant breathlessness at rest, worsening on minimal exertion, with significant distress. SpO2 is 91% on 4 L home oxygen. There is no infection, no PE, no heart failure exacerbation, and supplemental oxygen has been maximised. She has clear goals-of-care discussions documented as comfort-focused.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, RR 28, SpO2 91% on 4 L home O2, BP 124/76.
data_table.Examination: Bibasal velcro crackles, no fever, no oedema, no pleural rub.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate pharmacological intervention for the breathlessness?

options.text: Oral morphine immediate-release 2.5 mg 4-hourly as needed plus regular 4-hourly, with laxative cover and antiemetic available
Diazepam 5 mg orally regularly
Nebulised salbutamol 5 mg 6-hourly
Increase oxygen to 8 L via simple face mask
Furosemide 40 mg intravenous daily

stem: A 68-year-old man with metastatic lung cancer is being established on a continuous subcutaneous infusion via syringe driver. He has pain, agitation, nausea, and audible respiratory secretions. The community palliative care nurse asks which drugs can be safely combined in a single syringe with water for injection as diluent.
lead_in: Which is the most appropriate combination plan?

options.text: Morphine, midazolam, metoclopramide and hyoscine butylbromide combined in one syringe driver with water for injection; check compatibility chart and visual inspection for precipitation
Run two separate syringe drivers, one with opioid alone and one with everything else
Combine all four drugs but use 0.9% sodium chloride as the diluent
Add dexamethasone to the same syringe to manage anorexia
Bolus all four drugs subcutaneous PRN rather than continuous infusion

stem: An 81-year-old woman with permanent atrial fibrillation, hypertension, ischaemic heart disease (prior MI 5 years ago), and type 2 diabetes presents for medication review. Her medications are perindopril 5 mg, amlodipine 5 mg, metformin 1 g BD, and aspirin 100 mg daily. CHA2DS2-VASc is 6, HAS-BLED is 1. She has no contraindications to anticoagulation. eGFR is 58.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 76 irregular, BP 132/76.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate prescribing change based on START criteria?

options.text: Start apixaban 5 mg twice daily and cease aspirin
Continue aspirin alone and add clopidogrel for stroke prevention
Start aspirin plus warfarin (triple antithrombotic)
Reduce metformin dose without other changes
Stop perindopril given age >80

stem: An 86-year-old woman is referred for consideration of transcatheter aortic valve implantation for severe symptomatic aortic stenosis. She lives alone, walks 50 metres slowly before stopping, has unintentionally lost 4 kg over 6 months, says she feels exhausted most days, and reports decreased grip when opening jars. She avoids most physical activity. Clinical Frailty Scale is 6.

data_table.Background: Severe symptomatic AS being considered for TAVI.
data_table.Fried phenotype: Weight loss, exhaustion, weakness, slowness, low activity - meets 5/5.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Comprehensive geriatric assessment with multidisciplinary input prior to procedural decision, including prehabilitation if intervention proceeds
Proceed to TAVI based on aortic valve area and symptoms alone
Decline TAVI on age criterion alone
Refer for surgical aortic valve replacement instead
Watchful waiting until syncope or heart failure develops

stem: A 67-year-old woman with metastatic ovarian cancer and known peritoneal disease presents with 3 days of colicky abdominal pain, vomiting, and absolute constipation. CT abdomen shows multi-level small bowel obstruction with no transition point amenable to surgery. Surgical team has reviewed and considers her inoperable. She wants to maximise comfort. She has been able to tolerate sips.

data_table.Examination: Distended abdomen, tinkling bowel sounds, no peritonism.
data_table.Imaging: Multi-level SBO, peritoneal metastases, no surgical target.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate pharmacological management plan?

options.text: Continuous subcutaneous infusion of morphine (pain), haloperidol or metoclopramide (antiemetic - metoclopramide avoided if complete obstruction with colic), hyoscine butylbromide (antisecretory and antispasmodic), with consideration of octreotide if secretions persist; allow comfort sips orally

Nil by mouth with a nasogastric tube on free drainage and intravenous fluids alone, without combined opioid analgesia, antiemetic and antisecretory pharmacotherapy, accepting the associated discomfort from the tube and the lack of oral intake throughout the inoperable obstruction

Metoclopramide 10 mg intravenously four-hourly as the sole antiemetic for malignant bowel obstruction symptom control, on the basis that prokinetic action helps malignant bowel obstruction regardless of completeness or presence of colicky abdominal pain, with no opioid, antisecretory or antispasmodic agent added

Dexamethasone 8 mg orally daily as monotherapy for malignant bowel obstruction symptom control, without concurrent opioid analgesia, antiemetic, antisecretory or antispasmodic agent, on the basis of anti-inflammatory action around peritoneal tumour deposits and reduction of bowel-wall oedema

Oral stimulant and bulk-forming laxatives (senna 15 mg nocte, ispaghula husk 3.5 g twice daily) to relieve constipation and re-establish bowel motions in this patient with multi-level complete mechanical small bowel obstruction from peritoneal disease

stem: A 62-year-old man with metastatic prostate cancer involving the lumbar spine has back pain with radiation down the right leg in an L5 dermatomal distribution, with burning and electric shock quality. He is on oral sustained-release morphine 60 mg BD with breakthrough morphine, which controls the deep aching back pain but the radicular leg pain remains 7/10. MRI confirms epidural disease at L4-L5 without cord compression. He is receiving palliative radiotherapy.

data_table.Pain: Deep back pain 3/10 on opioid; radicular L5 burning electric 7/10.
data_table.Imaging: L4-L5 epidural metastases, no cord compression.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Add a gabapentinoid (gabapentin 100 mg three times daily titrated, or pregabalin 25-75 mg twice daily titrated) for the neuropathic component
Double the current sustained-release morphine dose, with breakthrough immediate-release morphine prescribed at one-sixth of the new total daily dose and laxatives continued
Add ibuprofen 400 mg three times daily for the inflammatory component of bony metastatic pain, with omeprazole 20 mg daily for gastric protection and renal review at 1 week
Add regular paracetamol 1 g four times daily only and continue current morphine, with a pain diary and follow-up review in 2 weeks for further analgesic escalation
Rotate to methadone monotherapy at an equianalgesic dose calculated by palliative care, ceasing morphine entirely and accepting a 5-day overlap with breakthrough immediate-release morphine

stem: A 76-year-old woman has been on pantoprazole 40 mg daily for 8 years, originally started during a hospital admission for gastroenteritis. She has no history of peptic ulcer, no NSAID use, no upper GI bleeding, no Barrett oesophagus, and no current reflux symptoms. She has osteoporosis with a recent T-score -2.7 at the femoral neck and one fall in the past year.

data_table.Indication review: No documented ongoing indication; started during gastroenteritis admission 8 years ago.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate deprescribing plan?

options.text: Step-down to pantoprazole 20 mg daily for 4 weeks, then alternate-day, then cease over 8 to 12 weeks; provide PRN antacid for rebound symptoms
Continue pantoprazole 40 mg daily indefinitely with annual GP medication review, on the basis that benefits outweigh harms in this elderly patient
Stop pantoprazole abruptly tonight with no step-down or PRN antacid, and review at 4 weeks for rebound symptoms
Switch pantoprazole to ranitidine 150 mg BD indefinitely as a safer long-term acid suppressant given her fracture risk
Increase to twice-daily pantoprazole 40 mg BD and add prophylactic calcium-vitamin D for bone density given her T-score -2.7
