stem: A 79-year-old man presents with recurrent presyncope and one collapse over the past month. Lying blood pressure is 142/82, standing at 1 minute 108/68 with reproduced symptoms. His medications are perindopril 10 mg, amlodipine 10 mg, indapamide 2.5 mg, tamsulosin 400 mcg, mirtazapine 30 mg nocte, and oxybutynin 5 mg twice daily.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 72, lying BP 142/82, standing BP 108/68 with symptoms.
data_table.Examination: No focal neurology, dry mucosae, JVP not elevated.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first management step?

options.text: Sequential withdrawal of contributing medications (start with tamsulosin and one antihypertensive) and non-pharmacological measures (slow positional change, salt and fluid liberalisation if no heart failure, compression)

Start fludrocortisone 0.1 mg orally daily for volume expansion without first reviewing or withdrawing the contributing antihypertensives, alpha-blocker, antidepressant or anticholinergic agents driving the orthostatic blood pressure drop and reproducible symptoms

Refer for head-up tilt-table testing as the first investigation, despite reproducible orthostatic blood pressure drop and reproduction of presyncope symptoms at the bedside with simple lying and standing blood pressure measurements

Refer for permanent pacemaker insertion to manage the presyncope and collapse episodes, despite the orthostatic blood pressure profile, absence of documented bradyarrhythmia, and absence of conduction-disease features on ECG

Increase indapamide from 2.5 mg to 5 mg orally daily for tighter blood pressure control despite the ongoing standing-BP drop, symptomatic orthostasis, dry mucous membranes and reproduced presyncope on standing at one minute

stem: A 64-year-old woman with metastatic glioblastoma multiforme is being treated at a tertiary centre in New South Wales. She raises voluntary assisted dying (VAD) with her treating oncologist. She has decision-making capacity, has been an Australian resident for over a year, has a prognosis of less than 6 months as documented by two specialists, and is suffering intolerably. She is currently able to communicate clearly. She is 64 years old.

data_table.Prognosis: Less than 6 months documented by two specialists.
data_table.Residency: Australian for >1 year, NSW for >12 months.

lead_in: Which is the single most accurate statement regarding her eligibility under NSW VAD legislation?

options.text: She is potentially eligible if she also meets the formal request process; the treating doctor may either accept the role of coordinating practitioner or refer her to another practitioner who is willing and trained
She is ineligible under the NSW VAD Act on the basis of being under 65 years of age, as the legislation restricts access to people aged 65 or older with terminal illness
She is ineligible because the NSW VAD Act explicitly excludes primary brain tumours including high-grade gliomas from the list of qualifying conditions for voluntary assisted dying
The treating oncologist is legally required to facilitate the VAD process even if they hold a conscientious objection, and cannot transfer this responsibility to another practitioner
Family members and the designated medical power of attorney may submit the formal VAD request on her behalf if she loses decision-making capacity during the assessment period

stem: An 82-year-old man with moderate dementia (MMSE 18) is admitted with a hip fracture requiring surgical fixation. The orthopaedic team asks whether he can consent to surgery. He can describe in his own words that his hip is broken, that surgery is being recommended to fix it, that without surgery he will not walk again and may die from complications, and that surgery carries risks of bleeding, infection, and worsening confusion. He says he wants the operation. His daughter has enduring guardianship.

data_table.Background: Moderate dementia, MMSE 18, lives with daughter who has enduring guardianship.
data_table.Capacity discussion: Patient describes condition, treatment, alternatives, risks; consistent choice.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step regarding consent?

options.text: Accept his consent for the surgery; he demonstrates decision-specific capacity (understands, retains, weighs the information, and communicates a choice) despite the dementia diagnosis
Defer to his daughter as enduring guardian because of the dementia diagnosis
Apply to the Guardianship Tribunal for a one-off consent order
Use MMSE score alone to determine capacity (MMSE >24 = capacity)
Document the patient as lacking capacity due to dementia and proceed under best-interests provisions

subtopic_detail: Postmenopausal IDA mandates upper and lower GI endoscopy
stem:
A 64-year-old postmenopausal woman attends her GP with three months of progressive fatigue and exertional dyspnoea climbing two flights of stairs. She has no overt PR bleeding, no melaena and no haematemesis but notes mild epigastric discomfort relieved by food. She takes ibuprofen 400 mg PRN for osteoarthritis (about three times per week) and is otherwise well. She has never had a colonoscopy.

Her father died of colorectal cancer at 67. She does not drink alcohol and has never smoked. Her diet includes red meat twice weekly. There is no overt haemorrhage source on history. Examination shows conjunctival pallor without jaundice or lymphadenopathy. Abdomen is soft with mild epigastric tenderness, no masses, PR exam reveals no haemorrhoids and the stool sample sent for FOBT is positive. Coeliac serology is pending. She has not had bariatric surgery and is not vegetarian. She wants to know what investigation is most appropriate now.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/74 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, RR 16, SpO2 98% on room air, T 36.7 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival pallor, koilonychia, no lymphadenopathy, abdomen soft with mild epigastric tenderness, PR no masses, FOBT positive.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 86 g/L, MCV 71 fL, MCH 23 pg, ferritin 6 micrograms/L, transferrin saturation 8%, CRP 4 mg/L, eGFR 78 mL/min/1.73m^2, coeliac serology pending.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Capsule endoscopy of the small bowel
Oral ferrous sulfate trial and reassess Hb in three months
CT colonography as first-line in place of colonoscopy
Repeat FBC and ferritin in 6 weeks before any endoscopic referral
Bidirectional upper and lower GI endoscopy at the same session

subtopic_detail: Subacute combined degeneration - parenteral B12 indicated
stem:
A 72-year-old woman presents with six months of progressive fatigue and three months of paraesthesiae in both feet that have ascended to mid-calf. She reports unsteadiness in the dark and a recent fall when reaching for an upper shelf. She has type 1 diabetes for 20 years on basal-bolus insulin, autoimmune hypothyroidism on levothyroxine 75 micrograms and takes metformin 1 g BD for adjunctive insulin resistance.

She has been on long-term proton pump inhibitor for reflux. She does not drink alcohol and is not vegan. She has had no bariatric surgery. On examination she has a beefy red tongue, brisk knee jerks but absent ankle jerks, impaired joint position and vibration sense to the mid-shins and a positive Romberg. There is no anaemic murmur. The GP requests urgent bloods. The MMSE is 28/30 with reduced recall. She is independently mobile with a four-wheel walker she has been using for the last month.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, T 36.6 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Beefy red tongue, glossitis, conjunctival pallor; absent ankle jerks, brisk knee jerks, reduced JPS and vibration to mid-shins, positive Romberg; no peripheral neuropathy of stocking distribution beyond mid-calf.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, MCV 114 fL, WCC 4.2, platelets 142, hypersegmented neutrophils on blood film, serum B12 78 pmol/L (RR >150), red cell folate 480 nmol/L, TSH 2.4, ferritin 145, LDH elevated, anti-intrinsic factor antibody positive.
data_table.Medications: Insulin glargine + aspart, metformin 1 g BD, levothyroxine 75 mcg, esomeprazole 20 mg.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Oral cyanocobalamin 1000 micrograms daily indefinitely and review symptoms in clinic in 4 weeks
Hydroxocobalamin 1 mg IM on alternate days until improvement plateaus, then 1 mg every 2 months
Start oral folic acid 5 mg daily while awaiting the Schilling test or holotranscobalamin level
Cease the metformin and recheck the B12 level at routine follow-up in 3 months
Transfuse 2 units of packed red cells today given the new neurological symptoms and anaemia

stem:
A 68-year-old woman with seropositive rheumatoid arthritis on methotrexate 20 mg weekly and prednisolone 5 mg daily presents with worsening fatigue. She had a flare two months ago managed with a prednisolone pulse. She has no overt bleeding, no melaena, no menstruation since age 52 and a normal colonoscopy three years ago. She has no chronic kidney disease (eGFR 76) and no malignancy.

Her appetite is preserved and BMI is 26 kg/m^2. She takes paracetamol regularly and avoids NSAIDs because of methotrexate. She has no overt source of blood loss. On examination she has active synovitis of MCPs and wrists with mild conjunctival pallor and no organomegaly. There is no telangiectasia and no hepatomegaly. She lives independently and is a retired nurse. Her ESR is 78 mm/h and CRP 42 mg/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 126/78 mmHg, HR 84 bpm.
data_table.Examination: Active synovitis MCPs/wrists, conjunctival pallor, no hepatosplenomegaly or lymphadenopathy.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 98 g/L, MCV 84 fL (normocytic), ferritin 142 micrograms/L, transferrin saturation 12%, serum iron 6 micromol/L (RR 10-30), TIBC 38 micromol/L, CRP 42 mg/L, ESR 78, soluble transferrin receptor elevated, reticulocyte index low, B12 and folate normal.

lead_in: Which result pattern most strongly indicates that iron deficiency is contributing in addition to anaemia of chronic disease?

options.text: Normocytic indices with ferritin 142 micrograms/L in isolation
Low serum iron with normal TIBC and elevated ESR
Hb 98 g/L with active synovitis, suggesting any anaemia in this context must be iron deficiency
Transferrin saturation 12% AND elevated soluble transferrin receptor
MCV 84 fL and low reticulocyte index

stem:
A 58-year-old woman with well-controlled SLE on hydroxychloroquine presents with 10 days of fatigue, exertional dyspnoea and dark urine, with mild scleral icterus for 3 days. She has no fever, weight loss or recent infections, has not started any new medications, and has never been transfused. Examination: pallor, scleral icterus, 2 cm spleen tip, no lymphadenopathy, no acrocyanosis. Bloods: Hb 62 g/L, MCV 102, reticulocytes 11 percent, LDH 920 U/L, haptoglobin under 0.1, unconjugated bilirubin 64 micromol/L, DAT IgG strongly positive and C3d weakly positive, blood film spherocytes and polychromasia, cold agglutinin titre negative.

She is haemodynamically stable but has new exertional angina on transferring to the bed. ECG shows no ischaemic changes; troponin is mildly elevated (28 ng/L, normal under 14).

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 102 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 97%, T 36.8 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Pale, scleral icterus, 2 cm palpable spleen tip, no lymphadenopathy, no acrocyanosis.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 72 g/L, MCV 102 fL, reticulocytes 11%, LDH 820 U/L, haptoglobin <0.1 g/L, unconjugated bilirubin 58 micromol/L, DAT IgG strongly positive C3d weakly positive, blood film spherocytes and polychromasia, cold agglutinin titre negative.

lead_in: Which combination of treatments is most appropriate as first-line management?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily, transfuse the least incompatible packed red cells with close clinical and laboratory monitoring, and add folate replacement
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily, strictly avoid blood transfusion regardless of clinical severity, and arrange weekly outpatient FBC review
Urgent splenectomy as first-line therapy, with IV immunoglobulin 1 g/kg as bridging treatment, and folate replacement during admission
Plasma exchange with fresh frozen plasma replacement as first-line, rituximab 375 mg/m^2 weekly for four doses, and folate replacement during admission
Continue hydroxychloroquine only and recheck FBC in 1 week before considering steroid initiation

subtopic_detail: Indications for red cell exchange transfusion
stem:
A 28-year-old man with homozygous HbSS sickle cell disease presents with three days of bilateral pleuritic chest pain, fever and dyspnoea. He was admitted six days ago for a typical vaso-occlusive crisis of the lower limbs and has been on regular morphine PCA, IV fluids and incentive spirometry. He has had four prior admissions for VOC this year and one previous episode of acute chest syndrome two years ago.

He is fully vaccinated including pneumococcal and is on penicillin V prophylaxis. He has no known allergies. He is normally on hydroxycarbamide 20 mg/kg daily but adherence has been poor. He works as a delivery driver. On examination he is in respiratory distress, with new bilateral basal crepitations and oxygen saturation of 88% on room air, improving to 93% on 6 L via Hudson mask.

There is no calf swelling. CXR shows new bilateral lower lobe infiltrates. Hb has dropped from baseline 88 to 64 g/L. He has a leucocytosis with WCC 22 and CRP 180. He is started on IV ceftriaxone and azithromycin.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 deg C, HR 124 bpm, RR 28, BP 102/64 mmHg, SpO2 88% RA, 93% on 6 L O2.
data_table.Examination: Respiratory distress, bilateral basal crepitations, no focal lower limb signs.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 64 g/L (baseline 88), HbS 78%, WCC 22 x10^9/L, platelets 280, reticulocytes 14%, CRP 180, troponin negative, ABG pH 7.36 pCO2 38 pO2 58 on 6 L, CXR new bilateral lower lobe infiltrates, D-dimer 4.2.
data_table.Medications: Morphine PCA, IV fluids, ceftriaxone, azithromycin, hydroxycarbamide 20 mg/kg (poor adherence).

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Simple top-up transfusion of 1 unit packed red cells
Empirical therapeutic dose enoxaparin for presumed pulmonary embolism
Urgent red cell exchange transfusion targeting HbS less than 30%
Continue current oxygen, fluids and antibiotics with hourly observations only
Increase hydroxycarbamide dose to drive HbF production

stem:
A 74-year-old woman attends ED with one day of right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild exertional dyspnoea. She had a knee arthroplasty 8 weeks ago. She has hypertension on perindopril, osteoarthritis, no haemoptysis, no calf swelling, no malignancy and is otherwise active. Examination: comfortable at rest, clear chest, no calf signs, SpO2 96 percent on room air. ECG sinus tachycardia 102.

CXR normal. Bloods: troponin negative, FBC normal, eGFR 68. Wells score is 1.5 (recent surgery 1.5; PE most likely diagnosis criterion not counted). Age-adjusted D-dimer returns at 680 microgram/L FEU.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102 bpm, BP 138/82 mmHg, RR 18, SpO2 96% RA, T 36.7 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Clear chest, no calf signs, comfortable at rest.
data_table.Investigations: Troponin negative, ECG sinus tachycardia, CXR normal, eGFR 68, FBC normal, Wells score 1.5 (PE unlikely).

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Exclude PE based on Wells unlikely plus D-dimer 680 microgram/L below the age-adjusted cut-off of 740, and discharge with safety netting
Proceed to CTPA because the D-dimer is above the standard fixed cut-off of 500 microgram/L
Start therapeutic anticoagulation empirically and image with CTPA within 24 hours
Perform V/Q scan as the first-line confirmatory test because CXR is normal
Repeat D-dimer in 24 hours before deciding on imaging

stem:
A 67-year-old man with newly diagnosed metastatic colorectal cancer (liver metastases) presents with a confirmed unprovoked left iliofemoral DVT and segmental subsegmental PE on CTPA. He started FOLFOX chemotherapy 10 days ago. He is haemodynamically stable, normotensive and not hypoxic. He has chronic kidney disease with eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m^2, no liver dysfunction (bilirubin 16, ALT 28), and no prior GI bleeding.

He has a colostomy after primary resection. There is no upper GI lesion documented on endoscopy 3 months ago. He has no thrombocytopenia (platelets 188) and no anaemia. He is not on antiplatelets. He has no history of intracranial haemorrhage. He weighs 78 kg. He is on ondansetron for nausea, dexamethasone PRN with chemotherapy, paracetamol for analgesia and atorvastatin 40 mg.

He is keen to take an oral agent and avoid daily injections if possible. He understands that anticoagulation must continue for at least the duration of active malignancy. He has no platelet transfusion history and no autoimmune disease.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 124/78 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, SpO2 97% RA.
data_table.Examination: Left leg swelling to mid-thigh, palpable colostomy site, no jaundice.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 118 g/L, platelets 188, eGFR 38, bilirubin 16, ALT 28, INR 1.0, no upper GI lesion on endoscopy 3 months ago.
data_table.Medications: FOLFOX chemotherapy, ondansetron, dexamethasone PRN, paracetamol, atorvastatin 40 mg.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate anticoagulation choice?

options.text: Rivaroxaban 15 mg BD for 21 days then 20 mg daily
Dabigatran 150 mg BD after 5 days of LMWH lead-in
Warfarin bridged with LMWH until INR 2-3 stable
Apixaban 10 mg BD for 7 days then 5 mg BD
Aspirin 100 mg daily as secondary prevention

stem:
A 72-year-old man is on day 8 post coronary artery bypass grafting. He has been on prophylactic enoxaparin 40 mg SC daily since day 1 plus an intraoperative and 48-hour post-op unfractionated heparin infusion. He develops a new right calf DVT confirmed on ultrasound. Platelets have fallen from 280 to 78 (a 72 percent drop). No bleeding, no skin necrosis, no schistocytes on film.

PF4-heparin ELISA is strongly positive and a serotonin release assay is pending. 4Ts score is 7. He has CKD with eGFR 38 (creatinine 168 micromol/L) and severe hepatic dysfunction from chronic right heart failure (bilirubin 62, INR 1.6).

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/82 mmHg, HR 92 bpm, T 37.0 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Right calf swollen and tender, no skin necrosis, no bleeding, sternotomy wound clean.
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 78 x10^9/L (pre-op 280), Hb 102 g/L, INR 1.1, fibrinogen 4.2 g/L, no schistocytes, PF4 antibody strongly positive ELISA, 4Ts 7 (high probability), eGFR 42.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate anticoagulation strategy?

options.text: Stop all heparin (UFH and LMWH) and commence IV bivalirudin at adjusted dose given combined renal and hepatic impairment, with close aPTT monitoring
Stop heparin and commence fondaparinux 7.5 mg SC daily off-label at standard dose
Stop heparin and commence IV argatroban at standard dose
Stop heparin and immediately commence warfarin bridging to therapeutic INR 2.0 to 3.0
Stop all heparin and observe expectantly without alternative anticoagulation until platelets recover

stem: A 32-year-old woman presents with one week of mucocutaneous bruising, gum bleeding, two short epistaxis episodes, and today new heavy menstrual bleeding requiring an overnight pad change every 90 minutes. She takes no medications, has not been recently vaccinated, has no recent viral illness, no pregnancy. No lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly. Bloods: isolated platelets 4 x10^9/L with normal Hb, WCC, differential, coagulation profile, renal and liver function. Blood film: large platelets, no schistocytes, no blasts. HIV, hepatitis B and C, H. pylori, ANA all negative. The team plans urgent treatment.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 118/72 mmHg, HR 86 bpm, T 36.6 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Petechiae lower limbs and buccal mucosa, bruising, gingival oozing, no lymphadenopathy or hepatosplenomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: Platelets 8 x10^9/L, Hb 132, WCC 6.4 normal differential, INR 1.0, APTT 30, blood film large platelets no blasts, HIV/HBV/HCV negative, ANA negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line treatment?

options.text: IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days plus IVIG 1 g/kg as combination first-line therapy
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily as monotherapy and review platelet count in 1 week
Platelet transfusion of 2 adult therapeutic doses to correct count above 50 x10^9/L
Rituximab 375 mg/m^2 weekly for 4 weeks as first-line therapy
Bone marrow biopsy first to confirm the diagnosis before commencing any treatment

subtopic_detail: Urgent FBC + blood film + bone marrow
stem:
A 46-year-old woman presents to her GP with three weeks of progressive fatigue, easy bruising of the limbs, gum bleeding and a low-grade fever. She had two episodes of unexplained epistaxis lasting 15 minutes each. She has no past medical history of note and takes no medications. She has lost 3 kg unintentionally in the last month and has drenching night sweats.

She has no foreign travel and no contact with TB. On examination she is pale, with widespread bruising and petechiae, gum hypertrophy and bleeding, a 4 cm palpable spleen and shotty cervical lymphadenopathy. Bloods at her GP show pancytopenia: Hb 76 g/L, WCC 38 x10^9/L (with 70% blasts on differential), platelets 14 x10^9/L. Blood film reports myeloid blasts with Auer rods.

Coagulation profile shows fibrinogen 1.0 g/L (low) and a raised D-dimer. She has not received transfusion. She is haemodynamically stable but the GP is concerned about possible acute promyelocytic leukaemia (APML). She has no current bleeding source other than gums.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72 mmHg, HR 96 bpm, T 37.6 deg C.
data_table.Examination: Pale, widespread bruising and petechiae, gum hypertrophy and bleeding, 4 cm splenomegaly, shotty cervical nodes.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 76 g/L, WCC 38 x10^9/L (70% blasts with Auer rods), platelets 14 x10^9/L, INR 1.6, fibrinogen 1.0 g/L, D-dimer 6.5, LDH 980, urate 0.52 mmol/L.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge home with routine outpatient haematology referral in 2 weeks for further workup
Start empirical broad-spectrum antibiotics and observe in ED for 24 hours before specialist referral
Transfuse 2 units of packed red cells and 1 pool of platelets then reassess clinically
Same-day transfer to haematology for urgent bone marrow biopsy with empirical ATRA if APML suspected
Repeat the full blood count in 48 hours to confirm the pancytopenia before any specialist referral

stem:
A 68-year-old man with stage A (Binet) CLL diagnosed 18 months ago has been on watch-and-wait. His lymphocyte count has been stable around 18-22 x10^9/L. He attends with three weeks of unilateral right cervical lymph node enlargement that is now 5 cm, firm and rapidly growing. He has lost 6 kg in the last month, has drenching night sweats and a temperature of 38.4 deg C this morning.

His Hb is 102 g/L (was 132), LDH is 920 U/L (was 220) and uric acid is 0.48 mmol/L. He has no infection elsewhere. CT chest/abdomen/pelvis shows bulky cervical, mediastinal and abdominal lymphadenopathy with a dominant 5 x 4 cm right cervical node. PET-CT shows the dominant node has SUVmax 18 with significantly higher avidity than other nodes. He has not had previous chemotherapy. He has not received rituximab. His original CLL FISH showed del(13q) only. He has no concurrent infection on cultures.

data_table.Examination: 5 cm firm right cervical lymph node, generalised lymphadenopathy, 3 cm splenomegaly.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 102 g/L (was 132), WCC 24 (lymphocytes 18), platelets 142, LDH 920 (was 220), uric acid 0.48, beta-2 microglobulin elevated, blood film smudge cells with some larger atypical cells, PET-CT dominant node SUVmax 18.

lead_in: Which finding most strongly suggests Richter transformation requiring biopsy?

options.text: Lymphocyte count rising from 18 to 22 x10^9/L over 18 months without lymphadenopathy or B symptoms
Smudge cells on the blood film with no rising LDH, new lymphadenopathy or constitutional symptoms
PET avidity SUVmax >10 in a dominant node alongside rising LDH and B symptoms in a known CLL patient
Hb 102 g/L alone without rising LDH or any new lymphadenopathy on recent examination today
Original FISH showing del(13q) as the sole cytogenetic abnormality at initial diagnosis years earlier

stem:
A 24-year-old previously well woman has been diagnosed with classical Hodgkin lymphoma after excisional left supraclavicular lymph node biopsy. Immunohistochemistry: CD30 positive, CD15 positive, CD20 negative Reed-Sternberg cells in a mixed inflammatory infiltrate. She reports drenching night sweats, fevers above 38, and 8 kg weight loss over 6 weeks. PET-CT shows supradiaphragmatic-only nodal involvement (left supraclavicular, mediastinal, bilateral cervical). Bloods: Hb 116, WCC normal, ESR 68, LDH normal, HIV negative.

Echocardiogram shows LVEF 60 percent. Pulmonary function tests are normal. She has not commenced any treatment yet. She has no children but wishes to preserve fertility.

data_table.Examination: 4 cm firm left supraclavicular lymph node, bilateral cervical nodes, mild splenomegaly, no rash.
data_table.Investigations: Excisional node biopsy: CD30+ CD15+ CD20- bi-nucleate Reed-Sternberg cells in mixed inflammatory infiltrate. PET-CT supradiaphragmatic only.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step before commencing chemotherapy?

options.text: Refer urgently for fertility preservation counselling and oocyte or embryo cryopreservation, then commence ABVD chemotherapy
Commence ABVD chemotherapy immediately and defer fertility discussion until after first cycle
Commence BEACOPP chemotherapy as first-line for B symptoms instead of ABVD
Proceed directly to involved-site radiotherapy as monotherapy without chemotherapy
Repeat excisional lymph node biopsy to confirm the immunohistochemistry findings before treatment

stem: A 70-year-old man is being evaluated for symptomatic multiple myeloma. He has back pain (mid-thoracic, worse at night), 4 kg unintentional weight loss, two recent pneumonias, T6 spinal tenderness without neurological deficit. Bloods: Hb 92 g/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (eGFR 28; baseline 78), corrected calcium 2.78 mmol/L (RR 2.10 to 2.60), albumin 28, IgG kappa paraprotein 42 g/L, kappa free light chain 320 mg/L (ratio 28), urinary Bence Jones protein positive. CT shows multiple lytic lesions and a T6 compression fracture. Bone marrow biopsy: 45 percent clonal plasma cells.

data_table.Examination: T6 spinal tenderness, no neurological deficit, no peripheral neuropathy.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 92 g/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (eGFR 28), corrected Ca 2.78, albumin 28, IgG kappa paraprotein 42 g/L, FLC kappa 320 mg/L (ratio 28), urinary BJP positive, lytic lesions on CT, compression fx at T6.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate combination of next steps in management?

options.text: Urgent MRI whole spine for cord compression risk, IV hydration with isotonic crystalloid, IV zoledronic acid (dose-adjusted for renal function), and refer to haematology to commence bortezomib-based induction

Repeat bone marrow biopsy and skeletal survey for staging before commencing any myeloma-directed therapy, with analgesia and oral hydration in the interim and outpatient haematology review within 2 weeks
Commence high-dose dexamethasone 40 mg daily as monotherapy induction, arrange oral hydration at home, and discharge with outpatient haematology and renal follow-up in 1 to 2 weeks
Commence high-dose lenalidomide-based induction immediately at standard dose, with IV hydration and analgesia, and arrange MRI spine and inpatient haematology review during the admission
Commence emergency haemodialysis as the primary intervention to clear paraprotein, give IV zoledronic acid for hypercalcaemia, and defer all chemotherapy until renal function recovers to baseline

stem:
A 38-year-old man is admitted with newly diagnosed Burkitt lymphoma with extensive abdominal disease, bulky retroperitoneal lymphadenopathy and bone marrow involvement. He is haemodynamically stable. Pre-chemotherapy bloods show urate 0.62 mmol/L (RR 0.20-0.42), potassium 4.6, phosphate 1.6 mmol/L, calcium 2.30, creatinine 92 (eGFR 86), LDH 4800 U/L (>10x upper limit), WCC 14 with 8% blasts on film. He has no known G6PD deficiency but has not been formally tested.

He is not pregnant. He is to start intensive R-CODOX-M/IVAC chemotherapy within 24 hours. He has no significant cardiac history. He is in a tertiary haematology unit with continuous monitoring. He has good IV access. He has no allopurinol allergy. The haematology team classifies him as high risk for tumour lysis syndrome by Cairo-Bishop criteria. The unit has rasburicase available. Renal output is currently 80 mL/hr. He weighs 75 kg.

data_table.Examination: Bulky abdominal mass, otherwise well.
data_table.Investigations: Urate 0.62 mmol/L, K 4.6, phosphate 1.6, corrected Ca 2.30, creatinine 92, LDH 4800, WCC 14 with 8% blasts.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate prophylactic strategy for tumour lysis syndrome in this high-risk patient?

options.text: Rasburicase 0.2 mg/kg IV daily plus IV hydration 3 L/m^2/day with close electrolyte monitoring
Allopurinol 300 mg daily and IV fluid hydration 2 L/m^2/day, without any rasburicase use
Urinary alkalinisation with intravenous sodium bicarbonate infusion targeting urine pH above 7.5 consistently
Delay chemotherapy by 7 days to allow oral allopurinol to reduce baseline serum urate substantially
Prophylactic upfront haemodialysis arranged via nephrology prior to commencing the first chemotherapy cycle

stem:
A 54-year-old woman with AML on day 12 of induction chemotherapy presents to the haematology ward with a temperature of 38.5 deg C on two readings 30 minutes apart. She has had mild rigors. She has no localising symptoms. Her central venous catheter exit site is clean. Her oral mucosa shows grade 2 mucositis without obvious infection. Her last chemotherapy was cytarabine plus daunorubicin completed 8 days ago.

She has no penicillin allergy. She has been on aciclovir and fluconazole prophylaxis. She has had no recent travel. She is haemodynamically stable. Her current bloods show neutrophil count 0.2 x10^9/L (severe neutropenia), Hb 92, platelets 38, creatinine 72, lactate 1.4, CRP 78. Blood cultures from the line and a peripheral site are drawn before any antibiotic is given. CXR is clear.

Urine dipstick is negative. There is no diarrhoea or cough. She has good IV access. Her MASCC score is calculated as 18 (lower risk, but with mucositis). She has had no antibiotics in the last 90 days. She has no recent C. difficile.

data_table.Examination: Grade 2 oral mucositis, clean CVC exit site, no rash, no focal signs.
data_table.Investigations: Neutrophils 0.2 x10^9/L, Hb 92, platelets 38, creatinine 72, lactate 1.4, CRP 78, CXR clear, blood cultures sent.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Oral amoxicillin-clavulanate plus ciprofloxacin home outpatient regimen
Meropenem 1 g IV every 8 hours as first-line
Piperacillin-tazobactam plus vancomycin plus caspofungin from the outset
Ceftriaxone 1 g IV daily
Piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g IV every 6 hours after cultures

stem:
A 42-year-old previously well non-smoker presents to ED with one week of progressive facial swelling, neck swelling, dyspnoea and headache worse on bending forward. She has noticed dilated veins on her chest wall. She has had two episodes of pre-syncope in the last 24 hours. She has no haemoptysis or chest pain. On examination she has facial plethora, periorbital oedema, distended jugular veins to the angle of the jaw, dilated collateral veins on the anterior chest wall and a positive Pemberton sign.

Stridor is absent at rest. There is no airway compromise currently but she is sitting forward in bed and saturating 95% on 2 L O2. CT chest with contrast shows a large anterior mediastinal mass compressing the SVC with extensive thrombus. She has not been previously diagnosed with malignancy. Her FBC, U&Es, LFTs and LDH (elevated at 950) are pending tissue diagnosis.

data_table.Examination: Facial plethora, periorbital oedema, distended JVPs, dilated chest wall collaterals, positive Pemberton sign, no stridor at rest.
data_table.Investigations: CT: large anterior mediastinal mass compressing SVC with thrombus; LDH 950; no tissue diagnosis yet.

lead_in: In the absence of airway compromise or critical neurological symptoms, which step is most important BEFORE starting empirical corticosteroids?

options.text: Start dexamethasone 16 mg IV stat regardless of biopsy timing
Start mediastinal radiotherapy empirically before tissue diagnosis
Obtain tissue diagnosis (core biopsy of accessible peripheral node or mediastinal biopsy)
Therapeutic anticoagulation alone for the SVC thrombus
Endovascular SVC stenting as definitive management

stem:
A 56-year-old man with cirrhosis presents with massive haematemesis. He arrives in haemorrhagic shock (BP 78/42, HR 142, GCS 13). The massive transfusion protocol is activated and he receives 6 units packed red cells, 4 units FFP and 1 pool of platelets via rapid infuser over 60 minutes. He is being continued on the MTP and IV tranexamic acid 1 g over 10 minutes was given on arrival.

Repeat bloods now: Hb 78, platelets 62, INR 2.1, fibrinogen 1.1 g/L, potassium 6.2 mmol/L, ionised calcium 0.84 mmol/L (RR 1.10 to 1.30), pH 7.18, lactate 8.4, base excess minus 12, magnesium 0.62, temperature 35.4 degrees C. ECG shows tall T waves in V2 to V4 with PR 200 ms; QRS 100 ms.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 78/42, HR 142, GCS 13, T 35.4 (mild hypothermia).
data_table.Examination: Cold peripheries, ongoing haematemesis, jaundice, ascites.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 g/L (post-transfusion), platelets 62, INR 2.1, fibrinogen 1.1, K 6.2, ionised Ca 0.84, pH 7.18, lactate 8.4, BE -12, Mg 0.62; ECG tall T waves V2-V4.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate single next intervention?

options.text: IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL given over 2 to 3 minutes via a peripheral large-bore cannula
IV insulin 10 units with 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose to shift potassium intracellularly
IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol bolus to correct metabolic acidosis
Active rewarming to address hypothermia as the priority complication
Stop the massive transfusion protocol and reassess once haemodynamics improve

subtopic_detail: Adult community-acquired sepsis: empirical regimen per eTG
stem:
A 72-year-old man presents to a regional emergency department with 36 hours of dysuria, rigors and increasing confusion. He has type 2 diabetes (metformin), benign prostatic hyperplasia (tamsulosin) and no documented antibiotic allergies. He was independent at baseline and lives with his wife. He has not travelled recently and is fully vaccinated. Triage observations show temperature 38.9 degrees C, heart rate 118 bpm, respiratory rate 26 per minute, blood pressure 96/54 mmHg and SpO2 95 percent on room air.

He is peripherally cool with capillary refill 4 seconds and a tender suprapubic region. Bedside urinalysis is positive for nitrites, leucocytes and blood. Venous blood gas shows pH 7.31, lactate 3.6 mmol/L, bicarbonate 18 mmol/L. Initial bloods reveal WCC 16.4 x10^9/L, neutrophils 14.1 x10^9/L, CRP 248 mg/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 92), eGFR 32 mL/min/1.73m^2. Two large-bore cannulae are sited.

Blood and urine cultures have just been taken. The team is preparing 30 mL/kg crystalloid resuscitation per Surviving Sepsis. He is not pregnant, not neutropenic and has no indwelling devices.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9 C, HR 118, RR 26, BP 96/54, SpO2 95 percent room air, CRT 4 s.
data_table.Examination: Confused, mottled peripheries, tender suprapubic, no flank tenderness elicited.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 16.4 x10^9/L, neutrophils 14.1, CRP 248 mg/L, lactate 3.6 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L (baseline 92), eGFR 32, urinalysis nitrites+ leucocytes+ blood+.
data_table.Medications: Metformin 1 g BD, tamsulosin 400 mcg nocte. No antibiotic allergy.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen to commence within the next hour?

options.text: IV gentamicin 5 mg/kg single dose plus IV amoxicillin 2 g every 6 hours
IV ceftriaxone 1 g daily plus IV metronidazole 500 mg every 12 hours
Oral trimethoprim 300 mg daily for 7 days after a single IV gentamicin dose
IV piperacillin-tazobactam 4.5 g every 8 hours as sole agent
IV meropenem 1 g every 8 hours pending blood culture results

subtopic_detail: qSOFA, vasopressor initiation threshold and MAP target
stem:
A 58-year-old woman with diet-controlled type 2 diabetes presents from a nursing aged-care facility with 24 hours of productive cough, fevers and lethargy. Background includes COPD (GOLD 2, FEV1 62 percent), ischaemic heart disease with two coronary stents (aspirin, clopidogrel ceased 6 months post-PCI), and chronic kidney disease stage 3a (baseline creatinine 110 micromol/L). She has no penicillin allergy. On arrival, T 39.1 degrees C, HR 124 bpm, RR 28 per minute, BP 84/48 mmHg, SpO2 91 percent on 4 L/min nasal prongs, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6).

Chest examination reveals right basal bronchial breathing and crackles. CXR confirms right lower lobe consolidation. Initial bloods: WCC 21 x10^9/L, neutrophils 18.6, CRP 312 mg/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L, eGFR 24, bicarbonate 17 mmol/L. Blood cultures and a respiratory PCR have been collected. IV ceftriaxone 1 g and IV azithromycin 500 mg are running. She has received 30 mL/kg of compound sodium lactate (Hartmann) over 90 minutes.

Repeat BP after fluid resuscitation is 86/52 mmHg, HR 118, MAP 63. Urine output is 12 mL/hr. She has no signs of pulmonary oedema and JVP is not elevated. An arterial line and central line are being placed. She has an advanced care directive consenting to ICU-level care.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.1, HR 118, RR 28, BP 86/52 (MAP 63) after 30 mL/kg, SpO2 91 percent on 4 L NP.
data_table.Examination: GCS 13, mottled knees, CRT 4 s, RLL crackles, no pulmonary oedema.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 21 x10^9/L, lactate 4.8 mmol/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (baseline 110), bicarb 17, CRP 312, CXR RLL consolidation.
data_table.Medications: Ceftriaxone 1 g IV, azithromycin 500 mg IV running. Aspirin 100 mg.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Continue further 20 mL/kg crystalloid bolus and reassess in 30 minutes
Start IV noradrenaline infusion targeting MAP at least 65 mmHg
Commence IV hydrocortisone 200 mg/day without starting a vasopressor
Switch antibiotics to IV meropenem 1 g 8-hourly before any vasopressor
Transfuse 1 unit of packed red cells to optimise oxygen delivery

stem:
A 68-year-old woman presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 12 hours of severe headache, fever, neck stiffness and one episode of vomiting. Her husband reports she has become drowsy in the last hour. Background includes systemic lupus erythematosus on prednisolone 10 mg daily and azathioprine 100 mg daily, and well-controlled hypertension. She has no penicillin allergy and is fully vaccinated, including pneumococcal and the recent meningococcal ACWY booster offered to immunosuppressed patients.

There has been no overseas travel and no household contact illness. On arrival, T 39.6 degrees C, HR 112 bpm, RR 22, BP 144/86 mmHg, SpO2 98 percent on room air. GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6). She has neck stiffness, photophobia and no rash. There are no focal neurological deficits, no papilloedema and no recent seizure. CT brain is being arranged before lumbar puncture because of her age, immunosuppression and reduced GCS.

Bloods are pending. Blood cultures have been taken. The team is preparing empirical antibiotic and adjunctive steroid therapy without delay. There is no clinical evidence of raised intracranial pressure. The Trust protocol mirrors eTG and Therapeutic Guidelines recommendations.

data_table.Vital signs: T 39.6, HR 112, RR 22, BP 144/86, SpO2 98 percent.
data_table.Examination: GCS 13, neck stiffness, photophobia, no rash, no focal deficit, no papilloedema.
data_table.Investigations: Bloods pending. CT awaiting. Blood cultures taken. No coagulopathy known.
data_table.Medications: Prednisolone 10 mg daily, azathioprine 100 mg daily, perindopril.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate empirical regimen to administer now, before CT or LP?

options.text: IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly alone after CT brain results, without Listeria cover or adjunctive steroid
IV vancomycin 1.5 g 12-hourly plus IV meropenem 2 g 8-hourly without any adjunctive dexamethasone
IV dexamethasone 10 mg with or just before IV ceftriaxone 2 g and IV benzylpenicillin 2.4 g
IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly plus IV aciclovir 8-hourly empirically, with no Listeria cover
Delay all antimicrobial therapy until lumbar puncture is performed to confirm the causative organism

stem:
A previously well 34-year-old primary school teacher presents to the emergency department with three days of worsening headache, fever to 38.6 degrees C and now a generalised seizure witnessed by paramedics, lasting two minutes with full post-ictal recovery over 20 minutes. Her husband describes 24 hours of out-of-character irritability, word-finding difficulty and difficulty naming family pets. She has no past medical history, takes no regular medications, has no allergies and is up to date with vaccinations.

There has been no overseas travel, no animal bites and no household sick contacts. On examination she is afebrile post-paracetamol, GCS 13 (E3 V4 M6), with expressive dysphasia, mild right pronator drift and no neck stiffness. There is no rash. Vital signs HR 96, BP 132/78, SpO2 98 percent. A non-contrast CT brain is normal. LP cannot proceed for 60 minutes while a CT venogram is reviewed.

Bloods show WCC 9.8 x10^9/L, CRP 22 mg/L, sodium 134 mmol/L, glucose 5.4 mmol/L. There is no coagulopathy. A consultant suspects herpes simplex encephalitis based on the temporal-lobe-pattern features.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.6 (peak), HR 96, BP 132/78, SpO2 98 percent.
data_table.Examination: GCS 13, expressive dysphasia, right pronator drift, no neck stiffness, no rash.
data_table.Investigations: CT brain normal. WCC 9.8, CRP 22, sodium 134, glucose 5.4 mmol/L. LP pending in 60 minutes.
data_table.Medications: Nil regular. No allergies.

lead_in: What is the single best next intervention?

options.text: Order MRI brain and EEG before initiating any antimicrobial therapy
Wait for CSF HSV PCR result before starting any antiviral therapy
Commence IV ceftriaxone 2 g 12-hourly as the priority therapy
Commence IV aciclovir 8-hourly empirically without waiting for LP
Give IV phenytoin loading dose and observe for further seizures

subtopic_detail: Empirical regimen and ECG monitoring for aortic root abscess
stem:
A 62-year-old man with a bioprosthetic aortic valve replacement five years ago for severe aortic stenosis presents with three weeks of low-grade fever, malaise, anorexia and a 4 kg weight loss. He had a dental scaling six weeks ago without antibiotic prophylaxis. On admission, T 38.2 degrees C, HR 92, BP 132/78. He has a soft early diastolic murmur not present at his last cardiology review.

There are two small painful nodules on his left index finger pad and a single splinter haemorrhage. There is no embolic stroke on examination, no skin emboli to soles. Two of three blood cultures drawn 12 hours apart grow viridans group streptococci. A transthoracic echocardiogram suggests mild aortic regurgitation; transoesophageal echocardiography demonstrates a 10 mm mobile vegetation on the bioprosthetic valve and an early perivalvular abscess. ECG on admission shows PR 168 ms with normal QRS.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.2, HR 92, BP 132/78, SpO2 98 percent.
data_table.Examination: Early diastolic murmur (new), Osler nodes left index finger, splinter haemorrhage. No focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: TTE mild AR. TOE: 10 mm vegetation + perivalvular abscess. Cultures: viridans strep x 2 of 3. ECG PR 168 ms.
data_table.Medications: Benzylpenicillin 1.8 g IV 4-hourly + gentamicin per eTG. No allergies.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate additional monitoring step over the next 72 hours?

options.text: Weekly CT chest with contrast to screen for septic pulmonary or systemic emboli
Single daily 12-lead ECG on the ward round, no continuous telemetry monitoring required
Twice-weekly serum vancomycin trough levels for therapeutic drug monitoring
Daily transthoracic echocardiography to track vegetation size and perivalvular extension
Continuous ECG / telemetry to detect progressive PR prolongation or AV block

stem:
A 27-year-old man who has sex with men presents to a sexual-health clinic 14 days after a single episode of condomless receptive anal intercourse with a partner of unknown serostatus. He reports 5 days of fever to 38.5 degrees C, sore throat, generalised maculopapular rash on the trunk, mouth ulcers, myalgia and tender cervical lymphadenopathy. He is not on PrEP.

He has no past medical history and is on no medication. He is otherwise systemically well, alert, drinking and eating. There is no meningism. On examination, T 38.4 degrees C, HR 96, BP 124/76, multiple posterior cervical nodes 1 cm, palatal ulcers, truncal maculopapular rash. Bloods: WCC 4.1 with relative lymphopenia, ALT 92 U/L, AST 84 U/L, CRP 38 mg/L, EBV serology negative for acute infection, CMV IgM negative, monospot negative. He attends specifically asking whether he might have just acquired HIV, and the clinic is following ASHM guidelines for testing in acute infection.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.4, HR 96, BP 124/76, SpO2 99 percent.
data_table.Examination: Maculopapular rash trunk, posterior cervical LN, palatal ulcers, mild pharyngitis.
data_table.Investigations: Lymphopenia, ALT 92, EBV/CMV/monospot negative. STI screen pending.
data_table.Medications: Nil. Not on PrEP.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial diagnostic test for suspected acute HIV infection?

options.text: Antibody-only rapid finger-prick HIV 1/2 test as the sole screening investigation
A combined 4th-generation HIV antigen/antibody test plus HIV RNA viral load
HIV Western blot as the primary screening test in suspected acute seroconversion
CD4 lymphocyte count alone as the initial diagnostic investigation in this presentation
Repeat HIV antibody test in 12 weeks before any testing now

subtopic_detail: Non-occupational PEP within 72 hours after high-risk exposure
stem:
A 22-year-old woman presents 36 hours after an episode of condomless receptive vaginal intercourse with a man known to be HIV positive on antiretroviral therapy. Her partner has been undetectable on viral load for 14 months on his last clinic letter, but she cannot reach him to confirm. She has no other STI risk factors recently, is on the combined oral contraceptive pill, has had a normal cervical screening three months ago, and her last HIV test (12 months ago) was negative.

She has no significant medical history, no allergies and normal renal function. She has not been on PrEP. She is anxious about acquiring HIV and asks specifically about post-exposure prophylaxis. The clinic follows the ASHM National PEP Guidelines. There are no contraindications to standard PEP. She is not pregnant on point-of-care testing. Hepatitis B serology is negative, hepatitis C antibody negative. She is up to date with HPV vaccination. She agrees to follow-up testing per protocol.

data_table.Vital signs: T 36.6, HR 78, BP 118/72, normal otherwise.
data_table.Examination: Unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: Baseline HIV Ag/Ab negative (today), STI swabs sent, HBV/HCV negative, pregnancy test negative, creatinine 70 micromol/L.
data_table.Medications: Combined oral contraceptive pill. No allergies.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Reassure that PEP is not indicated because the source partner is reportedly virally suppressed
Commence two-drug PrEP (tenofovir-emtricitabine) daily and review HIV serology at 4 and 12 weeks
Commence three-drug HIV PEP (tenofovir-emtricitabine plus dolutegravir) within 72 hours, baseline HIV and STI testing, and arrange ASHM follow-up
Repeat baseline HIV serology in 12 weeks without commencing any antiretroviral therapy now
A single intramuscular dose of cabotegravir as one-off post-exposure prophylaxis therapy

subtopic_detail: QuantiFERON-TB Gold over Mantoux in BCG-vaccinated patients
stem:
A 28-year-old woman who arrived from Vietnam 6 months ago is starting a graduate nursing program at a metropolitan tertiary hospital. She received BCG vaccination in childhood. She is asymptomatic, with no fever, cough, weight loss or night sweats. She has no household TB contacts. She is not immunocompromised, not pregnant, and on no medications. Examination is unremarkable. Pre-employment screening with QuantiFERON-TB Gold returns a positive result.

CXR is clear with no parenchymal abnormality, no apical scarring and no calcified granulomata. She has no symptoms or signs of active TB on review. LFTs and HIV serology are normal.

data_table.Examination: No lymphadenopathy. Chest clear. No erythema nodosum.
data_table.Investigations: CXR clear. FBC normal, LFTs normal, HIV negative.
data_table.Medications: Nil. No allergies.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Commence treatment for latent TB infection with rifampicin 600 mg daily for 4 months after baseline LFTs
Confirm the positive result with a Mantoux tuberculin skin test before treating
Commence full 4-drug active TB therapy with rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol under directly observed therapy
No treatment; arrange annual chest X-ray surveillance and clinical review for 5 years
Repeat QuantiFERON in 8 weeks; treat only if the second test remains positive

subtopic_detail: Cellulitis vs erysipelas vs necrotising soft tissue infection
stem:
A 58-year-old man with type 2 diabetes (metformin, sitagliptin) and obesity (BMI 38) presents with a 30 hour history of pain in his right calf, out of proportion to the modest superficial erythema. He had a small abrasion at the time of mowing the lawn 3 days ago. He now feels systemically unwell. On arrival, T 38.9 degrees C, HR 124, RR 26, BP 96/58, SpO2 96 percent.

The right calf is tense, exquisitely tender beyond the area of redness, with patchy dusky violaceous discolouration and a small area of haemorrhagic bullae developing over the lateral calf in the last 90 minutes. He has no penicillin allergy. He has reduced sensation over the calf compared with the contralateral side. Bedside ultrasound shows fascial-plane gas. Bloods: WCC 19.4 x10^9/L, sodium 130 mmol/L, glucose 16.4 mmol/L, CRP 312 mg/L, creatinine 156 micromol/L, haemoglobin 124 g/L, lactate 3.8 mmol/L. He has no documented HIV or other immunosuppression. He has not received antibiotics yet. The surgical registrar is reviewing.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.9, HR 124, RR 26, BP 96/58, SpO2 96 percent.
data_table.Examination: Pain out of proportion, dusky calf, haemorrhagic bullae, reduced sensation, fascial-plane gas on US.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 19.4, Na 130, glucose 16.4 mmol/L, CRP 312, creatinine 156, Hb 124, lactate 3.8. LRINEC > 8.
data_table.Medications: Metformin, sitagliptin. No allergies.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Urgent surgical exploration and debridement plus IV meropenem 1 g 8-hourly and IV clindamycin 600 mg 8-hourly
IV flucloxacillin 2 g 6-hourly as monotherapy and surgical review in the morning
Limb elevation and oral cefalexin 500 mg 6-hourly with GP follow-up in 48 hours
Hyperbaric oxygen therapy alone without surgical exploration or debridement of necrotic tissue
MRI of the lower limb with contrast to confirm fasciitis before any surgical decision is made

subtopic_detail: Early treatment of high-risk hospitalised patients
stem:
A 79-year-old woman with type 2 diabetes, COPD and chronic heart failure presents in early August with 36 hours of fever 38.7 degrees C, myalgia, dry cough and progressive breathlessness. She had her annual quadrivalent influenza vaccination 6 weeks ago. Chronic medications include metformin, perindopril, bisoprolol, furosemide and inhaled corticosteroids. On arrival: T 38.7, HR 110, RR 24, BP 134/76, SpO2 92 percent on room air.

Bibasal crackles without focal consolidation. CXR clear. Influenza A PCR positive. Bloods: WCC 8.2, CRP 56, eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m^2, creatinine 134 micromol/L (was 96 last month). She is being admitted for supportive care.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.7, HR 110, RR 24, BP 134/76, SpO2 92 percent room air.
data_table.Examination: Bibasal crackles, no consolidation, mild work of breathing.
data_table.Investigations: Influenza A PCR positive, CXR clear, eGFR 64, WCC 8.2, CRP 56.
data_table.Medications: Metformin, perindopril, bisoprolol, furosemide, ICS.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate antiviral and supportive management?

options.text: Oral oseltamivir 75 mg once daily (renal-dose reduced) for 5 days, plus targeted supportive care without empirical antibiotics
Oral oseltamivir 75 mg twice daily standard dose with concurrent IV ceftriaxone for empirical bacterial cover
Single oral dose of baloxavir marboxil 40 mg as one-off antiviral therapy
No antiviral therapy because symptom onset is approaching 48 hours and she was vaccinated 6 weeks ago
IV zanamivir 600 mg twice daily as first-line antiviral therapy in renal impairment

subtopic_detail: Empirical IV antibiotics per eTG and oral step-down
stem: A 32-year-old woman has 24 hours of right flank pain, rigors and dysuria. She has had three urinary tract infections this year, all treated orally. She is not pregnant and has no allergies.

data_table.Vital signs: T 38.8 degrees C, HR 108 /min, BP 110/68 mmHg
data_table.Examination: Right costovertebral angle tenderness
data_table.Investigations: WCC 14.8 x10^9/L, CRP 134 mg/L, creatinine 78 micromol/L, urine nitrites positive

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate empirical antibiotic regimen?

options.text: Intravenous meropenem 1 g eight-hourly
Oral nitrofurantoin twice daily for 5 days
Oral trimethoprim daily for 14 days at home
Intravenous gentamicin and amoxicillin
Oral ciprofloxacin twice daily for 7 days

stem:
A 28-year-old woman presents with a 6 month history of fatigue, alopecia, oral ulcers, photosensitive malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, and intermittent symmetrical polyarthralgia of small joints. She has no nephritic features, no neurological symptoms and no serositis. She is on no regular medications, has no allergies, does not smoke and has occasional alcohol. She has not been pregnant and is using condoms.

On examination she is afebrile, BP 124/76. There is a malar rash sparing the nasolabial folds, scarring alopecia, oral ulcers and tender MCPs without synovitis. There is no rash on sun-protected areas. Bloods: ANA strongly positive (homogeneous, titre 1:1280), anti-dsDNA positive (340 IU/mL), anti-Smith positive, C3 0.62 g/L (low), C4 0.08 g/L (low), CRP 6 (normal), ESR 64 mm/hr, FBC: Hb 108 g/L, platelets 124 x10^9/L, leukopenia 3.2 x10^9/L.

Urinalysis: no protein, no blood. Renal function and LFTs normal. She meets ACR/EULAR 2019 classification criteria for SLE. The rheumatologist plans to commence first-line therapy as per Australian Rheumatology Association guidance.

data_table.Examination: Malar rash, alopecia, oral ulcers, tender MCPs, no synovitis, no serositis.
data_table.Investigations: ANA 1:1280, anti-dsDNA 340, anti-Smith +, C3/C4 low, Hb 108, lymphopenia. Urinalysis clear.
data_table.Medications: Nil. Not pregnant. Condom contraception.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line maintenance therapy plus baseline assessment?

options.text: Hydroxychloroquine up to 5 mg/kg per day plus baseline ophthalmology screening
Long-term oral prednisolone 20 mg daily as sole maintenance
Oral methotrexate 15 mg once weekly as monotherapy without hydroxychloroquine
IV rituximab as initial first-line therapy for cutaneous-musculoskeletal SLE
Oral NSAID monotherapy (e.g. naproxen 500 mg BD) with paracetamol as required

subtopic_detail: Sapporo criteria and warfarin target INR for venous thrombosis
stem: A 34-year-old woman presents with a first unprovoked left popliteal DVT confirmed on Doppler ultrasound. She has had two prior first-trimester miscarriages and one mid-trimester fetal death, all with no anatomical or chromosomal cause identified. Her sister has SLE. Bloods sent: lupus anticoagulant positive on dilute Russell viper venom time at presentation and again 12 weeks later, anti-cardiolipin IgG strongly positive at both timepoints, anti-beta-2-glycoprotein-I IgG positive at both timepoints. She has been commenced on therapeutic LMWH and a long-term anticoagulation plan is being formulated, with a working diagnosis of primary antiphospholipid syndrome.

data_table.Examination: Left calf swollen, tender, warm. Otherwise unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: DVT on US. LA positive x2 (12 weeks apart), aCL IgG strong, anti-B2GPI IgG positive x2. APTT prolonged, does not correct on mix.
data_table.Medications: Therapeutic LMWH commenced. Copper IUD.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate long-term anticoagulation strategy?

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily indefinitely
Warfarin titrated to INR target 2.0 to 3.0 indefinitely
Aspirin 100 mg daily monotherapy for life
Warfarin titrated to INR target 3.0 to 4.0
Three months of LMWH then cessation of anticoagulation

subtopic_detail: Sight-saving high-dose steroid and temporal artery biopsy timing
stem:
A 72-year-old woman presents with 3 weeks of new-onset right temporal throbbing headache, scalp tenderness when combing hair, and jaw claudication when chewing tougher foods. Today she reports brief loss of vision in her right eye lasting 6 minutes, fully resolved. She has a 4 month history of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle stiffness lasting 90 minutes each morning, consistent with polymyalgia rheumatica.

She has type 2 diabetes (metformin), hypertension (perindopril) and hyperlipidaemia (atorvastatin). She has no penicillin or steroid allergy. On examination, T 36.9, HR 80, BP 144/86. Her right temporal artery is non-pulsatile and tender. Visual acuity is currently 6/9 right and 6/6 left with no afferent pupillary defect. Fundoscopy is unremarkable. There is shoulder and hip girdle tenderness without active synovitis.

Bloods: ESR 92 mm/hr, CRP 142 mg/L, FBC normal, glucose 8.1 mmol/L, UEC normal, LFTs normal. The team plans urgent ophthalmology assessment and is determining the immediate management while awaiting temporal artery biopsy.

data_table.Examination: Tender non-pulsatile right TA, scalp tenderness, mild jaw claudication, shoulder/hip girdle tenderness.
data_table.Investigations: ESR 92, CRP 142, glucose 8.1, FBC/UEC/LFT normal. Acuity 6/9 R, 6/6 L. Fundoscopy unremarkable.
data_table.Medications: Metformin, perindopril, atorvastatin. No allergies.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: Defer all corticosteroid therapy until the temporal artery biopsy result returns for confirmation
Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily and outpatient temporal artery biopsy in 6 weeks
IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days then high-dose oral prednisolone with biopsy within 1-2 weeks
Oral aspirin 100 mg daily and clinical observation without commencing any corticosteroid therapy
MRI of the head with contrast as the definitive diagnostic test prior to any steroid

subtopic_detail: Acute monoarthritis discrimination and intra-articular steroid timing
stem:
A 64-year-old man presents with a 24 hour history of an exquisitely painful, hot, swollen right knee. He has had three prior episodes of acute right first metatarsophalangeal joint pain in the past 4 years, each lasting 5-7 days and self-managed with NSAIDs. He is on hydrochlorothiazide for hypertension, has chronic kidney disease (eGFR 38), and a history of duodenal ulcer 2 years ago on proton pump inhibitor maintenance.

He has no fever today but reports brief rigors 12 hours ago. On examination, T 37.8, HR 92, BP 142/86. The right knee is held in slight flexion, with a tense effusion, marked warmth and erythema spreading 4 cm beyond the joint line. Active and passive movement is severely restricted by pain. There are no other joints involved. Bloods: WCC 12.4, CRP 142, urate 0.52 mmol/L, creatinine 168 micromol/L, eGFR 38.

Joint aspiration is performed: cloudy yellow fluid, leukocyte count 28 000 cells/microL with 85 percent neutrophils, Gram stain negative, polarised microscopy reveals negatively birefringent needle-shaped crystals. Cultures are pending.

data_table.Vital signs: T 37.8, HR 92, BP 142/86, SpO2 99 percent.
data_table.Examination: Right knee tense effusion, hot, erythema beyond joint, ROM severely limited.
data_table.Investigations: WCC 12.4, CRP 142, urate 0.52, creatinine 168, eGFR 38. Aspirate WCC 28 000, 85 percent neutrophils, negatively birefringent needle crystals, Gram stain negative.
data_table.Medications: HCT, PPI. No allergies. CKD 3b.

lead_in: What is the single best acute pharmacological management while awaiting cultures?

options.text: Empirical IV flucloxacillin 2 g 6-hourly without diagnostic joint aspiration or microbiology samples
Oral indometacin 50 mg three times daily for 5 days with a proton pump inhibitor for gastroprotection
Allopurinol 300 mg orally daily started immediately during the acute flare to lower the serum urate
Intra-articular methylprednisolone 40 mg plus oral colchicine 1 mg then 500 micrograms 1 hour later
Oral colchicine 1 mg six times daily continued until profuse diarrhoea develops as a dosing endpoint

subtopic_detail: Distinguishing PMR from GCA overlap and steroid dose
stem:
A 68-year-old woman presents to her GP with a 6 week history of bilateral shoulder and hip girdle pain and stiffness, worst in the mornings with 90 minutes of stiffness improving through the day. Over the past week she has developed a new left-sided temporal headache that is constant and aching, and yesterday her jaw ached after chewing toast. Her vision is normal and there is no scalp tenderness on direct questioning.

She has no fevers, no rash. Past medical history includes hypertension on perindopril and type 2 diabetes on metformin. Examination: T 36.6, BP 132/78. Shoulder and hip girdle tender, passive range of movement painful but full; temporal arteries palpable and slightly tender on the left; normal fundoscopy, normal visual acuity, no neurological deficit. Bloods: ESR 78 mm/hr, CRP 92 mg/L, CK normal, TSH normal, anti-CCP and rheumatoid factor negative.

data_table.Examination: Shoulder/hip girdle tenderness, painful but full passive ROM, no synovitis, normal TAs.
data_table.Investigations: ESR 62, CRP 48, CK normal, TSH normal, anti-CCP/RF negative.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, metformin. No allergies.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial management?

options.text: Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily with arrangement of an urgent rheumatology review
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg (60 mg) daily commenced immediately, with urgent temporal artery biopsy arranged within 1 to 2 weeks
IV pulse methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days followed by oral prednisolone 60 mg daily
NSAID monotherapy with naproxen 500 mg twice daily plus PPI cover and review in 2 weeks
Oral methotrexate 15 mg weekly as initial steroid-sparing monotherapy with folate cover

stem:
A 64-year-old man is brought to a metropolitan emergency department by paramedics with right-sided weakness and expressive aphasia first noticed by his wife when he woke at 06:30. He last spoke normally at 22:00 the night before. He arrives at 07:40. He has hypertension and atrial fibrillation; he takes apixaban 5 mg twice daily, last dose 18:00 yesterday. National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale (NIHSS) is 14.

Non-contrast computed tomography (CT) brain shows no haemorrhage and no early ischaemic change. CT perfusion shows a 12 mL ischaemic core and 78 mL of penumbra with mismatch ratio 7.5.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88 irregular, BP 168/92, SpO2 97% room air, RR 16, BSL 6.4 mmol/L.
data_table.Imaging: Non-contrast CT no haemorrhage. CTP core 12 mL, penumbra 78 mL, mismatch 7.5.
data_table.Medications: Apixaban 5 mg BD, last dose 18:00 prior day.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate reperfusion strategy?

options.text: Intravenous alteplase 0.9 mg/kg now
Intravenous tenecteplase 0.25 mg/kg bolus then endovascular thrombectomy
Endovascular thrombectomy without prior thrombolysis
Aspirin 300 mg orally and admit to stroke unit
Andexanet alfa reversal then intravenous alteplase

stem: A 58-year-old woman presents 90 minutes after sudden-onset left hemiparesis and dysarthria witnessed at work. NIHSS is 9. Non-contrast CT brain shows no haemorrhage. Blood pressure on three measurements 5 minutes apart is 198/112, 196/108 and 194/106. She has no other contraindications to intravenous thrombolysis.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 196/108 mean of three, SpO2 98% room air.
data_table.NIHSS: 9 (left arm 3, left leg 2, facial 1, dysarthria 2, sensory 1).
data_table.Imaging: Non-contrast CT no haemorrhage, no early ischaemic change.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Proceed with alteplase as benefit outweighs the BP risk
Intravenous labetalol 10 to 20 mg bolus, recheck, then alteplase if BP <185/110
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg and reassess in 30 minutes
Withhold thrombolysis and treat as ineligible due to severe hypertension
Intravenous glyceryl trinitrate infusion at 5 mcg/min titrated to BP <140/90

stem: A 71-year-old woman presents to a regional hospital 2 hours after sudden right hemiparesis and global aphasia. NIHSS is 18. Non-contrast CT brain shows hyperdense left middle cerebral artery (MCA) sign and an ASPECTS score of 8. The nearest comprehensive stroke centre with endovascular thrombectomy is 90 minutes away by helicopter retrieval; her local hospital does intravenous thrombolysis only.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84 regular, BP 158/82, SpO2 98% room air, BSL 5.6 mmol/L.
data_table.Imaging: Hyperdense left MCA, ASPECTS 8, no haemorrhage.
data_table.NIHSS: 18 (motor 6, aphasia 3, gaze 2, sensory 2, neglect 2, facial 1, dysarthria 1, level of consciousness 1).

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Administer alteplase locally and arrange urgent retrieval for thrombectomy
Aspirin 300 mg and admit locally without retrieval
Direct retrieval to thrombectomy centre, withholding alteplase until arrival
Decompressive hemicraniectomy referral
Heparin infusion targeting aPTT 60 to 80 seconds

stem: A 68-year-old man received intravenous alteplase 2 hours ago for acute ischaemic stroke. NIHSS was 11 pre-lysis, improved to 6 at 1 hour. He now has acute deterioration with NIHSS rising to 19, new vomiting, BP 220/118, HR 52, and reduced level of consciousness. He is on the stroke unit.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 220/118, HR 52, SpO2 94% room air, GCS 11.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Stop any infusing alteplase, urgent non-contrast CT brain, cross-match and prepare cryoprecipitate
Intravenous mannitol 1 g/kg and reassess in 30 minutes
Increase alteplase rate to complete remaining dose faster
Aspirin 300 mg and antiemetic
Prothrombin complex concentrate (PCC) 50 units/kg

stem: A 56-year-old woman wakes at 06:00 with left-sided weakness. She last spoke normally at 23:00 the previous night. She arrives at the emergency department at 06:45. NIHSS is 12. Non-contrast CT brain at 07:00 shows no haemorrhage and no early ischaemic change.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 162/88, HR 76, SpO2 98% room air.
data_table.Timeline: Last known well 23:00; symptom discovery 06:00; arrival 06:45; CT 07:00.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next investigation to determine thrombolysis eligibility?

options.text: Magnetic resonance imaging brain with diffusion-weighted imaging and FLAIR
Repeat non-contrast CT in 4 hours
Carotid Doppler ultrasound
Computed tomography venogram
Electroencephalogram

stem: A 34-year-old man with known epilepsy is brought to the emergency department by ambulance. He has been seizing continuously for 8 minutes with generalised tonic-clonic activity. Intravenous access is in place. He weighs approximately 80 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 168/96, SpO2 91% room air, T 37.6 C, BSL 5.8 mmol/L.
data_table.Airway: Bag-valve-mask, jaw thrust, oral suction in use.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate first-line pharmacological treatment?

options.text: Midazolam 10 mg intramuscular
Lorazepam 0.1 mg/kg intravenous (maximum 4 mg)
Phenytoin 20 mg/kg intravenous infusion
Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg intravenous infusion
Propofol 2 mg/kg intravenous bolus and intubation

subtopic_detail: Second-line agent selection after benzodiazepine failure
stem: A 28-year-old woman has been seizing for 18 minutes. She received two doses of intravenous midazolam 5 mg, 5 minutes apart, with no cessation. She has no known epilepsy, is 16 weeks pregnant, and weighs 65 kg.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 140, BP 156/94, SpO2 88% on 15 L non-rebreather, T 38.2 C, BSL 6.2 mmol/L.
data_table.Background: 16 weeks gestation, G2P1, no epilepsy.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next pharmacological agent?

options.text: Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg intravenous over 10 minutes
Sodium valproate 40 mg/kg intravenous
Phenytoin 20 mg/kg intravenous infusion
Magnesium sulfate 4 g intravenous over 20 minutes
Repeat midazolam 5 mg intravenous

stem: A 45-year-old man has had ongoing seizure activity for 45 minutes despite two doses of intravenous midazolam 10 mg and intravenous levetiracetam 60 mg/kg. He is now in the resuscitation bay with the anaesthetic registrar.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 178/102, SpO2 86% on 15 L non-rebreather.
data_table.Treatments given: Midazolam 10 mg x2 IV. Levetiracetam 60 mg/kg IV completed.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Rapid sequence induction with propofol and intubation, then propofol or midazolam infusion with continuous EEG
Add a third antiepileptic (phenytoin 20 mg/kg) and wait 20 minutes
Therapeutic hypothermia to 33 degrees Celsius
Ketogenic diet via nasogastric tube
Lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis

stem: A 42-year-old man presents to a regional hospital with 5 days of progressive ascending lower limb weakness, now involving the proximal upper limbs and mild facial droop. He had gastroenteritis 3 weeks ago. Examination shows symmetrical weakness 3/5 in the legs and 4/5 in the arms with absent ankle and knee reflexes. Cranial nerve examination shows bilateral mild facial weakness. Sensation is intact.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 148/96 (was 124/78 on admission), SpO2 96% room air, RR 22.
data_table.Examination: Symmetrical LL weakness 3/5, UL 4/5, areflexia, bilateral facial droop, sensation intact.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Intravenous immunoglobulin (IVIG) 0.4 g/kg/day for 5 days and admission to a monitored bed with respiratory and autonomic surveillance
Methylprednisolone 1 g IV daily for 5 days
Pyridostigmine 60 mg orally four times daily
Outpatient nerve conduction studies and review in 1 week
Empirical aciclovir 10 mg/kg IV three times daily

stem: A 38-year-old woman presents with 3 weeks of intermittent diplopia worse in the evenings, fatigable proximal limb weakness, and dysphagia for solids that worsens through a meal. Reflexes are preserved. There is no sensory disturbance and no recent viral or gastrointestinal illness. Ice pack applied to the right eyelid for 2 minutes improves ptosis.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 124/72, SpO2 99% room air, RR 14, FVC 42 mL/kg.
data_table.Examination: Fatigable proximal weakness, preserved reflexes, no sensory level, positive ice pack test.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate confirmatory investigation?

options.text: Acetylcholine receptor antibody assay
Lumbar puncture for cytological dissociation
Nerve conduction studies for demyelination
Stool culture for Campylobacter jejuni
Magnetic resonance imaging spine

stem: A 52-year-old woman with seropositive myasthenia gravis on pyridostigmine 60 mg four times daily and prednisolone 15 mg daily presents to a metropolitan emergency department with 24 hours of worsening dysphagia, breathlessness on lying flat, and inability to lift her head off the pillow. She was started on azithromycin 500 mg by her general practitioner 3 days ago for sinusitis. She is alert but tachypnoeic.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 122, BP 142/86, SpO2 92% on 4 L nasal prongs, RR 28.
data_table.Bedside: FVC 12 mL/kg, negative inspiratory force -18 cmH2O, single breath count 8.
data_table.Examination: Bulbar weakness, neck flexor 2/5, paradoxical abdominal breathing.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management priority?

options.text: Stop azithromycin, transfer to intensive care for likely intubation, and start plasma exchange or intravenous immunoglobulin
Increase pyridostigmine to 120 mg orally hourly
Methylprednisolone 1 g IV without stopping azithromycin
Edrophonium test to differentiate myasthenic from cholinergic crisis
Non-invasive ventilation as a long-term plan, no specific MG-directed therapy

stem: A 67-year-old woman presents to a regional emergency department with 12 hours of fever, severe headache, neck stiffness and progressive confusion. She has type 2 diabetes mellitus. She has no penicillin allergy. Kernig sign is positive. There are no focal neurological signs and Glasgow Coma Scale (GCS) is 13.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 118, BP 102/64, SpO2 96% room air, T 39.2 C, RR 22.
data_table.Examination: Neck stiffness, Kernig positive, GCS 13, no focal signs, no rash.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate empirical antimicrobial regimen?

options.text: Ceftriaxone 2 g intravenous 12-hourly plus benzylpenicillin 2.4 g intravenous 4-hourly plus dexamethasone 10 mg intravenous 6-hourly
Ceftriaxone 2 g intravenous 12-hourly alone
Vancomycin 30 mg/kg intravenous loading dose plus meropenem 2 g intravenous 8-hourly
Aciclovir 10 mg/kg intravenous 8-hourly alone
Defer antibiotics until lumbar puncture results return

stem: A 54-year-old man presents to a tertiary emergency department with fever, headache, neck stiffness and a single focal seizure 1 hour ago. GCS is 12. He has a known history of HIV with CD4 count 180. There are no focal motor signs but he is post-ictal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, BP 138/82, SpO2 97% room air, T 38.9 C.
data_table.Examination: Post-ictal, GCS 12, no focal motor deficit, neck stiffness present.
data_table.Background: HIV on antiretroviral therapy, CD4 180.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate sequence of immediate steps?

options.text: Blood cultures, empirical antibiotics and dexamethasone, then CT brain before lumbar puncture
Immediate lumbar puncture without imaging
CT brain first, then antibiotics only if CT clear
Magnetic resonance imaging brain first, then lumbar puncture
Treat empirically and avoid lumbar puncture entirely

stem: A 42-year-old man with suspected bacterial meningitis has received blood cultures and is about to be given his first dose of intravenous ceftriaxone. The registrar asks about dexamethasone timing.

data_table.Plan: Ceftriaxone 2 g IV being drawn up. Blood cultures collected.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate plan for dexamethasone?

options.text: Dexamethasone 10 mg intravenous with or just before the first antibiotic dose, continued 6-hourly for 4 days only if CSF confirms pneumococcus
Dexamethasone 10 mg intravenous after the first antibiotic dose, continued for 10 days regardless of organism
Dexamethasone only after CSF Gram stain confirms organism
Hydrocortisone 100 mg intravenous 6-hourly
No steroids - steroid use is not part of bacterial meningitis management

stem: A 74-year-old woman is admitted with a left middle cerebral artery territory ischaemic stroke. Echocardiogram and 72-hour cardiac monitor reveal paroxysmal atrial fibrillation. She has hypertension and previous transient ischaemic attack. Her CHA2DS2-VASc is 6. HAS-BLED is 2. She has no contraindication to anticoagulation. The stroke is moderate sized on MRI without haemorrhagic transformation.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/78, HR 76 (in sinus rhythm now).
data_table.Imaging: Moderate left MCA infarct, no haemorrhagic transformation on day 5 MRI.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate timing to start anticoagulation?

options.text: Apixaban 5 mg twice daily commenced on day 6 to 8 after stroke onset
Aspirin 100 mg daily plus clopidogrel 75 mg daily long-term
Warfarin commenced immediately on day 1
Aspirin 100 mg daily alone
Anticoagulation deferred until 6 weeks post-stroke

stem: A 68-year-old man presents to his general practitioner having had a 45-minute episode of right arm weakness and word-finding difficulty that resolved 3 hours ago. He has hypertension and type 2 diabetes mellitus. Blood pressure today is 162/94 and he is in sinus rhythm. Examination is now normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 162/94, BSL 9.2 mmol/L.
data_table.Examination: Now normal; no residual deficit.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate management plan?

options.text: Same-day specialist stroke clinic or emergency department referral for imaging and carotid assessment
Outpatient referral within 4 weeks
Aspirin 100 mg and review in 7 days
Increase antihypertensive and review in 2 weeks
Reassurance as the episode has resolved

stem: A 62-year-old man presents 2 hours after sudden severe headache, vomiting, and left hemiparesis. Non-contrast CT brain shows a 12 mL right basal ganglia haemorrhage without intraventricular extension. He takes amlodipine for hypertension. He is on no antiplatelet or anticoagulant. Glasgow Coma Scale is 13.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 84, BP 198/112, SpO2 98% room air.
data_table.Imaging: 12 mL right basal ganglia bleed, no IVH, no midline shift.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate blood pressure target and timeframe?

options.text: Systolic blood pressure 140 mmHg within 1 hour using titrated intravenous antihypertensive
Permissive hypertension - no antihypertensive treatment
Systolic blood pressure <100 mmHg within 1 hour
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg
Lower over the next 24 hours to <160 mmHg

stem: A 26-year-old man presents to a metropolitan emergency department after a witnessed first generalised tonic-clonic seizure lasting 90 seconds. He bit his tongue and was post-ictal for 20 minutes. He has fully recovered. He drinks 4 standard drinks on Fridays and Saturdays. No illicit drug use. He works as a courier driver. Examination, electrolytes, glucose and ECG are normal. Non-contrast CT brain is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 124/72, T 36.8 C, BSL 5.4 mmol/L.
data_table.Investigations: U&E, glucose, calcium, magnesium, CRP, ECG normal. CT brain normal.
data_table.Driving: Class C licence; works as a courier.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Discharge with outpatient MRI brain and electroencephalogram (EEG), neurology follow-up within 4 weeks, no antiepileptic started, and advise non-driving per Austroads
