Start sodium valproate 500 mg orally twice daily and discharge with a 6-month GP follow-up, without outpatient MRI brain or electroencephalogram first
Admit for 48-hour inpatient video EEG monitoring as the next investigation, deferring outpatient MRI and outpatient neurology review until after admission
Discharge with no neurology follow-up, no MRI, no EEG, and no specific driving advice provided that examination remains normal at the time of discharge
Perform a lumbar puncture for cerebrospinal fluid analysis prior to discharge, despite the afebrile, alert and fully recovered status of the patient

stem: A 19-year-old university student is admitted with confirmed invasive meningococcal disease (CSF and blood cultures positive for Neisseria meningitidis serogroup B). She lives in shared university accommodation with 4 housemates and attended a 5-hour party 2 days before admission with 12 other people. She is on appropriate antibiotics.

data_table.Background: Confirmed IMD serogroup B.
data_table.Contacts: 4 household contacts; 12 party attendees with prolonged close contact.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate public health response for close contacts?

options.text: Notify public health unit; offer ciprofloxacin 500 mg orally single dose (or rifampicin) to household and prolonged close contacts; arrange meningococcal B vaccination via public health
Treat the index case only; contacts only need treatment if they develop symptoms
Offer benzathine penicillin intramuscular to all contacts
Casual contacts (classmates, gym buddies) also require prophylaxis
Defer notification until microbiology confirms serogroup

stem: A 64-year-old man presents with 4 months of progressive proximal lower limb weakness, dry mouth, erectile dysfunction, and difficulty rising from a chair. He has a 50 pack-year smoking history. On examination, knee reflexes are absent at rest but become elicitable after 10 seconds of sustained quadriceps contraction. Strength initially weak but improves with repeated effort. No ptosis, no ocular involvement.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 128/74, SpO2 97% room air.
data_table.Examination: Proximal LL weakness, areflexic at rest with post-exercise facilitation, no ocular involvement.
data_table.Autonomic: Dry mouth, ED, postural drop 22 mmHg.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Computed tomography (CT) thorax and voltage-gated calcium channel antibody assay
Acetylcholine receptor antibody assay alone, in keeping with suspected myasthenia gravis
Lumbar puncture for albuminocytological dissociation suggestive of Guillain-Barre syndrome
Magnetic resonance imaging of the lumbar spine to exclude a compressive cauda equina lesion
Overnight polysomnography to investigate sleep apnoea contributing to weakness

subtopic_detail: KDIGO eGFR/ACR matrix + KHA-CARI referral thresholds
stem:
A 64-year-old man attends his GP for a chronic disease check. He has type 2 diabetes for 12 years, hypertension, and a BMI of 33 kg/m^2. Medications include perindopril 5 mg, metformin 1 g BD, empagliflozin 10 mg, and atorvastatin 40 mg. He denies haematuria, frothy urine, oedema or new urinary symptoms and has had no recent illness, NSAIDs or contrast exposure.

He has never been seen by a nephrologist. Examination shows BP 142/86 mmHg, no peripheral oedema, normal heart sounds and chest. Fundi show background diabetic retinopathy. Today's results in stable conditions: serum creatinine 168 micromol/L (was 162 three months ago and 158 six months ago); eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m^2; urine albumin to creatinine ratio (ACR) on a first-morning sample is 42 mg/mmol, confirmed on a repeat sample two weeks later at 38 mg/mmol; serum potassium 4.6 mmol/L; HbA1c 58 mmol/mol; haemoglobin 128 g/L. He has had no episodes of AKI in the past year.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 142/86 mmHg, HR 76 bpm, BMI 33 kg/m^2.
data_table.Examination: No peripheral oedema, JVP not raised, fundi: background diabetic retinopathy.
data_table.Investigations: Creatinine 168 micromol/L (stable), eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m^2, urine ACR 42 mg/mmol (confirmed 38 mg/mmol on repeat), K 4.6 mmol/L, HbA1c 58 mmol/mol, Hb 128 g/L.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg, metformin 1 g BD, empagliflozin 10 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in his renal management?

options.text: Continue GP-led care and recheck eGFR and ACR in 6 months without specialist input
Refer only if eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m^2 on the next test
Stop empagliflozin because the eGFR has fallen below 45 mL/min/1.73m^2
Stop perindopril given the modest creatinine rise and switch to amlodipine
Refer to nephrology for assessment given persistent ACR above 30 mg/mmol

subtopic_detail: Iron repletion before ESA, KDIGO Hb thresholds
stem:
A 72-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73m^2, secondary to long-standing hypertension and obstructive uropathy after pelvic radiotherapy) is seen in renal outpatients. She reports six weeks of fatigue and exertional dyspnoea climbing one flight of stairs. She denies overt bleeding, melaena, haematuria or menorrhagia (post-menopausal). Medications: amlodipine 10 mg, irbesartan 300 mg, atorvastatin 40 mg, colecalciferol 1000 IU.

She does not take NSAIDs. There has been no recent infection or hospitalisation. Examination: BP 138/82, conjunctival pallor, mild ankle oedema, otherwise unremarkable. Bloods (today): Hb 96 g/L, MCV 88 fL, ferritin 78 microgram/L, transferrin saturation 14 percent, CRP 4 mg/L, B12 and folate normal, reticulocyte count low, creatinine 232 micromol/L (stable), eGFR 22, K 4.4 mmol/L, PTH 18 pmol/L, corrected Ca 2.30 mmol/L, phosphate 1.4 mmol/L. Faecal occult blood is negative on three samples.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/82 mmHg, HR 84 bpm, SpO2 97 percent on room air.
data_table.Examination: Conjunctival pallor, mild ankle oedema. JVP not raised. No abdominal mass; PR exam unremarkable.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 96 g/L, MCV 88, ferritin 78 microgram/L, TSAT 14%, CRP 4 mg/L, retics low, eGFR 22, PTH 18 pmol/L, Ca 2.30, PO4 1.4.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in managing her anaemia?

options.text: Commence subcutaneous darbepoetin alfa and review Hb in 4 weeks
Give IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose) targeting TSAT 20-30% and ferritin 100-500, then reassess Hb
Trial oral ferrous sulfate 325 mg daily and recheck iron studies in 3 months
Transfuse 2 units of packed red cells today and arrange outpatient ESA
Investigate for occult GI malignancy with colonoscopy before any treatment

subtopic_detail: Sequencing phosphate binder vs activated vitamin D vs cinacalcet
stem: A 58-year-old man with CKD stage 5 not yet on dialysis (eGFR 12 mL/min/1.73m^2 due to ADPKD) is reviewed in nephrology clinic. He is asymptomatic of bone pain or pruritus but has cramping. He follows a low-phosphate diet with the renal dietitian. Medications: amlodipine, irbesartan, atorvastatin, sodium bicarbonate 840 mg TDS, colecalciferol 1000 IU. He is not yet anuric. Bloods at today's visit (consistent with the trend over the last 3 months): corrected calcium 2.18 mmol/L, phosphate 1.95 mmol/L (rising from 1.5 three months ago), PTH 78 pmol/L (rising from 45), 25-OH vitamin D 78 nmol/L, alkaline phosphatase 142 U/L, bicarbonate 22 mmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 134/82 mmHg, HR 72 bpm.
data_table.Examination: No bone tenderness; mature radiocephalic AV fistula on left forearm with good thrill.
data_table.Investigations: Corrected Ca 2.18 mmol/L, phosphate 1.95 mmol/L (rising), PTH 78 pmol/L (rising), 25-OH vit D 78 nmol/L, ALP 142 U/L, HCO3 22, eGFR 12.
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine, irbesartan, atorvastatin, NaHCO3 840 mg TDS, colecalciferol 1000 IU.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in managing his CKD-MBD?

options.text: Commence oral calcium carbonate 600 mg with each meal as a phosphate binder
Start oral calcitriol 0.25 microgram daily to suppress the rising PTH
Commence oral cinacalcet 30 mg daily as a calcimimetic
Add a non-calcium phosphate binder (sevelamer) and reinforce dietary phosphate restriction
Refer urgently for subtotal parathyroidectomy given the rising PTH

subtopic_detail: AEIOU + advance care planning in frail older adult
stem:
An 82-year-old woman with CKD stage 5 (eGFR 8 mL/min/1.73m^2 due to renovascular disease and longstanding T2DM) is admitted with fatigue, anorexia and one week of intermittent confusion. She lives alone with package supports, has a Clinical Frailty Scale of 7, and a Charlson index of 9 (T2DM with retinopathy and neuropathy, IHD with PCI, HF with EF 35 percent, COPD).

She has been counselled previously about home haemodialysis and peritoneal dialysis and has expressed a preference 'not to live on a machine' but has not formalised this. She is alert, oriented to person and place only. Bloods: K 5.4 mmol/L, HCO3 19 mmol/L, urea 38 mmol/L, creatinine 412 micromol/L, Hb 92 g/L, no acidaemia on VBG (pH 7.34), no pulmonary oedema on CXR, urine output 1100 mL/day. She has not been exposed to NSAIDs, contrast or new nephrotoxins.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 mmHg, HR 88 bpm, RR 18, SpO2 96 percent on RA, T 36.7.
data_table.Examination: Mild asterixis, mild peripheral oedema, no pericardial rub. Clear chest.
data_table.Investigations: K 5.4, HCO3 19, urea 38 mmol/L, creatinine 412 micromol/L, Hb 92, pH 7.34, normal CXR, UO 1100 mL/day.
data_table.Medications: Furosemide 40 mg, amlodipine, aspirin, metoprolol, atorvastatin, gliclazide MR 60 mg, insulin glargine 14 units.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Insert a tunnelled vascath and commence urgent in-centre haemodialysis today
Hold a formal goals-of-care conversation and offer renal supportive (conservative) care
Commence inpatient peritoneal dialysis training and discharge home on PD
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter for accurate urine output then discharge with GP review
Transfuse 1 unit of packed red cells targeting Hb 110 g/L to relieve her fatigue

subtopic_detail: Pre-renal vs intrinsic - urine sodium and FENa interpretation
stem:
A 68-year-old man presents to ED with five days of vomiting, diarrhoea and reduced oral intake after a community gastroenteritis outbreak. Past history: hypertension, T2DM, IHD with previous CABG. Medications: perindopril 8 mg, indapamide 2.5 mg, metformin 1 g BD, empagliflozin 10 mg (held 48 hours ago by his GP), atorvastatin 40 mg, aspirin 100 mg. He has not taken any NSAIDs or had recent imaging contrast.

On arrival: BP 96/58 mmHg lying, 78/44 mmHg sitting, HR 112, dry mucous membranes, JVP not visible, no peripheral oedema, soft non-tender abdomen, bladder not palpable. Bloods: Na 148 mmol/L, K 4.0, urea 22 mmol/L, creatinine 198 micromol/L (baseline 88 three months ago), eGFR 28, HCO3 19, lactate 2.4, glucose 9 mmol/L, CRP 12. Urinalysis: SG 1.030, no blood, no protein. Spot urine: sodium 8 mmol/L, urine creatinine 12 mmol/L, urine osmolality 612 mOsm/kg. Renal tract US: normal-sized kidneys, no hydronephrosis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 96/58 lying, 78/44 sitting, HR 112, T 36.6.
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, capillary refill 3 sec, JVP flat, no oedema.
data_table.Investigations: Urea 22, Cr 198 (baseline 88), urine Na 8, urine osm 612, FENa < 1%, US normal, no obstruction.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, indapamide, metformin, empagliflozin (held), aspirin, atorvastatin.

lead_in: Which finding best supports a pre-renal aetiology over established acute tubular necrosis?

options.text: Postural hypotension on arrival with dry mucous membranes on examination
Creatinine has more than doubled from her three-month baseline value
Urine sodium 8 mmol/L with FENa under 1% and concentrated urine
Hypernatraemia (sodium 148 mmol/L) reflecting a free water deficit clinically
Absence of hydronephrosis on bedside renal tract ultrasound today

stem: A 71-year-old woman with CKD stage 3b (eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73m^2) and T2DM (HbA1c 56 mmol/mol) is scheduled tomorrow for an elective coronary angiogram for stable angina. She takes perindopril, atorvastatin, aspirin, metformin and empagliflozin. She is euvolaemic on examination with no peripheral oedema, JVP not raised, clear chest, BP 134/78 mmHg, K 4.1 mmol/L, creatinine 132 micromol/L. She has no decompensated heart failure or current sepsis. The cardiologist plans iso-osmolar low-volume iodinated contrast.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 134/78 mmHg, HR 72 bpm, SpO2 98% RA.
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic, clear chest, no oedema, JVP not elevated.
data_table.Investigations: Cr 132 micromol/L, eGFR 38, K 4.1, HCO3 25, HbA1c 56 mmol/mol.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, atorvastatin, aspirin, metformin, empagliflozin.

lead_in: Which combined peri-procedural plan most appropriately reduces her risk of contrast-associated AKI and metabolic complications?

options.text: Continue all current medications and prescribe IV 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1 mL/kg/h for 6 hours before and 6 hours after contrast
Withhold metformin and empagliflozin on the day of and 48 hours after contrast, give IV 0.9 percent sodium chloride 1 mL/kg/h pre and post, and recheck creatinine before reinstating
Commence oral N-acetylcysteine 1200 mg twice daily on the day of and after the procedure, continue all usual medications
Give IV sodium bicarbonate infusion in place of normal saline, with IV furosemide 40 mg before contrast to maintain urine output
Withhold all antihypertensives for 48 hours before angiogram and recheck creatinine on the day

stem: A 34-year-old man presents to his GP with two weeks of progressive ankle and periorbital swelling, weight gain of 6 kg, and frothy urine. He has no joint pains, rashes, recent sore throat, skin infection, or haemoptysis. He takes no regular medications. Examination: BP 138/86 mmHg, periorbital and bilateral pitting peripheral oedema to the knees, chest clear, no purpura. Bloods: albumin 22 g/L, cholesterol 8.8 mmol/L, creatinine 88 micromol/L, eGFR over 90, normal FBC and LFTs, complement C3 and C4 normal, ANA and ANCA negative, hepatitis B and C and HIV negative, HbA1c 38 mmol/mol. Urinalysis: protein 4+, blood trace, no leucocytes or nitrites, no red cell casts on microscopy. Spot urine protein-creatinine ratio 480 mg/mmol.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/86, HR 78, afebrile.
data_table.Examination: Periorbital + bilateral pitting peripheral oedema; chest clear; no rash.
data_table.Investigations: Albumin 22 g/L, cholesterol 8.8 mmol/L, Cr 88, eGFR > 90, UPCR 480 mg/mmol, urinalysis protein 4+ blood trace, C3/C4 normal, ANA/ANCA/HBV/HCV/HIV negative.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next investigation to establish the underlying diagnosis?

options.text: Renal biopsy with light microscopy, immunofluorescence and electron microscopy
Serum and urine electrophoresis with free light chain assay to exclude paraprotein
Anti-phospholipase A2 receptor (anti-PLA2R) antibody titre as a standalone diagnostic test
Renal tract ultrasound with Doppler to assess kidney size and vascular flow
Empirical trial of high-dose oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg daily and recheck in 8 weeks

subtopic_detail: ACR/UPCR treatment threshold and ACEi/ARB role
stem: A 27-year-old previously well man is referred to nephrology after two episodes of frank haematuria coinciding with a sore throat. Renal biopsy six weeks ago confirmed IgA nephropathy with mesangial proliferation and no crescents. He has no rash, joint pain or systemic symptoms. Family history of CKD is negative. Today, after 12 weeks of lifestyle advice and observation, his BP is 138/88 mmHg, eGFR is 78 mL/min/1.73m^2 and stable, ACR is 78 mg/mmol (approximately 0.78 g/g; estimated 24-hour proteinuria 1.1 g) on first-morning samples on two occasions. Microscopic haematuria persists. He takes no regular medications. Hepatitis serology is negative.2 mmol/L. He has no signs of nephrotic syndrome and complement is normal.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 138/88 mmHg, HR 72.
data_table.Examination: No oedema, no rash, no joint swelling.
data_table.Investigations: Biopsy: IgA nephropathy, no crescents. eGFR 78 (stable), ACR 78 mg/mmol (confirmed), microscopic haematuria, K 4.2.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in his management?

options.text: Continue lifestyle measures alone and recheck urine ACR in six months' time
Commence high-dose IV cyclophosphamide induction immediately without further investigation
Commence high-dose oral prednisolone daily as first-line agent today
Refer for elective tonsillectomy as the patient's definitive disease-modifying therapy
Maximise ACE inhibitor or ARB, targeting BP < 120/70 mmHg and proteinuria < 1 g/day

stem:
A 64-year-old woman is admitted with three weeks of malaise, weight loss, sinus crusting and small-volume haemoptysis, on a background of two months of arthralgia. She has no history of smoking, no exposure to silica or solvents. Examination: BP 156/92 mmHg, saturation 95% on RA, scattered fine crackles bilaterally, mild ankle oedema, palpable purpura on the lower legs. Bloods on admission: creatinine 312 micromol/L (was 84 three months ago), eGFR 14, urea 28, K 4.8, Hb 96 g/L, platelets 380, WCC 11, CRP 124, ESR 92, albumin 28 g/L.

Urinalysis: blood 3+, protein 2+, red cell casts seen on phase-contrast microscopy. UPCR 180 mg/mmol. Serology: MPO-ANCA positive, PR3-ANCA negative, ANA negative, anti-GBM negative, complement C3 and C4 normal, hepatitis B/C and HIV negative. CT chest: bilateral peripheral ground-glass opacities. Renal biopsy is being arranged urgently.

data_table.Examination: Fine crackles bilaterally, palpable purpura lower legs, sinus crusting.
data_table.Investigations: Cr 312 (was 84), urea 28, K 4.8, Hb 96, CRP 124, MPO-ANCA positive, anti-GBM negative, urine red cell casts, UPCR 180 mg/mmol, CT chest peripheral GGO.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial induction regimen?

options.text: Oral prednisolone alone titrated to symptom control over weeks
IV methylprednisolone then oral prednisolone, plus rituximab (or cyclophosphamide), with PJP prophylaxis
Therapeutic plasma exchange alone as the sole intervention for induction
Oral mycophenolate mofetil 1 g twice daily as monotherapy for induction
Await renal biopsy result before starting any disease-modifying immunosuppression

stem:
A 38-year-old woman is admitted with three days of fatigue, easy bruising, and confusion. She had a vague URTI two weeks ago, denies diarrhoea, and is not pregnant (LMP one week ago). Medications: nil regular. No new drugs or supplements. Examination: T 37.8, BP 146/90, HR 104, GCS 14 (oriented to person, intermittent disorientation to place), petechiae on shins, mild jaundice, no lymphadenopathy.

Bloods: Hb 78 g/L with schistocytes on blood film, platelets 18 x10^9/L, LDH 1820 U/L, haptoglobin undetectable, indirect bilirubin elevated, DCT negative, INR 1.0, APTT normal, fibrinogen 3.2 g/L, creatinine 142 micromol/L (was 70), urea 12, troponin mildly elevated, urinalysis blood 1+ protein 1+. Stool culture for Shiga toxin-producing E. coli has been sent but is not yet back. ADAMTS13 activity has been sent.

data_table.Examination: GCS 14, intermittent disorientation, petechiae, mild jaundice.
data_table.Investigations: Hb 78 + schistocytes, plt 18, LDH 1820, haptoglobin undetectable, DCT negative, INR 1.0, fibrinogen 3.2, Cr 142 (was 70), troponin mildly raised.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step before ADAMTS13 results return?

options.text: Await stool Shiga toxin PCR and ADAMTS13 activity before any TMA-specific therapy
Transfuse 1 unit of platelets to raise the platelet count above 50 x10^9/L
Start eculizumab as the first-line therapy for presumed complement-mediated TMA
Commence urgent therapeutic plasma exchange and high-dose corticosteroids for empirical TTP
Commence broad-spectrum IV antibiotics for presumed sepsis-related disseminated intravascular coagulation

subtopic_detail: Acute interstitial nephritis vs acute tubular necrosis
stem:
A 62-year-old woman is referred to ED with a creatinine rise noted on routine bloods. Six weeks ago she was commenced on a proton pump inhibitor for reflux and three weeks ago she had a course of amoxicillin-clavulanate for sinusitis. She reports a non-pruritic maculopapular rash on her trunk over the last week, intermittent low-grade fever, and mild fatigue. She denies vomiting, diarrhoea, dehydration, NSAID use, or contrast exposure.

Her usual medications are perindopril and metformin. Examination: BP 134/82, HR 84, T 37.6, mild non-blanching erythematous rash trunk and proximal limbs, no oedema, JVP not raised, clear chest. Bloods: Cr 198 micromol/L (baseline 70), eGFR 28, K 4.4, HCO3 21, eosinophils 0.8 x10^9/L (raised), CRP 24. Urinalysis: blood trace, protein 1+, leucocytes 2+, nitrites negative. Urine microscopy: white cells present, no bacteria, no red cell casts; eosinophiluria reported on Wright stain. Renal tract US: normal-sized kidneys, no hydronephrosis.

data_table.Examination: Non-pruritic maculopapular rash trunk + proximal limbs, no oedema.
data_table.Investigations: Cr 198 (baseline 70), eGFR 28, peripheral eosinophils 0.8, urine WBC + eosinophiluria, no casts, US normal.
data_table.Medications: PPI (6/52), amoxicillin-clavulanate completed 1/52 ago, perindopril, metformin.

lead_in: Which is the most likely diagnosis and most appropriate next step?

options.text: Pre-renal AKI - hold the ACE inhibitor and rehydrate with IV crystalloid
Acute tubular necrosis - give IV crystalloid resuscitation and observe with serial bloods
Pyelonephritis - commence IV gentamicin and ceftriaxone after blood and urine cultures
Rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis - urgent biopsy and pulse IV methylprednisolone
Acute interstitial nephritis - withdraw the offending drug(s) and consider corticosteroids if no improvement

subtopic_detail: CK threshold, IV crystalloid, hyperkalaemia surveillance
stem:
A 52-year-old man is brought to ED after being found on the floor of his home approximately 18 hours after a fall complicated by alcohol intoxication. He has no head injury but is unable to bear weight on the left side due to pain. Past history: hypertension on perindopril, gout on allopurinol, harmful alcohol use. Examination: GCS 15, BP 132/82, HR 104, RR 18, T 36.8, SpO2 97% RA, dependent oedema and skin tenderness over the left thigh and calf, dark tea-coloured urine when catheterised.

Bloods on arrival: Cr 168 micromol/L (baseline 88), K 5.6, HCO3 19, Na 138, urea 12, glucose 6.0, CK 84,000 U/L, troponin not elevated, lactate 2.6, AST 380, ALT 110. Urinalysis: dipstick positive for blood 4+, but microscopy shows no red blood cells. ECG: sinus tachycardia, no peaked T waves. He has not taken statins recently and no other myotoxic drug exposure is identified.

data_table.Examination: Tender left thigh + calf, dark urine, dependent oedema.
data_table.Investigations: CK 84,000 U/L, Cr 168 (baseline 88), K 5.6, HCO3 19, urine dipstick blood 4+ but no RBC on micro, ECG sinus tachy.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril, allopurinol; no statin.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: IV furosemide 80 mg bolus to force diuresis through depleted tubules
Urgent haemodialysis via a temporary vascath to clear circulating myoglobin
Aggressive IV isotonic crystalloid (1-2 L/h) titrated to urine output 200-300 mL/h
IV mannitol 1 g/kg bolus to scavenge oxygen free radicals and force diuresis
Restrict fluids and observe given a normal blood pressure on arrival

stem:
A 74-year-old man with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 22 mL/min/1.73m^2) and heart failure attends ED with malaise and palpitations. Medications: irbesartan 300 mg, spironolactone 25 mg, furosemide 40 mg, metoprolol, atorvastatin. He was started on trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole 5 days ago for a UTI. Examination: BP 138/82, HR 52 regular, alert. Bloods on arrival: K 7.3 mmol/L, Na 134, Cr 248 micromol/L (was 198 last month), HCO3 19, glucose 6.4.

ECG shows sinus bradycardia with prolonged PR, broad QRS approximately 140 ms, and tall peaked T waves in V2-V5. You have given IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL over 2 minutes and the QRS narrows on repeat ECG.

data_table.Examination: Alert, well-perfused, mild peripheral oedema.
data_table.Investigations: K 7.3, Cr 248 (was 198), HCO3 19, ECG: peaked T waves, broad QRS 140 ms, prolonged PR.
data_table.Medications: Irbesartan, spironolactone, furosemide, metoprolol, TMP-SMX (5/7).

lead_in: Which combination is the most appropriate next set of interventions?

options.text: Repeat IV calcium gluconate 10 percent 10 mL every 30 minutes as the sole intervention, continue all current medications unchanged, and arrange urgent renal review for dialysis without further potassium-lowering therapy

IV actrapid insulin 10 units with 50 mL of 50 percent dextrose plus nebulised salbutamol 10 mg, stop irbesartan, spironolactone and trimethoprim-sulfamethoxazole, and arrange urgent renal review for dialysis

Oral sodium polystyrene sulfonate 30 g and IV furosemide 80 mg bolus as the shift and removal strategy, continue irbesartan and spironolactone at current doses, and admit for telemetry monitoring overnight
IV sodium bicarbonate 100 mmol over 30 minutes as the primary shift therapy, continue irbesartan and spironolactone at half dose, and arrange routine renal review at the next outpatient clinic
Withhold further potassium-lowering interventions, continue all current medications unchanged, and recheck the potassium in 4 hours, planning shift therapy only if it remains above 6.5 mmol/L

stem:
A 68-year-old woman is admitted from a residential aged care facility with two days of vomiting and reduced oral intake. She has long-standing heart failure on furosemide 80 mg daily and metolazone 2.5 mg three times weekly. Other medications include pantoprazole for several years, digoxin, perindopril and atorvastatin. Examination: BP 122/72, HR 96 with frequent ectopics, dry mucous membranes, no oedema.

Bloods on admission: K 2.6 mmol/L, Mg 0.55 mmol/L, Ca 2.30 corrected, Na 132, HCO3 32, Cr 142, eGFR 38, digoxin level pending. ECG: sinus rhythm 96, prominent U waves, occasional ventricular ectopics, QT prolonged at 480 ms. She has received 40 mmol of oral KCl slow-release tablets six hours ago at the facility but the potassium has not improved on the repeat venous sample. She is not on insulin and has no diabetic ketoacidosis.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 122/72, HR 96, ectopics frequent.
data_table.Examination: Dry mucous membranes, no oedema.
data_table.Investigations: K 2.6, Mg 0.55, Na 132, HCO3 32, Cr 142, ECG: U waves, QT 480 ms, ectopics.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in correcting her electrolytes?

options.text: Start an IV potassium infusion at 40 mmol/hour via peripheral cannula
Increase oral potassium chloride slow-release tablets to 80 mmol immediately
Replace magnesium intravenously (e.g. magnesium sulfate 10 mmol) alongside potassium replacement
Stop pantoprazole and recheck potassium in 48 hours
Give IV sodium bicarbonate for the alkalosis

subtopic_detail: Rate of correction and osmotic demyelination prevention
stem: A 62-year-old woman with a history of harmful alcohol use is brought to ED after being found drowsy. She has eaten poorly for two weeks. Examination: GCS 11, BP 110/70, HR 96, RR 14, T 36.5, weight 58 kg, mucous membranes moist, no peripheral oedema, no focal neurology. Bloods on arrival: Na 108 mmol/L, K 3.0, urea 2.4 mmol/L, glucose 4.2, serum osmolality 232 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 460 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 38 mmol/L, TSH normal, random cortisol normal. She has had one self-limited generalised tonic-clonic seizure since arrival.

data_table.Vital signs: GCS 11, BP 110/70, HR 96, T 36.5, weight 58 kg.
data_table.Examination: Mucous membranes moist, no oedema, no focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: Na 108, K 3.0, urea 2.4, glucose 4.2, serum osm 232, urine osm 460, urine Na 38, TSH and cortisol normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate immediate management?

options.text: IV 3% hypertonic saline 150 mL boluses, capping 24-hour rise at 8-10 mmol/L
IV 0.9% sodium chloride at 250 mL/h with hourly sodium measurement
Free water restriction to 800 mL daily as the sole acute intervention
Oral tolvaptan 15 mg now to block V2 receptors and aquarese free water
Allow spontaneous correction by treating the underlying cause over 24 hours

subtopic_detail: Outpatient SIADH workup - drug and paraneoplastic causes
stem:
A 72-year-old man is referred from his GP after an asymptomatic sodium of 124 mmol/L on a routine pre-operative panel. He has a 50-pack-year smoking history and a chronic cough for three months with mild weight loss. Medications: amlodipine, atorvastatin, sertraline (started six months ago) and carbamazepine (long-standing for trigeminal neuralgia). He denies polydipsia and is otherwise well. Examination: BP 132/78 lying and standing, JVP not raised, mucous membranes moist, no peripheral oedema, normal CVS and respiratory exam.

Bloods: Na 124, K 3.9, urea 3.0, creatinine 76 micromol/L, glucose 5.0, serum osmolality 258 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 412 mOsm/kg, urine sodium 48 mmol/L, TSH 1.8 mIU/L, 9 am cortisol 380 nmol/L.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 132/78 lying and standing, HR 76.
data_table.Examination: Euvolaemic, no oedema, no postural BP drop.
data_table.Investigations: Na 124, serum osm 258, urine osm 412, urine Na 48, TSH 1.8, cortisol 380.
data_table.Medications: Amlodipine, atorvastatin, sertraline, carbamazepine.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step in management?

options.text: Cease sertraline and carbamazepine simultaneously and recheck sodium in 2 weeks
Arrange CT chest with contrast and review medications with a structured taper plan
Commence tolvaptan 15 mg daily and titrate to sodium response over the next week
Empirical hypertonic 3 percent saline 100 mL bolus and admit for ongoing infusion
Restrict fluid intake to 800 mL daily and reassure that no further investigation is needed

subtopic_detail: Central vs nephrogenic - water deprivation + desmopressin
stem:
A 45-year-old woman is referred to endocrine clinic with three months of polyuria and polydipsia (estimated 6 to 7 L per day), worse at night. She has bipolar disorder on lithium 750 mg daily for 12 years, stable, with no recent mood episodes. Medications: lithium, escitalopram. BP 116/72, weight 64 kg, mucous membranes slightly dry. Bloods: Na 148 mmol/L, K 4.2, creatinine 92 micromol/L, eGFR 64, corrected calcium 2.34 mmol/L, glucose 5.2, HbA1c 38, TSH 1.6, lithium 0.7 mmol/L.

Plasma osmolality 308 mOsm/kg, urine osmolality 198 mOsm/kg. Water deprivation: urine osmolality 220 mOsm/kg after 6 hours, rising only to 245 mOsm/kg after subcutaneous desmopressin 2 microgram. Her psychiatrist has communicated that lithium remains the preferred mood stabiliser.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 116/72, HR 78, weight 64 kg.
data_table.Examination: Slightly dry mucous membranes, no focal neurology.
data_table.Investigations: Na 148, plasma osm 308, urine osm 198, water deprivation: urine osm 220 -> 245 after dDAVP, lithium 0.7, Ca 2.34.
data_table.Medications: Lithium 750 mg, escitalopram.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate ongoing management strategy?

options.text: Discontinue lithium immediately and switch to sodium valproate, then reassess polyuria in 6 weeks
Continue lithium, add amiloride 5 to 10 mg daily, ensure free access to water and monitor sodium and lithium levels
Commence intranasal desmopressin 10 microgram twice daily and continue lithium unchanged
Restrict fluid intake to 1.5 L daily and recheck sodium and lithium level in 4 weeks
Start a high-protein high-sodium diet to enhance free water clearance and continue lithium

subtopic_detail: Mixed disorder with delta-delta in DKA
stem: A 24-year-old woman with type 1 diabetes is brought to the emergency department with 2 days of vomiting and increasing drowsiness. She has not taken her basal insulin for 3 days. She is breathing deeply and rapidly, and her breath smells of ketones.

data_table.Vital signs: Pulse 124 /min, blood pressure 102/64 mmHg, respiratory rate 34 /min, SpO2 98% on 2 L/min oxygen, temperature 36.8°C
data_table.Examination: GCS 13; very dry mucous membranes; mildly tender abdomen
data_table.Investigations: Sodium 132 mmol/L (135-145), potassium 5.2 mmol/L (3.5-5.2), chloride 88 mmol/L (95-110), bicarbonate 6 mmol/L (22-32), albumin 36 g/L (35-50), glucose 32 mmol/L, beta-hydroxybutyrate 7.8 mmol/L (<0.6), lactate 1.8 mmol/L (<2.0); arterial gas pH 7.19 (7.35-7.45), PaCO2 16 mmHg (35-45)

lead_in: Which is the most accurate description of her acid-base disorder?

options.text: High anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation and a concurrent metabolic alkalosis
Pure high anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate Kussmaul respiratory compensation
Mixed high anion gap and normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with appropriate compensation
Primary respiratory alkalosis with secondary metabolic compensation through bicarbonate loss
Normal anion gap metabolic acidosis with a primary respiratory alkalosis overlay

subtopic_detail: Drug dose adjustment and avoidance in CKD
stem:
A 78-year-old woman with CKD stage 4 (eGFR 24 mL/min/1.73m^2) is reviewed after a fall. Medications: perindopril 5 mg, metformin 1 g BD, gabapentin 600 mg three times daily, morphine MR 30 mg twice daily, ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD (day 2 of 5 for uncomplicated UTI started by her GP), and apixaban 5 mg BD for atrial fibrillation. She weighs 58 kg.

She is drowsy and ataxic, but rousable, with no focal neurology and no head injury. BP 132/76. Bloods: Cr 220 micromol/L (was 195 last month), eGFR 24, K 4.8, HCO3 21, INR 1.1.

data_table.Examination: Drowsy, ataxic gait, no focal neurology.
data_table.Medications: Perindopril 5 mg, metformin 1 g BD, gabapentin 600 mg TDS, morphine MR 30 mg BD, ciprofloxacin 500 mg BD (day 2), apixaban 5 mg BD.

lead_in: Which combination of medication changes is most urgently required?

options.text: Reduce gabapentin dose, switch morphine to a less renally cleared opioid such as buprenorphine or fentanyl, and reduce apixaban to 2.5 mg BD given age over 80 and weight under 60 kg
Stop metformin permanently, continue gabapentin and morphine at current doses, and continue apixaban 5 mg BD
Switch apixaban to warfarin titrated to an INR of 2.0 to 3.0, continue gabapentin and morphine at current doses, and continue all other regular medications unchanged
Stop ciprofloxacin and switch to oral nitrofurantoin 100 mg twice daily for the remaining UTI course, with continuation of all other current medications at present doses
Stop perindopril today, continue all other regular medications at current doses, and recheck creatinine and potassium at the GP in 1 week

stem:
A 58-year-old woman presents to a tertiary emergency department with 2 hours of sudden dyspnoea and pre-syncope, 8 days after a right total knee replacement at a Central Coast LHD hospital. She is alert but ashen and cool. Heart rate 132 sinus, blood pressure 76/44 mmHg unresponsive to 1 L of compound sodium lactate, respiratory rate 32, SpO2 88% on 15 L non-rebreather.

Bedside transthoracic echocardiogram shows a severely dilated and hypokinetic right ventricle with septal bowing. Computed tomography pulmonary angiogram (CTPA) confirms bilateral central pulmonary artery filling defects. High-sensitivity troponin 480 ng/L (reference <14). Her surgical wound is dry and well-healed. There is no history of intracranial pathology, recent gastrointestinal bleeding, or stroke.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 76/44 after 1 L crystalloid, SpO2 88% on 15 L NRB, RR 32, T 36.6.
data_table.Echo: Severe RV dilatation and hypokinesis, septal bowing, no LV dysfunction.
data_table.Imaging: CTPA: bilateral central PA filling defects.
data_table.Bloods: hs-troponin 480 ng/L (<14), lactate 4.2 mmol/L, INR 1.0, platelets 240.
data_table.Surgical: Day 8 post right TKR; wound dry and clean.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next intervention?

options.text: Intravenous alteplase 100 mg over 2 hours plus unfractionated heparin
Therapeutic enoxaparin 1 mg/kg subcutaneously twice daily
Apixaban 10 mg orally twice daily for 7 days then 5 mg twice daily
Inferior vena caval filter placement after heparin loading
Bolus 1 L compound sodium lactate then reassess before further intervention

stem: A 24-year-old woman with known asthma (Step 3: budesonide-formoterol maintenance and reliever therapy) presents to a HNE LHD emergency department with progressive wheeze and dyspnoea for 8 hours. She is tachypnoeic and speaking in 2-word sentences. After 1 hour of back-to-back salbutamol 8 puffs via spacer every 20 minutes, ipratropium 8 puffs every 20 minutes, and oral prednisolone 50 mg, her status is reassessed.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 132, BP 138/84, SpO2 91% on 8 L Hudson mask, RR 32, T 37.0, peak expiratory flow 35% predicted.
data_table.Examination: Diffuse polyphonic wheeze, accessory muscle use, no silent chest, mild diaphoresis.
data_table.Bloods: Venous blood gas: pH 7.41, pCO2 36 mmHg, HCO3 22, K 3.4 mmol/L.
data_table.Treatment so far: 3 salbutamol/ipratropium nebulised sets, prednisolone 50 mg oral.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next pharmacological step?

options.text: Intravenous magnesium sulfate 2 g over 20 minutes
Intravenous aminophylline loading 5 mg/kg over 20 minutes
Intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg in place of oral prednisolone
Intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg
Initiate non-invasive positive pressure ventilation at 10/5 cmH2O

subtopic_detail: Adult step-up - SMART therapy and ICS-formoterol
stem:
A 32-year-old woman with adult-onset asthma uses salbutamol 6 to 8 puffs daily over the past month, has woken twice in the past week with cough and wheeze, and has used 2 short courses of prednisolone in the past 12 months. She is currently on budesonide-formoterol 200/6 microgram one inhalation twice daily as a preventer with salbutamol as a reliever.

Spirometry today: forced expiratory volume in 1 second (FEV1) 68% predicted, FEV1/forced vital capacity ratio 0.66, bronchodilator response +14%. Inhaler technique is verified satisfactory; adherence is self-reported at 5 of 7 days per week.

data_table.Symptom control: Daytime symptoms most days, 2 nocturnal episodes/week, salbutamol 6-8 puffs/day.
data_table.Current preventer: Budesonide-formoterol 200/6 mcg 1 puff bd + salbutamol reliever.
data_table.Exacerbations: 2 oral prednisolone courses in last 12 months.

lead_in: Which adjustment best optimises her asthma control?

options.text: Switch to budesonide-formoterol 200/6 mcg as both maintenance and reliever (SMART)
Add tiotropium 2.5 mcg 2 puffs daily without changing current preventer
Add montelukast 10 mg nocte and continue current preventer plus reliever
Commence daily oral prednisolone 5 mg as maintenance therapy
Refer for omalizumab subcutaneous injection

subtopic_detail: Near-fatal asthma - silent chest and intubation
stem: A 19-year-old man brought by ambulance is in extremis from acute asthma. He has had multiple presentations including one previous ICU admission. On arrival he is drowsy, slumped, with minimal chest movement. The chest is silent on auscultation. SpO2 84% on 15 L non-rebreather, heart rate 138 sinus, blood pressure 96/58 mmHg, respiratory rate 8 and shallow. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.18, pCO2 78 mmHg, pO2 56 mmHg, HCO3 24, lactate 5.2 mmol/L. He has received 3 salbutamol-ipratropium nebulisers, intramuscular adrenaline 0.5 mg, intravenous hydrocortisone 200 mg, and intravenous magnesium 2 g.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 96/58, SpO2 84% on 15 L NRB, RR 8 shallow, GCS 11.
data_table.Examination: Silent chest, minimal chest wall movement, diaphoretic, peripherally shut down.
data_table.ABG: pH 7.18, pCO2 78 mmHg, pO2 56 mmHg, HCO3 24, lactate 5.2 mmol/L.
data_table.Treatment so far: 3x neb salbutamol/ipratropium, IM adrenaline 0.5 mg, IV hydrocortisone 200 mg, IV magnesium 2 g.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Rapid sequence intubation with ketamine and rocuronium
Bilevel non-invasive positive pressure ventilation 14/6 cmH2O via full face mask
Intravenous adrenaline infusion at 5 microgram/min titrated upwards
Repeat intravenous magnesium 2 g over 20 minutes
Heliox (70:30 helium-oxygen) via tight-fitting mask

stem: A 68-year-old man with chronic obstructive pulmonary disease (COPD), 40-pack-year smoking history and previous FEV1 42% predicted presents with 4 days of worsening dyspnoea, increased sputum volume and a change from clear to yellow-green sputum. He is afebrile, heart rate 96, blood pressure 132/78, respiratory rate 22, SpO2 88% on room air, 92% on 2 L nasal prongs. Chest x-ray shows hyperinflation without consolidation. He has had 2 exacerbations in the past 12 months and lives independently with his wife.

data_table.Examination: Bilateral wheeze, prolonged expiration, no crackles, no consolidation.
data_table.Imaging: CXR: hyperinflation, no infiltrate.
data_table.Bloods: C-reactive protein 38 mg/L, WCC 11.2.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate antibiotic decision?

options.text: Amoxicillin 500 mg orally 8-hourly for 5 days
Doxycycline 100 mg orally 12-hourly for 5 days
Amoxicillin-clavulanate 875/125 mg orally 12-hourly for 7 days
Azithromycin 500 mg orally daily for 3 days
Withhold antibiotic and treat with bronchodilators and steroid alone

subtopic_detail: Stable COPD - inhaler escalation by phenotype
stem: A 72-year-old man with COPD (post-bronchodilator FEV1 48% predicted) is reviewed in the respiratory clinic. He has been on tiotropium 18 mcg once daily for 18 months. He reports increasing dyspnoea on walking the dog and 3 moderate exacerbations in the past 12 months (one hospitalised). He has no asthma history. Eosinophil count is 0.42 x10^9/L (reference 0.02-0.5).

data_table.Symptoms: Modified MRC dyspnoea 3, COPD assessment test 22.
data_table.Lung function: Post-BD FEV1 48% predicted, FEV1/FVC 0.58, no asthma reversibility.
data_table.Exacerbations: 3 moderate exacerbations in past 12 months, 1 hospitalisation.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step in pharmacotherapy?

options.text: Add an inhaled corticosteroid-long-acting beta agonist combination to current tiotropium
Replace tiotropium with inhaled corticosteroid monotherapy
Add long-acting beta agonist to tiotropium without inhaled corticosteroid
Add azithromycin 250 mg orally three times weekly
Add oral theophylline 200 mg twice daily

stem: A 74-year-old woman with severe COPD presents with acute exacerbation. Despite 90 minutes of optimised medical therapy (controlled oxygen via Venturi mask titrated to SpO2 88-92%, nebulised salbutamol and ipratropium, oral prednisolone 50 mg, intravenous ceftriaxone), she remains dyspnoeic. She is alert and cooperative. Arterial blood gas: pH 7.26, pCO2 78 mmHg, pO2 62 mmHg on 28% FiO2, HCO3 32 mmol/L. There is no pneumothorax on chest x-ray.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 110, BP 142/86, SpO2 90% on 28% Venturi, RR 28, alert.
data_table.ABG: pH 7.26, pCO2 78 mmHg, pO2 62 mmHg on 28% FiO2, HCO3 32, BE +5.
data_table.Imaging: CXR: hyperinflation, no pneumothorax, no consolidation.
data_table.Medical therapy so far: 90 min: controlled O2, neb bronchodilator, oral prednisolone, IV antibiotic.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Bilevel non-invasive ventilation starting at IPAP 12 EPAP 5 cmH2O
Increase oxygen via Hudson mask to 8 L/min and reassess in 30 minutes
Intubate and commence invasive mechanical ventilation
Intravenous doxapram infusion as a respiratory stimulant
Continuous positive airway pressure at 7.5 cmH2O via full face mask

subtopic_detail: Type 1 vs type 2 failure - mechanism inversion
stem: A medical registrar is teaching about respiratory failure. She draws four pathophysiological mechanisms on the board: (1) ventilation-perfusion mismatch with preserved alveolar ventilation; (2) alveolar hypoventilation with normal alveolar-arterial oxygen gradient; (3) right-to-left shunt unresponsive to oxygen therapy; (4) impaired diffusion across the alveolar-capillary membrane.
lead_in: Which clinical scenario best matches pattern 2 (alveolar hypoventilation with normal A-a gradient)?

options.text: Opioid overdose with respiratory rate 6 and pinpoint pupils
Acute pulmonary embolism with sudden dyspnoea and SpO2 88%
Severe lobar pneumonia with consolidation and oxygen-refractory hypoxaemia
Pulmonary fibrosis with chronic exertional dyspnoea and clubbing
Acute severe asthma with diffuse wheeze and rising pCO2

stem: A 26-year-old man is hit in the chest while playing rugby. Brought to the emergency department 30 minutes later he is increasingly agitated, with severe dyspnoea, asymmetric chest expansion, hyper-resonance over the right hemithorax with absent breath sounds, and tracheal deviation to the left. Heart rate 138, blood pressure 78/44, SpO2 84% on 15 L non-rebreather, distended neck veins.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 138, BP 78/44, SpO2 84% on 15 L NRB, RR 36, agitated.
data_table.Examination: Right hemithorax: hyper-resonant, absent breath sounds, reduced expansion; trachea deviated left; raised JVP.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate immediate intervention?

options.text: Needle thoracostomy at right second intercostal space mid-clavicular line
Needle thoracostomy at right fifth intercostal space anterior axillary line
Urgent erect chest x-ray to confirm pneumothorax before intervention
Bedside thoracic ultrasound to confirm absent lung sliding
Insert 32 French intercostal catheter immediately as primary intervention

stem: A 22-year-old tall, thin male non-smoker presents with sudden right-sided pleuritic chest pain and mild dyspnoea that began 6 hours ago while sitting still. He has no past medical history. He is comfortable, heart rate 88, blood pressure 124/76, SpO2 97% room air, respiratory rate 16. Chest x-ray shows a right-sided pneumothorax measuring 1.8 cm at the level of the hilum (interpleural distance). There is no mediastinal shift.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 88, BP 124/76, SpO2 97% RA, RR 16, comfortable.
data_table.Imaging: Right pneumothorax, interpleural distance 1.8 cm at hilar level, no mediastinal shift.
data_table.Examination: Mildly reduced right-sided breath sounds, no tracheal deviation.
data_table.History: First episode, primary (no underlying lung disease), non-smoker.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate management?

options.text: Needle aspiration via the 2nd intercostal space mid-clavicular line
Conservative observation with high-flow oxygen and admission
Insertion of 14 French Seldinger intercostal catheter to underwater seal
Discharge home with primary care follow-up in 1 week
Surgical referral for video-assisted thoracoscopic bullectomy and pleurodesis

stem: A 64-year-old man with heart failure on furosemide presents with progressive dyspnoea and a left-sided pleural effusion. Diagnostic thoracentesis is performed. Pleural fluid analysis: protein 31 g/L, lactate dehydrogenase (LDH) 280 U/L; serum protein 64 g/L, serum LDH 220 U/L. Pleural fluid pH 7.42, glucose 5.6 mmol/L, no organisms on Gram stain, cytology pending. He received intravenous furosemide for 3 days prior to thoracentesis.

data_table.Pleural fluid: Protein 31 g/L, LDH 280 U/L, pH 7.42, glucose 5.6 mmol/L.
data_table.Recent treatment: IV furosemide 3 days prior to tap.
data_table.Background: Heart failure, on furosemide.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate interpretation?

options.text: Exudate by Light criteria; warrants exudate workup including CT chest
Transudate consistent with heart failure given clinical context and diuretic effect
Parapneumonic effusion requiring intercostal catheter insertion
Malignant effusion; arrange pleurodesis as definitive management
Tuberculous effusion; commence empirical antituberculous therapy

stem: A 58-year-old woman with community-acquired pneumonia not improving after 48 hours of intravenous ceftriaxone and azithromycin develops a moderate left-sided pleural effusion. Bedside ultrasound shows a complex septated collection. Thoracentesis: pleural fluid pH 7.05, glucose 1.6 mmol/L, LDH 1850 U/L, protein 48 g/L, white cell count 28 x10^9/L (neutrophil predominant), Gram stain shows gram-positive cocci in chains, no growth yet on culture.

data_table.Pleural fluid: pH 7.05, glucose 1.6 mmol/L, LDH 1850 U/L, protein 48 g/L, WCC 28 (neutrophilic).
data_table.Microbiology: Gram-positive cocci in chains on Gram stain; culture pending.
data_table.Imaging: Bedside US: moderate left effusion with multiple internal septations.
data_table.Treatment so far: 48 h IV ceftriaxone + azithromycin for CAP.
data_table.Clinical: Persistent fever, raised WCC, ongoing dyspnoea.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Intercostal catheter drainage and continue current antibiotics
Continue antibiotics for 5 more days before considering drainage
Repeat diagnostic thoracentesis in 24 hours to reassess pH
Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery (VATS) decortication now
Broaden antibiotics to meropenem and vancomycin without drainage

stem: A 67-year-old woman with metastatic breast carcinoma presents with breathlessness from a large right-sided pleural effusion. Cytology of a previous thoracentesis confirmed malignant cells. She has had three therapeutic taps in the past 6 weeks, with rapid re-accumulation each time. She has a good performance status (ECOG 1) and life expectancy estimated at 9 to 12 months. Bedside ultrasound shows the lung re-expands fully after drainage. She prioritises symptom control and minimising hospital time.

data_table.Diagnosis: Metastatic breast cancer, cytology-positive malignant pleural effusion.
data_table.Recurrence pattern: 3 therapeutic thoracenteses in 6 weeks, rapid re-accumulation.
data_table.Lung re-expansion: Full re-expansion after drainage on US.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate definitive intervention?

options.text: Indwelling pleural catheter for ambulatory drainage at home
Talc slurry pleurodesis via intercostal catheter
Continue intermittent therapeutic thoracentesis as required
Video-assisted thoracoscopic surgery and mechanical pleurodesis
Systemic chemotherapy escalation without local pleural intervention

stem: A 34-year-old man who arrived in Sydney from Vietnam 18 months ago presents with 6 weeks of low-grade fever, drenching night sweats, weight loss of 8 kg, and progressive right-sided pleuritic chest pain. Chest x-ray shows a moderate right pleural effusion without parenchymal consolidation. Thoracentesis: straw-coloured fluid, protein 52 g/L (serum 70), LDH 540 U/L (serum 240), pH 7.36, glucose 3.4 mmol/L, white cell count 4.8 x10^9/L (lymphocyte predominant 88%), adenosine deaminase (ADA) 78 U/L. Acid-fast bacilli smear is negative. Mantoux 18 mm.

data_table.Pleural fluid: Protein 52 g/L (S 70), LDH 540 (S 240), pH 7.36, glucose 3.4, WCC 4.8 (88% lymphs), ADA 78 U/L.
data_table.Imaging: CXR: moderate right effusion, no parenchymal consolidation.
data_table.Background: Migrated from Vietnam 18 months ago; constitutional symptoms 6 weeks.

lead_in: What is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Commence rifampicin, isoniazid, pyrazinamide and ethambutol after notification to NSW Health
Defer treatment pending pleural biopsy and mycobacterial culture (6 weeks)
Empirical antibiotics for community-acquired pneumonia and reassess in 1 week
Intercostal catheter drainage and pleurodesis to control reaccumulation
Quantiferon-TB Gold testing to confirm diagnosis before treatment

stem: Five patients have confirmed pulmonary embolism with haemodynamic instability requiring vasopressor support, and systemic thrombolysis is being considered for each.

data_table.Patient A: Transient ischaemic attack 4 months ago, fully recovered, on aspirin.
data_table.Patient B: Cerebral metastasis from lung cancer, diagnosed last month.
data_table.Patient E: Active duodenal ulcer seen at endoscopy 2 weeks ago, no bleeding since.

lead_in: Which patient has an absolute contraindication to systemic thrombolysis?

options.text: Patient A - transient ischaemic attack 4 months ago
Patient B - cerebral metastasis diagnosed last month
Patient C - warfarin for atrial fibrillation, INR 2.3
Patient D - uncomplicated vaginal birth 4 days ago
Patient E - active duodenal ulcer, no bleeding since

stem: A 68-year-old woman with severe COPD (post-bronchodilator FEV1 28% predicted) on optimised inhaled triple therapy is reviewed at the respiratory clinic 6 weeks after an exacerbation. She has stopped smoking 8 months ago. Arterial blood gas on room air at rest: pH 7.41, pCO2 48 mmHg, pO2 54 mmHg, SpO2 88%, HCO3 30 mmol/L. Repeat ABG 3 weeks later under stable conditions: pO2 56 mmHg, SpO2 88%. She has secondary polycythaemia (haematocrit 0.58) and lower-limb peripheral oedema with raised JVP suggesting cor pulmonale.

data_table.ABG (stable, RA, on 2 occasions): pO2 54-56 mmHg, SpO2 88%, pCO2 48 mmHg, pH 7.41.
data_table.Right heart: Raised JVP, peripheral oedema, ECG p-pulmonale - cor pulmonale.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate decision regarding long-term oxygen therapy?

options.text: Commence home oxygen at 1-2 L/min for at least 15 hours per day
Continue current therapy and reassess for LTOT in 6 months
Commence nocturnal-only home oxygen as initial trial
Defer until smoking cessation is verified for 12 months
Therapeutic venesection for polycythaemia before considering oxygen

subtopic_detail: Side-effect to drug mapping - inhaled therapy
stem: A 45-year-old man with asthma develops oral candidiasis, dysphonia and easy skin bruising 6 months after starting a new asthma controller. He uses the device twice daily with adequate technique.

data_table.Adverse effects: Oral candidiasis (white plaques on tongue/buccal mucosa), dysphonia (hoarse voice), easy skin bruising on forearms.
data_table.Duration of use: 6 months on new controller, twice daily, good inhaler technique.
data_table.Other meds: Salbutamol PRN, no oral corticosteroid courses in past 12 months.
data_table.Examination: Multiple ecchymoses forearms, oral thrush confirmed on swab.

lead_in: Which medication class is most likely responsible?

options.text: Inhaled corticosteroid
Long-acting beta agonist (LABA)
Long-acting muscarinic antagonist (LAMA)
Leukotriene receptor antagonist (montelukast)
Theophylline

subtopic_detail: ARDS - ventilator strategy and prone positioning
stem: A 56-year-old man admitted with severe community-acquired pneumonia has been intubated and ventilated for 36 hours in the intensive care unit. Despite optimised therapy he meets the Berlin definition of acute respiratory distress syndrome (ARDS). Current ventilator settings: volume control, tidal volume 7 mL/kg predicted body weight, respiratory rate 20, FiO2 0.8, positive end-expiratory pressure (PEEP) 12. PaO2/FiO2 ratio 92 mmHg. He has not been pharmacologically paralysed. Plateau pressure 32 cmH2O. No pneumothorax. Bilateral patchy infiltrates on chest x-ray.

data_table.Vent settings: VC, TV 7 mL/kg PBW, RR 20, FiO2 0.8, PEEP 12, P-plateau 32 cmH2O.
data_table.Imaging: Bilateral patchy infiltrates, no pneumothorax.
data_table.Background: Severe CAP, 36 h intubated, Berlin criteria met.

lead_in: Which intervention is the most appropriate next step?

options.text: Prone position the patient for at least 16 hours per day
Increase tidal volume to 10 mL/kg to improve minute ventilation
Switch to high-frequency oscillatory ventilation
Reduce PEEP to 5 cmH2O to lower plateau pressure
Commence inhaled nitric oxide at 20 parts per million

stem:
A 38-year-old woman presents to the emergency department with 12 hours of pleuritic right-sided chest pain and mild dyspnoea. She is on the combined oral contraceptive pill, has no prior venous thromboembolism, and recently completed a 5-hour flight from Perth 3 days ago. Examination is unremarkable. Heart rate 92, blood pressure 124/76, SpO2 97% room air, respiratory rate 18, afebrile.

Two-level Wells score for PE: 3 (clinical signs of DVT 0, alternative diagnosis less likely 3, HR >100 0, immobilisation/surgery 0, prior DVT/PE 0, haemoptysis 0, malignancy 0).

data_table.Examination: Unremarkable; no DVT signs, no haemoptysis.

lead_in: What is the most appropriate next investigation?

options.text: Age-adjusted D-dimer measurement
Immediate computed tomography pulmonary angiogram
Ventilation-perfusion (V/Q) scan
Bilateral lower limb compression ultrasound
Empirical therapeutic anticoagulation pending further workup

subtopic_detail: GPA - induction immunosuppression for severe disease
stem:
A 54-year-old woman is referred to your general medicine clinic with 8 weeks of nasal crusting, a saddle-nose deformity that has developed over the last month, intermittent haemoptysis, and progressive fatigue. She has lost 6 kg unintentionally. Over the past week she has noticed dark frothy urine. She has no significant past history and takes no regular medications. Examination shows nasal septal perforation, scattered bibasal crackles, and lower-limb pitting oedema to mid-shin.

Blood pressure is 158/92, HR 88, SpO2 96% on room air, afebrile. Bloods show haemoglobin 92 g/L, white cell count 12.4 x10^9/L, platelets 480, creatinine 184 micromol/L (baseline 70 six months ago), CRP 88. Urinalysis shows 3+ blood and 2+ protein with dysmorphic red cells and red cell casts on microscopy. Urine protein:creatinine ratio is 320 mg/mmol. Chest CT shows multiple bilateral cavitating nodules up to 2 cm. PR3-ANCA is strongly positive at 110 U/mL (negative <20); MPO-ANCA is negative. A renal biopsy shows pauci-immune crescentic glomerulonephritis with 60% cellular crescents.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 158/92, HR 88, SpO2 96% room air, afebrile.
data_table.Bloods: Hb 92, WCC 12.4, plt 480, creatinine 184 (baseline 70), CRP 88.
data_table.Urine: 3+ blood, 2+ protein, RBC casts, uPCR 320 mg/mmol.
data_table.Imaging: CT chest: multiple bilateral cavitating nodules up to 2 cm.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate induction regimen?

options.text: Pulsed IV methylprednisolone 500 mg daily for 3 days then oral prednisolone, with weekly oral methotrexate
Pulsed IV methylprednisolone 500 mg daily for 3 days then oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day with rituximab 375 mg/m2 weekly for 4 weeks
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day with azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day from day 1
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day with mycophenolate mofetil 1 g twice daily for 6 months
Plasma exchange alone for 7 sessions with adjunctive oral prednisolone 0.5 mg/kg/day, deferring cytotoxic therapy

subtopic_detail: EGPA - distinguishing features and asthma context
stem:
A 46-year-old man presents to your hospital clinic with 3 months of progressively poor asthma control despite escalating combination ICS/LABA and a 2-week course of oral prednisolone. Over the last 3 weeks he has developed numbness and weakness in the right foot with a foot drop, and a non-blanching purpuric rash on both shins. He has had nasal polyps removed twice and has a history of allergic rhinitis.

Today he reports new pleuritic left-sided chest pain and one episode of haemoptysis (small streak). Vital signs are HR 102, BP 134/82, SpO2 94% on room air, RR 22, afebrile. Examination shows scattered wheeze, palpable purpura on shins, and right common peroneal palsy with absent dorsiflexion. Bloods show haemoglobin 134, white cell count 16.8 with eosinophils 4.8 x10^9/L (reference <0.4), platelets 360, creatinine 92 (baseline 80), CRP 64.

IgE is 980 IU/mL (<100). p-ANCA/MPO-ANCA is positive at 78 U/mL. PR3-ANCA negative. Urinalysis shows trace blood, no protein. Chest CT shows patchy bilateral ground-glass infiltrates. Nerve conduction studies confirm mononeuritis multiplex.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 102, BP 134/82, SpO2 94% room air, RR 22, afebrile.
data_table.Bloods: Hb 134, WCC 16.8, eos 4.8 (ref <0.4), plt 360, creatinine 92, CRP 64.
data_table.Serology: MPO-ANCA 78 U/mL, PR3-ANCA negative, IgE 980 IU/mL.
data_table.Imaging: CT chest: patchy bilateral ground-glass infiltrates.

lead_in: Which feature most strongly supports EGPA over alternative ANCA-associated vasculitides?

options.text: MPO-ANCA positivity at 78 U/mL
Eosinophil count of 4.8 x10^9/L on a background of poorly controlled asthma and nasal polyposis
Palpable purpura on the shins with normal renal function
Mononeuritis multiplex involving the common peroneal nerve
Bilateral ground-glass pulmonary infiltrates on CT

subtopic_detail: Takayasu arteritis - imaging and initial treatment
stem:
A 28-year-old woman of South Asian background presents to your medical assessment unit with 4 months of fatigue, intermittent low-grade fever and 5 kg weight loss. Over the last 6 weeks she has developed claudication in the right arm after vacuuming, and a recent episode of transient left visual blurring lasting 10 minutes. Examination shows BP 168/96 in the left arm, unrecordable in the right arm, a right supraclavicular bruit, asymmetric radial pulses with right radial weaker than left, and a soft bruit over the abdominal aorta.

There is no rash, no synovitis. She has no recent travel, no IVDU. Bloods show haemoglobin 108, WCC 8.2, platelets 460, ESR 76 mm/h, CRP 58, creatinine 72. ANCA, ANA, hepatitis serology, IGRA and blood cultures are negative. An echocardiogram is normal. The renal arteries appear normal on ultrasound. The medical registrar is considering imaging.

data_table.Vital signs: BP left arm 168/96, right arm unrecordable, HR 84, afebrile today.
data_table.Examination: Right radial pulse diminished, right supraclavicular bruit, abdominal aortic bruit.
data_table.Bloods: Hb 108, WCC 8.2, plt 460, ESR 76, CRP 58, creatinine 72.
data_table.Serology: ANCA neg, ANA neg, IGRA neg, hepatitis neg, blood cultures neg.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next diagnostic investigation?

options.text: Temporal artery biopsy of a 2 cm segment of the right superficial temporal artery
CT angiography of the aorta and major branches from arch to iliac bifurcation
Carotid duplex ultrasound alone
Catheter-based digital subtraction angiography of the aortic arch
Whole-body FDG-PET without companion CT or MR

subtopic_detail: GCA - confirmatory testing once steroid started
stem:
A 74-year-old woman presents to your emergency department with a 3-day history of new right-sided temporal headache, scalp tenderness when brushing her hair, and jaw claudication after 3 minutes of chewing. She had one episode of transient monocular vision loss in the right eye lasting 5 minutes this morning. She has bilateral shoulder and hip-girdle stiffness for 6 weeks. Vital signs are HR 78, BP 142/82, SpO2 98% on room air, afebrile.

Examination shows a tender, nodular right temporal artery with diminished pulsation; visual acuity is 6/6 both eyes; fundoscopy is normal. Bloods show haemoglobin 116, WCC 9.4, platelets 480, ESR 92 mm/h, CRP 96, creatinine 78. After consultation with the on-call ophthalmologist and rheumatologist, you administer IV methylprednisolone 1 g and arrange admission. The team plans temporal artery biopsy.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 78, BP 142/82, SpO2 98% room air, afebrile.
data_table.Examination: Tender nodular right temporal artery, diminished pulsation. VA 6/6 bilaterally. Fundi normal.
data_table.Bloods: Hb 116, WCC 9.4, plt 480, ESR 92, CRP 96, creatinine 78.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate timing for temporal artery biopsy?

options.text: Within 24 hours of steroid initiation, prioritising urgent referral
Within 2 weeks of steroid initiation, with a minimum biopsy length of 1 cm
After 4 to 6 weeks of steroid response to confirm the diagnosis biochemically
Only if temporal artery ultrasound shows no halo sign or compression sign
Defer biopsy indefinitely if the patient improves clinically on steroid

subtopic_detail: Early RA - first-line DMARD and time-to-treatment
stem:
A 38-year-old woman presents to your general medicine clinic with 10 weeks of symmetrical pain and swelling in the MCP and PIP joints of both hands, both wrists, and the MTPs of both feet. She has morning stiffness lasting 90 minutes. She is otherwise well and not pregnant; she uses condoms for contraception. Examination shows synovitis at 14 joints (8 small joint involvement).

Bloods show haemoglobin 122, WCC 9.6, platelets 420, creatinine 72, ALT 28, ESR 48 mm/h, CRP 32, anti-CCP positive at 240 U/mL (negative <20), rheumatoid factor positive 96 IU/mL. Hepatitis B sAg and anti-HCV are negative. Chest X-ray is normal. Hand X-rays show periarticular osteopenia without erosions. She meets ACR/EULAR criteria for RA with a score of 8/10.

data_table.Examination: Synovitis at 14 joints; 8 small joints; symmetrical; morning stiffness 90 min.
data_table.Bloods: Hb 122, WCC 9.6, plt 420, creatinine 72, ALT 28, ESR 48, CRP 32.
data_table.Serology: Anti-CCP 240 (neg <20), RF 96, hep B sAg neg, anti-HCV neg.
data_table.Imaging: Hand XR: periarticular osteopenia, no erosions. CXR normal.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate initial DMARD strategy?

options.text: Sulfasalazine 1 g twice daily monotherapy with folic acid
Hydroxychloroquine 5 mg/kg/day monotherapy with baseline ophthalmology review
Methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid 5 mg on a different day, escalating to 25 mg weekly as tolerated, plus a short prednisolone bridge
Combination methotrexate, sulfasalazine and hydroxychloroquine triple therapy initiated simultaneously
Initiate a TNF-alpha inhibitor (adalimumab) upfront without trialling conventional DMARDs

subtopic_detail: Methotrexate safety - pre-prescription checks and monitoring
stem:
A 52-year-old man with newly diagnosed seropositive rheumatoid arthritis is to commence methotrexate. He drinks 18 standard drinks per week, has a BMI of 32, and was born in Vietnam. He has no significant past medical history and takes paracetamol as needed. Baseline bloods show haemoglobin 138, WCC 8.4, platelets 290, creatinine 78, eGFR 88, ALT 64 (reference <40), AST 52, albumin 38.

Hepatitis B surface antigen is negative, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs negative. Anti-HCV negative. HIV negative. IGRA negative. Chest X-ray is unremarkable. He has not had any vaccinations in adulthood.

data_table.Background: BMI 32, alcohol 18 std drinks/week, born Vietnam.
data_table.Bloods: Hb 138, WCC 8.4, plt 290, creatinine 78, eGFR 88, ALT 64 (<40), AST 52, albumin 38.
data_table.Serology: HBsAg neg, anti-HBc positive, anti-HBs neg, anti-HCV neg, HIV neg, IGRA neg.

lead_in: Which issue most needs to be addressed BEFORE initiating methotrexate?

options.text: Brisk alcohol reduction counselling, with a target of fewer than 4 standard drinks per week while on methotrexate
Workup for occult hepatitis B reactivation risk: HBV DNA and gastroenterology referral for antiviral prophylaxis
Repeat fasting LFTs in 4 weeks and defer methotrexate if ALT remains above 60
Vaccinate against influenza, pneumococcal disease, COVID-19 and varicella with live and inactivated vaccines as appropriate
Repeat IGRA in 8 weeks before initiating any DMARD therapy

subtopic_detail: RA in pregnancy - DMARD switch and flare management
stem: A 31-year-old woman with seropositive RA in remission for 18 months on methotrexate 20 mg weekly and folic acid presents to your clinic. She has been using condoms but tells you today that she and her partner want to start trying for a pregnancy. She has had no flares for 12 months and her last DAS28 was 1.8. She has no comorbidities, takes no other medications, and her last bloods 6 weeks ago showed normal FBC, UEC and LFTs. She asks how to plan this.

data_table.Current Tx: Methotrexate 20 mg weekly, folic acid 5 mg on a non-MTX day.
data_table.Disease activity: DAS28 1.8 at last review, remission 18 months.
data_table.Bloods: FBC, UEC, LFTs normal 6 weeks ago.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate pre-conception medication plan?

options.text: Cease methotrexate immediately, wait 1 month, then attempt conception while monitoring for flare
Cease methotrexate, switch to hydroxychloroquine 5 mg/kg/day with or without sulfasalazine, and attempt conception after a 1 to 3 month washout
Continue methotrexate until pregnancy is confirmed, then cease immediately
Cease methotrexate and switch to leflunomide as a steroid-sparing alternative
Continue methotrexate and add high-dose folic acid 5 mg daily to mitigate fetal harm

subtopic_detail: Psoriatic arthritis - pattern recognition and first-line therapy
stem:
A 44-year-old man presents to your general medicine clinic with 4 months of progressive pain and swelling in his right index DIP and left great toe DIP, with sausage swelling of the entire 3rd left toe. He has plaque psoriasis on his scalp and elbows for 10 years, managed with topical calcipotriol/betamethasone, and pitting of several nails. There is no axial pain.

Examination shows synovitis at the right 2nd DIP and left great toe DIP, dactylitis of the left 3rd toe, and three nail-pits on the left thumb. Bloods show normal FBC, UEC, LFTs; ESR 28, CRP 18; RF and anti-CCP negative; HLA-B27 not tested. Hand and foot X-rays show pencil-in-cup deformity at the right 2nd DIP and juxta-articular new bone formation at the left 1st DIP. There is no axial involvement on examination.

data_table.Examination: DIP synovitis right 2nd, left 1st toe; dactylitis left 3rd toe; nail pits; psoriasis scalp/elbows.
data_table.Bloods: Normal FBC/UEC/LFTs; ESR 28, CRP 18; RF neg, anti-CCP neg.
data_table.Imaging: Pencil-in-cup right 2nd DIP; juxta-articular new bone left 1st DIP.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate first-line systemic DMARD?

options.text: Methotrexate 15 mg weekly with folic acid, escalating as tolerated
Sulfasalazine 1 g twice daily, escalating to 2 g twice daily
Adalimumab 40 mg subcutaneously every 2 weeks as first-line therapy
Hydroxychloroquine 5 mg/kg/day as a steroid-sparing agent
Oral prednisolone 15 mg daily long-term as monotherapy

subtopic_detail: Systemic sclerosis - early detection of renal crisis
stem:
A 56-year-old woman with diffuse cutaneous systemic sclerosis (anti-RNA polymerase III positive) diagnosed 14 months ago presents to your emergency department with 5 days of progressive headache and visual blurring, and a new dry cough. She is on prednisolone 25 mg daily commenced 3 weeks ago for myositis overlap, plus mycophenolate 1 g twice daily, omeprazole, and amlodipine 5 mg.

She has no chest pain. Vital signs are BP 198/122, HR 102, SpO2 96% on room air, afebrile. Examination shows widespread skin tightening, bibasal crackles, normal heart sounds, and grade III hypertensive retinopathy on fundoscopy. Bloods show haemoglobin 88 g/L (was 122 a month ago) with schistocytes on film, platelets 78 (was 240), creatinine 286 (baseline 78), LDH 1850, haptoglobin <0.1, direct Coombs negative, ADAMTS13 activity 65%. Urinalysis 2+ protein, 1+ blood. CT brain is unremarkable.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 198/122, HR 102, SpO2 96% room air, afebrile.
data_table.Examination: Tight skin, bibasal crackles, grade III hypertensive retinopathy.
data_table.Bloods: Hb 88 (was 122), schistocytes+, plt 78 (was 240), creatinine 286 (baseline 78), LDH 1850, haptoglobin <0.1, Coombs neg, ADAMTS13 65%.
data_table.Imaging: CT brain normal.
data_table.Background: Diffuse SSc, RNA-pol III+, prednisolone 25 mg/day x 3 weeks.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate immediate treatment?

options.text: IV hydralazine and IV labetalol titrated to a 25% MAP reduction over 1 hour
Oral captopril 12.5 mg starting dose, uptitrated 6 to 8 hourly to achieve BP control even at the expense of further short-term creatinine rise
Urgent plasma exchange for thrombotic microangiopathy with adjunctive caplacizumab
High-dose IV methylprednisolone 1 g daily for 3 days to suppress the underlying autoimmune disease
Sublingual nifedipine 10 mg every 30 minutes until BP <160/100

subtopic_detail: Hydroxychloroquine retinopathy - screening protocol and dose
stem:
A 42-year-old woman with SLE diagnosed 18 months ago is reviewed in your medicine clinic. She is in clinical remission on hydroxychloroquine 400 mg daily and low-dose prednisolone 5 mg. Her weight is 58 kg, eGFR 78, and she has no liver disease. Past medications include tamoxifen 5 years ago for DCIS. Visual acuity is 6/6 bilaterally and she reports no visual symptoms.

The previous registrar arranged baseline ophthalmology assessment at diagnosis which was normal. She asks how often she needs eye reviews and whether her dose is appropriate.

data_table.Background: SLE x 18 months, weight 58 kg, eGFR 78, prior tamoxifen 5 years ago.
data_table.Eyes: VA 6/6 bilateral, no symptoms, baseline ophthalmology normal at diagnosis.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate hydroxychloroquine dose and retinopathy screening plan?

options.text: Continue 400 mg daily; arrange repeat ophthalmology screening at 5 years from initiation, then annually
Reduce to 300 mg daily (or alternate 200 mg/400 mg days); maintain annual ophthalmology screening from 5 years of cumulative use, earlier if risk factors are present
Continue 400 mg daily; screen at 10 years from initiation given remission status
Cease hydroxychloroquine entirely as she is in remission and switch to prednisolone alone
Continue 400 mg daily and rely on Amsler grid self-testing in place of formal ophthalmology review

subtopic_detail: Lupus nephritis - class IV induction therapy
stem:
A 26-year-old woman with SLE (positive ANA 1:640 homogeneous, anti-dsDNA 380 IU/mL, low C3 and C4) presents to your medicine clinic with 4 weeks of ankle swelling. She takes hydroxychloroquine 300 mg daily. Vital signs are BP 152/94, HR 84, afebrile. Examination shows malar rash, oral ulcers, pitting oedema to the knees and a clear chest. Bloods show haemoglobin 102, WCC 4.2, platelets 132, creatinine 124 (baseline 70 four months ago), albumin 22 g/L, ALT 32.

Urinalysis 3+ protein, 2+ blood; spot urine protein:creatinine ratio 480 mg/mmol; urine microscopy red cell casts. C3 0.42 g/L (low), C4 0.07 g/L (low), anti-dsDNA 380 IU/mL. Renal biopsy reports class IV (diffuse proliferative) lupus nephritis with active lesions (NIH activity index 12/24) and no chronic damage. She has not previously been on cyclophosphamide or mycophenolate.

data_table.Vital signs: BP 152/94, HR 84, afebrile.
data_table.Bloods: Hb 102, WCC 4.2, plt 132, creatinine 124 (baseline 70), albumin 22, ALT 32.
data_table.Urine: 3+ protein, 2+ blood, RBC casts, uPCR 480 mg/mmol.
data_table.Serology: ANA 1:640, anti-dsDNA 380, C3 0.42 low, C4 0.07 low.
data_table.Biopsy: Class IV LN, NIH activity 12/24, no chronicity.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate induction regimen?

options.text: IV methylprednisolone 500 mg for 3 days then oral prednisolone, continue hydroxychloroquine, plus mycophenolate 2 to 3 g/day OR cyclophosphamide 500 mg IV fortnightly for 6 doses
Oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day with azathioprine 2 mg/kg/day, continuing hydroxychloroquine
Rituximab 1 g x 2 doses 2 weeks apart, plus oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day, ceasing hydroxychloroquine to avoid combined immunosuppression
ACE inhibitor and statin alone, with deferred immunosuppression until creatinine doubles
Plasma exchange daily for 7 days plus high-dose oral prednisolone without cytotoxic therapy

stem:
A 71-year-old man presents to your general practice with 5 weeks of bilateral shoulder and hip-girdle pain with morning stiffness lasting 2 hours. He has difficulty rising from a chair and combing his hair. He has lost 2 kg, has no fever, no headache, no jaw claudication, no visual symptoms and no rash. Examination shows tender shoulder and hip-girdle muscles with restricted active range of motion.

There is no synovitis, no muscle weakness on confrontation testing, no temporal artery tenderness. Vital signs are HR 76, BP 138/82, afebrile. Bloods show haemoglobin 124, WCC 7.8, platelets 360, creatinine 84, ESR 68 mm/h, CRP 54, normal CK, normal TSH, normal calcium and PSA. Hand/shoulder X-rays show no erosions. RF and anti-CCP negative.

data_table.Symptoms: Bilateral shoulder/hip-girdle pain, morning stiffness 2 h, 5 weeks.
data_table.No: Fever, headache, jaw claudication, visual symptoms, rash, synovitis, weakness.
data_table.Bloods: Hb 124, WCC 7.8, plt 360, ESR 68, CRP 54, CK normal, TSH normal, Ca normal, PSA normal.

lead_in: Which is the most appropriate initial treatment?

options.text: Prednisolone 15 mg orally daily, with calcium, vitamin D and bone-protection assessment, expecting marked symptomatic improvement within 1 week
Prednisolone 1 mg/kg orally daily as for GCA, with high-dose pulse if visual symptoms occur
Methotrexate 15 mg weekly as first-line monotherapy with folic acid
NSAIDs (celecoxib 200 mg twice daily) as first-line, reserving steroid for non-response
Tocilizumab 8 mg/kg IV monthly as first-line biologic therapy

subtopic_detail: IgA vasculitis adult - renal indication for biopsy
stem:
A 34-year-old man presents to your general medicine clinic 3 weeks after an upper respiratory tract infection with a palpable purpuric rash on both lower legs and buttocks, bilateral ankle and knee arthralgia, and crampy abdominal pain. Vital signs are HR 82, BP 138/86, afebrile. Examination confirms non-blanching palpable purpura, no synovitis, soft non-tender abdomen, no peripheral oedema. Bloods show haemoglobin 142, WCC 9.6, platelets 320, creatinine 92 (baseline 78), CRP 28.

Coagulation profile normal. Urinalysis shows 2+ blood, 2+ protein. Spot urine protein:creatinine ratio 105 mg/mmol. Microscopy shows dysmorphic red cells without casts. Throat swab negative. ASOT normal. ANCA negative.

data_table.Vital signs: HR 82, BP 138/86, afebrile.
data_table.Examination: Palpable purpura legs/buttocks, no synovitis, soft abdomen.
data_table.Bloods: Hb 142, WCC 9.6, plt 320, creatinine 92 (baseline 78), CRP 28, coags normal.
data_table.Urine: 2+ blood, 2+ protein, uPCR 105 mg/mmol, dysmorphic RBCs no casts.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate next step?

options.text: Refer for urgent renal biopsy now, as proteinuria of this severity in adult IgA vasculitis warrants histological confirmation and guides immunosuppression
Reassure, manage symptomatically with paracetamol, and review in 6 weeks for spontaneous resolution
Start empirical oral prednisolone 1 mg/kg/day without biopsy and review in 4 weeks
Start an ACE inhibitor and review urine protein in 12 weeks before deciding on biopsy
Send a skin biopsy of a purpuric lesion for direct immunofluorescence as definitive testing

subtopic_detail: Antiphospholipid syndrome - obstetric pathway and aspirin/LMWH
stem: A 32-year-old woman is referred to your medicine clinic at 7 weeks gestation. She has had three consecutive first-trimester miscarriages between 6 and 9 weeks. She has no history of thrombosis. She is otherwise well, not on any medications, BMI 26. Investigations 14 weeks ago and again 12 weeks later show persistently positive lupus anticoagulant on two occasions, IgG anticardiolipin antibody 92 GPL (positive >40), and beta-2-glycoprotein-1 IgG 78 (positive >40). ANA is negative. Bloods show haemoglobin 132, WCC 8.2, platelets 244, normal coagulation studies, normal renal and liver function. She is normotensive.

data_table.Serology: Lupus anticoagulant + x 2 (12 wks apart), aCL IgG 92 (>40), b2GP1 IgG 78 (>40), ANA neg.
data_table.Bloods: Hb 132, WCC 8.2, plt 244, normal coags, normal UEC/LFTs.
data_table.Background: BMI 26, no thrombosis, no current medications.

lead_in: Which is the single most appropriate management for this pregnancy?
